NZ’s oldest Holocaust survivor Rachelle Calkoen on hate, the world today, and sharing her story with young people

New Zealand Herald September 04, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

At 103, New Zealand’s oldest Holocaust survivor Rachelle Calkoen has lived through Nazi occupation, hiding her Jewish heritage and surviving for years under a stolen identity.

Now, the Dutch-born New Zealander is sharing her story with a new generation to warn of the harms of intolerance – and has found an unlikely new “bestie” along the way.

Calkoen joined a film project about child Holocaust survivors who rebuilt their lives in New Zealand, to teach Year 7–10 students about standing up against hatred and preventing discrimination and prejudice.

The project is led by the Holocaust Centre and funded by the Ministry for Ethnic Communities.

It was through filming We Were Just Children that Calkoen met 17-year-old Bulls high school student Eva Dreliozis, who also features in the film.

Despite the more than eight-decade age difference, the pair have become fast friends.

“We didn’t know each other at first and I’m glad we do now because we’re besties now,” Dreliozis told the Herald, sitting alongside Calkoen and her dog Tilda at the centenarian’s Waikanae home.

“Rachelle reminds me a lot of my Nana ... we come here a lot and visit,” Dreliozis said, but “not enough” according to Calkoen.

Born in Holland in 1923, Calkoen remembered a “very happy childhood”, until “the Germans in ’40 came falling out of the sky”, with airborne soldiers descending on the Netherlands.

“We thought maybe a week or two and we probably would all be sent to concentration camps.”

Soon after, she recalled antisemitic affiches were erected on city buildings with “terrible” depictions of Jewish men.

Calkoen avoided captivity by hiding in a cupboard when Nazis searched her family’s home in 1942, and ended up living in hiding on stolen food coupons.

“It felt very insecure and you didn’t trust your friends anymore,” she said.

She also assumed a stolen identity, with a friend stealing another girl’s ID card from her pocket on the train and swapping the picture for Calkoen’s.

“If you weren’t Jewish, you had just an identity card with your photo and your thumbprint and your name and everything, but if you were Jewish, you had exactly the same, except a big ‘J’ on it.

“For probably three years, I lived with her name and her birthday,” she said.

Calkoen also credits her blonde hair and blue eyes with helping her and her sisters avoid detection during the German occupation.

“You lose your identity and you lose the certainty that you had as a child that you are a valued person in the family.

“The Holocaust is not just concentration camp and awful things happening, it’s not being valued for what you are, and being taken away from the people you love.”

She remembers the uncertainty of being separated from her family during the war, and fearing they were in concentration camps or killed.

Calkoen and her sisters survived, and in 1958 she and her husband moved to New Zealand, seeking to protect their children.

“It was far away from Germany,” she said.

“My husband had been in concentration camp. He was not Jewish, but he had two and a half years in concentration camp and not a very nice time, and we didn’t want our children to have that.”

Nearly 70 years on, Calkoen is “very happy” with her decision.

For Dreliozis, learning Calkoen’s story brought the history she learned in the classroom to life.

Dreliozis first studied the horrors of the Holocaust in a Year 12 history class.

“I remember sitting in that class and thinking, ‘Oh my God, how could this happen’,” she said.

As head of culture at her high school, she said she had heard stories of “horrific” racism and hate in schools, and credited it to the same psychology that led to the Holocaust.

“People naturally want to be a part of the group, it comes down to human biology, and you want to be a part of the ‘us’, and then whoever doesn’t conform to that is ‘them.’

“It all starts with one hateful comment to then turn into a group of people who buy into that ideology and it grows and it grows, more people could realise the weight of their words.”

Having survived persecution to live for more than a century, Calkoen feared the lessons of history were being forgotten, saying world leaders today “haven’t learned much”.

Asked about the state of the world today, Calkoen said she despaired at current events.

“I mean, every normal thinking [person] is appalled about what’s happening in Gaza and wherever in the world, it’s just awful,” she said.

“Even here, there is a lot of antisemitism that shouldn’t be here ... hate isn’t really founded in anything.

“You try to live as as good as you can live and there’s not much more you can do really.

“I do hope young people will be influenced by this and learn to think for themselves and not just do whatever other people do or tell them to do.”

Real estate agent Janet Dickson is unrepentant, saying she would refuse course if given another chance

New Zealand Herald September 04, 2026

Real estate agent Janet Dickson refused to do a Māori tikanga course. This week a tribunal refused to give her an exemption. She's now likely to lose her licence as a result. Photo / Annaleise Shortland

A real estate agent on the verge of losing her licence after being denied an exemption from a compulsory Māori tikanga course says if she had her time again, she would still refuse to do it.

“It’s totally irrelevant to the everyday work of real estate.

“That we should learn to bow down to the Māori gods. That’s a major part. I downloaded the course book to see what it was about ... and I’m going, pardon? You’re asking me to do what?” Janet Dickson told NZME.

“It’s [my real estate work] to do with property; it’s nothing to do with spiritual gods and tikanga.”

The Real Estate Tribunal this week rejected Dickson’s request for an exemption from the compulsory course.

With 30 years’ experience, she’s been left feeling teary and like her profession had betrayed her.

The decision concludes a nearly three-year battle argued before the Real Estate Authority, the High Court and the tribunal.

The authority has already signalled it is unlikely to reinstate Dickson’s licence after the tribunal’s decision, even though she said it hasn’t suspended or cancelled the licences of other agents found guilty of misconduct for “seriously negligent real estate agency work”.

The authority introduced the mandatory course, Te Kākano (the Seed), in 2023. The 90-minute course comprised three modules: Māori language and development, the Treaty of Waitangi and Māori land.

Dickson said when the course was introduced in late 2023, it drew outrage from many of the profession’s almost 17,000 real estate agents.

“We erupted with rage at having to do this course, which had nothing to do with our work whatsoever.”

But she said there wasn’t a co-ordinated response from the industry before the authority started sending threatening letters, which gave agents an ultimatum: either do the course or don’t work.

“People were cowed, and many people left the job because they just wouldn’t do it. They took early retirement.

“For me it was like, ‘Which part of the word no do you not understand?’ And then suddenly it became a national case.”

She said those at the authority, who were responsible for introducing the course, should have, given the response, put it aside and suggested something else.

But instead they dug their toes in, she said.

Dickson said her life had been in limbo since she took her stance and refused to do the course in November 2023, leaving her unable to work as an agent because it was a condition of her licence.

She describes the impact as “bad news” compounded by the recent loss of her husband and soulmate of 32 years, Grant Dickson, a bass and opera singer.

The two would travel overseas, she as his manager and pianist, while he worked as her personal assistant, between his music.

Dickson insists her stance isn’t racial. She grew up among Māori families, taught at Bay of Islands College, which was predominantly Māori, and passed School Certificate Māori.

Her father was chaplain to the 26th Battalion and good friends with Canon Wiremu “Wi” Te Tau Huata, a highly respected Māori Anglican chaplain.

“That has been my soul upbringing. When my father was ill, he was like a godfather to us”.

Contact the Open Justice team

Dickson said since the tribunal’s decision was published, she’s received support from up and down the country and said none of the responses were critical of her.

“I’m getting emails every day. People saying ‘Hang in there’ and ‘If only I’d done the same thing’, or whatever.

“It’s people I don’t even know saying ‘Gee, I wish I had done that in my field. I should have had the courage to stand up’.”

She said there had been no decision on whether to appeal the ruling, but it was up to her lawyer, Stephen Franks, and Don Brash from Hobson’s Pledge, who had funded her case.

Catherine Hutton is an Open Justice reporter, based in Wellington. She has worked as a journalist at the Waikato Times and RNZ. Most recently, she was working as a media adviser at the Ministry of Justice.

All Blacks: Why mental skills techniques used by Gilbert Enoka can apply to sport, business and everyday life

New Zealand Herald September 04, 2026

New Zealand high-performance athletes and team players benefit from mental skills coaching from sports psychologists such as Gilbert Enoka.

The All Blacks and the Springboks are level with one victory each in the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series. Mental skills coach Gilbert Enoka must make sure the players have their heads in the game for this weekend’s clash. Jane Phare looks at why mental skills coaching is an essential part of a winning formula, and why it can be used in everyday life.

Watch closely during a Blues game and you just might notice the team’s big lock Cameron Christie doing something a little odd. He knocks his wrists together.

Former All Black Dan Carter used to whack himself on the leg. It’s a technique highly trained sportspeople use to bring themselves back to the moment, focus on the now, not what was. The idea is to forget about what went wrong on the field or court, or board or council meeting, and concentrate on what needs to happen next.

Christie, 22, who also plays for North Harbour, has come up through the ranks since leaving Ōrewa College, playing in age-grade rugby and the New Zealand Under-20s. Throughout that journey, he’s had access to sports psychologists and is now a firm believer in the power of the mind.

He’s picked up “bits of gold”, he says, and added them to his toolbox to cope with pressure and perform better on the field.

Christie’s taken inspiration from role models like Sam Whitelock, Carter and, in particular, English rugby legend Jonny Wilkinson, who worked extensively with a mind coach and a psychiatrist throughout his career to visualise success and handle pressure.

Like Carter, Christie uses a physical reset to bring himself back to the present, to stop thinking about a mistake or a play that went wrong and focus on what to do next.

“So, I just tap my wrists together from over the top and then underneath. It just kind of brings you back to where your feet are.”

On Instagram, Carter talks about going into a state of “red head”, an unhelpful mindset when the brain is locked into a mistake that happened minutes ago. Mental skills coaching helps players to focus, get back into a calm “blue” state and get on with the game.

Carter describes three types of reaction in a state of red head – freeze, fight or flight – and how he would react when under pressure as playmaker for the All Blacks.

“I would freeze, I would go quiet. My teammates are looking at me going, ‘well, what’s the move, what’s the call?’ And I was like, ‘man, I’m still thinking about that mistake I made sort of 10 minutes ago’.”

Whereas his teammate Ma’a Nonu would go into a state of fight when things went wrong, Carter says.

“Like he was trying to take out the opponents, he was yelling at the referee, he was yelling at his teammates, he was trying to shoulder charge or physically trying to fight the opposition.”

The third reaction is flight, a state of mind where players “just want to get the hell out of there”.

Players might want to get substituted off or, in a work situation, people might call in sick.

“You just don’t want to be in that moment.”

Recognising that “red head” state early and having the tools to get out of it is the key, Carter says.

“If I made a mistake, I would whack myself on my leg ... recognising that I had made a mistake or recognising that I’d frozen and it’s like, right, now, next task, what do I need to do right now in this moment? And just catch the ball, just communicate to my half, whatever it was, that would get me back into the present and on task in that moment and I’m back in the state of blue.”

Auckland sports psychologist and mental skills coach Iain Saunders, a former police officer, uses a “win-win” model: what’s important now and what’s important next. The idea is not to ruminate on the past, things that can’t be changed, he says.

“It’s making sure that you’re living in the moment.”

Saunders, who has a masters degree in psychology, draws on years of experience with the Armed Offenders Squad and assessing candidates for New Zealand’s elite special tactics group to make sure they are the right fit under pressure. At the same time, he worked part-time as a sports psychologist, leaving the police two years ago to become a fulltime mental skills coach.

He’s worked with the Blues, Auckland Rugby, the Black Ferns and Pulse Netball and also has business and career clients who need help to manage stress and get past setbacks. Saunders says the same techniques apply both in professional sport and in everyday life and business.

Part of his job is to create the right culture, an environment that allows athletes, or people in business, to perform at their best.

Team members need to be connected by a common purpose and understand the team’s direction and values. There needs to be a clear vision about what they, and the team, need to do. And they need to know how to manage relationships, how to lead, how to be a good communicator and how to achieve goals together.

Saunders prefers creating an optimistic environment rather than teaching positive psychology.

“So if you’re in a game of rugby and you’re 20 behind after 10 minutes, there’s nothing positive about that, but you’ve got to be optimistic, right?”

Working with Pulse Netball, he gets the players to work on moving forward.

“It’s like a belief system.”

“The last centre pass in a game of netball has absolutely no bearing on how the next centre pass will go unless you allow it to occupy a part of your brain where you’re thinking about it. And then that makes you slower, it makes you more cluttered in your head.”

Forget the last goal, he’ll tell players.

“We don’t even want you to know what the score is really. It just doesn’t affect how much effort or how much skill you apply to the next centre pass. It’s got nothing to do with it.”

Don’t worry about the things you can’t change; concentrate on the next play, he tells them.

Christie says his mental skills are “a work in progress”, that he still catches himself ruminating over a mistake he’s made which distracts his focus.

“I want to be really instinctive when I’m on the field so I want to have an absence of [that] thought.”

He uses the physical reset method, the wrist tapping, but also uses visualisation and repeats “power phrases” in his head like “I back myself” to counter negative thoughts.

Learning those mental-skills techniques has become increasingly important in team sports, he says.

“It’s massive. I put a huge importance on it.”

So do his teammates.

“In the warm-up you’ll see boys meditating, potentially visualising ... ”

The goal is to quieten down the inner critic, or thoughts that the day’s performance will fall short.

“So then the innate skill you have within you can come out and you can just play freely.”

Christie says he uses the same techniques to get back into the “blue” mode of calmness in his personal life.

“[I can] use those techniques to get back into that state where I can make clear and rational decisions, where you can communicate and lead better.“

Former All Blacks captain Sean Fitzpatrick, currently in South Africa for the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry tour, says mental skills coaching by specialists wasn’t available in his day.

“So we basically learned through experience how to handle pressure. Whereas now it’s absolutely paramount because it’s the one thing that you can do to make a difference without the opposition knowing what you’re doing, how you prepare.”

The best-prepared team usually win, he says.

“So we used to just drum that into ourselves, ‘We need to prepare, prepare, prepare’, put pressure on each other and that was our mental coaching. We didn’t have a Gilbert Enoka telling us how to prepare. We just learned.”

The same pressures happen off the field in business, careers and family life, he says. Preparation is the key whether it’s to be the best golfer in the world or successful in business.

Fitzpatrick is chairman of the Laureus Sport for Good Foundation, a London-based global charity that raises millions to support sport-based projects for under-privileged youth around the world.

“It teaches you so many values, resilience, dealing with failure, getting on with a team, getting on with people.”

Saunders says back in the Fitzpatrick era and the early rugby sevens tournaments, it was more about surviving the training to create resilient individuals. Rugby clubs had a larger pool of talent from which to choose, because so many youngsters were playing the game back then.

“They could afford that attritional sort of selection of the fittest approach. But we’re probably trying to be a bit more broad than that now and realise there’s a scarcity of good athletes.”

Gilbert Enoka has been incredibly successful helping athletes to perform at a high level by creating an environment in which they can thrive and understanding what individuals need, Saunders says.

“He’s fairly famous for that.”

That builds confidence and trust, enabling people to stay calm in the face of big decisions.

A stress response, getting in the red, makes thinking foggy.

“That’s true of life as it is of sport,” Saunders says.

Getting out of that state and into a calm head space might mean taking some breaths, repeating a phrase or doing a physical movement.

“A common one in sport is just counting things you can see just to get you out of your head and pay attention to the external environment.”

In rugby, he says, stressed players are often told to just move.

“When you start moving, take five steps, it forces your brain to navigate within the game and then you’re back into the environment.”

Jane Phare is a senior journalist based in Auckland. Her roles at the Herald have included assistant editor of NZ Herald, editor of the Weekend Herald, founding editor of Viva, features editor and deputy print editor.

Mum calls for mandatory e-scooter helmets after crash leaves son with fractured pelvis and memory loss

New Zealand Herald September 04, 2026

A Greymouth teen is recovering after a ute hit him on his e-scooter. Photo / 123rf

By Melanie Earley of RNZ

A collision with a ute while on his e-scooter left her son with a fractured pelvis, internal bleeding and a large bump to his head, but Riana Grobbelaar fears it would have been much worse had he not been wearing a helmet.

Her son, 15, has spent more than a week in hospital after the crash, which happened while he was delivering newspapers in Greymouth on August 29.

“My son delivers papers on the main road, State Highway 6, in the Paroa area. He crosses that main road a few times and the speed goes from 100km/h to 80 so vehicles coming into Paroa area go quite fast.

“He said he was waiting to cross and looked and didn’t see anything, but after that he woke up with a lot of people around him.

“He can’t remember what exactly happened.”

Despite his injuries, Grobbelaar believed if he hadn’t been wearing a helmet he would’ve ended up with a serious head injury – or worse.

Doctors had been looking at whether he had a concussion, which could account for his memory loss.

“His helmet took a big hit. That was a rule in our house: no helmet, no scooter. He was really lucky, but he has a slow and long road to recovery.

“The helmet is full of bumps and scratches through the side.”

The e-scooter was wrecked, along with a puffer jacket he had been wearing, which had helped prevent more extensive bruising and cuts on his upper body.

Her son was using crutches and a wheelchair, and the family had spent Thursday having a ramp installed at the house for him.

Grobbelaar said she didn’t want any other families to go through what hers had been through.

Seeing other young people riding around Greymouth without helmets since the accident worried her, especially given the speed they could reach.

“A lot of the kids are driving on pathways and the speed they are driving at ... a vehicle could just back out of their driveway and imagine what accident that could cause.”

Grobbelaar was speaking out after seeing RNZ’s earlier coverage of a psychologist calling for helmets to be made compulsory for e-scooter riders in New Zealand.

Chris Parsons told Morning Report this week he was one of many people in the industry who believed attitudes towards e-scooter safety were generally too relaxed.

He said the country’s legislation was lagging behind other countries.

“In Australia, it’s mandatory to wear a helmet on an e-scooter.

“Queensland is looking at bringing in a range of measures, including the possibility that you have to have a learner’s licence and have to be over 16 before you ride an e-scooter. We’re in a situation where the law has to catch up with technology.”

He said there needed to be nationwide social education, particularly for young people, to prevent more “catastrophic” e-scooter accidents.

“For anyone with a serious brain injury, we’re looking at long-term rehabilitation and sometimes lifelong effects. The consequences are very serious.

“The brain is a very soft organ, the consistency of tofu, inside a bony structure of the skull, and people are moving at speed on an e-scooter and if it suddenly stops the brain keeps moving with catastrophic results.”

ACC figures released this year show claims for e-scooter injuries are on the rise, with children and young people among the most affected.

ACC paid out almost $16 million for scooter-related injuries in 2025, an increase of about 10% on the year prior. Just over $1.2 million had been paid out in January 2026.

Canterbury truck driver Jason Chapman was not medically cleared to drive when he crashed and died on SH7, Associate Coroner finds

New Zealand Herald September 04, 2026

Truck driver Jason Chapman died after he had a heart event and crashed. Photo / Screenshot

Jason Chapman was the guy who “would give the shirt off his back for anybody”.

The 51-year-old Canterbury truck driver was described by his employer as a “good and skilled driver”.

But Chapman had been battling heart disease and after his second heart attack in August 2023 he was stood down from commercial driving by his medical team. He never told his employer.

On November 13, 2025, Chapman crashed an empty logging truck into a hedge on State Highway 7, south of Culverden, after a heart event and died at the scene.

Associate Coroner Jennifer Smith has ruled Chapman died from ischaemic heart disease with a contribution from hypertension.

“Speed was not a factor in the crash. There was no evidence of yaw marks or brake marks on the road, suggesting that Jason was not in control of the vehicle as it travelled across the centreline into the hedge.

“Fortunately, there were no other road users injured in this crash.”

Smith said Chapman had a history of heart disease since 2018.

He had coronary artery bypass surgery at Christchurch Hospital followed by several angioplasty procedures with stent placement.

In October 2018 he passed his exercise tolerance test and was able to resume commercial driving.

After a heart attack in August 2023, Chapman was stood down again from driving. There was another attempt at angioplasty and Chapman had further bypass surgery in April 2024.

However, he continued to fail his exercise tolerance tests, the last in August 2024, and could not resume commercial driving.

Chapman’s GP and cardiologist provided reports to the coronial inquiry. The GP report confirmed their understanding Chapman had failed his most recent exercise tolerance test and was not able to drive under his commercial licence.

The cardiologist documented a discussion with Chapman in September 2024 after the failed exercise tolerance test and recorded Chapman’s disappointment at not being allowed to drive trucks.

“During a clinic visit in September 2024, [Jason] was clearly told by me, in person, that he was not able to resume driving commercial vehicles. I don’t remember the exact words of the conversation. However, I believe that he understood he would not be allowed to drive commercial vehicles, indefinitely,” the cardiologist report said.

The Associate Coroner said she was satisfied Chapman knew he should not be driving.

She questioned why he still held a full Class 1-5 NZ driver licence as well as a forklift and wheels endorsement.

Chapman’s employer told Smith he did not seek independent confirmation from medical specialists on Chapman’s ability to drive.

However, he did check the Transport Operator Register Online (TORO) system to confirm Chapman’s driver licence status.

The TORO system enables transport service licence holders, such as the employer in this case, to verify that only licensed drivers operate company vehicles and monitor licence status and activity.

TORO provides information on restrictions, endorsements, demerits and driver’s licence status and conditions.

In this case, the TORO check confirmed Chapman held a current Class 1-5 full licence with no conditions.

The employer said he believed any restriction would be reported if Chapman was not medically cleared to drive and that a TORO check would alert him.

Chapman was also subject to a random police check while driving the truck on September 2, 2025. Police found no issues with his logbook, loading or driving.

Waka Kotahi’s booklet Medical Aspects of Fitness to Drive: A Guide for Health Practitioners (“the Booklet”) states health practitioners must report a person if they are unfit to drive and are likely to continue driving despite advice not to do so. This reflected section 18 of the Land Transport Act 1998.

However, there is no general legal requirement for practitioners to report every medically unfit driver. The obligation only arises where a health practitioner believes the licence holder is “likely to continue to drive”.

Nor is there any legal obligation on licence holders to notify Waka Kotahi that they have been advised not to drive due to medical unfitness.

As a result, if a person accepts medical advice and gives no indication they intend to ignore it, neither Waka Kotahi nor police will necessarily be aware they have been deemed medically unfit to drive, and no restrictions will appear on their licence.

“That is what occurred here,” Smith said.

“Jason’s GP and cardiologist both knew he should not be driving, but neither had any reason to believe he intended to or had resumed commercial driving. Accordingly, they were under no obligation to report him.

“Thus, when Police stopped Jason on September 2, 2025, they had no way of knowing he was medically unfit to drive. Nor could his employer have ascertained that information when he checked the TORO system.

“I consider this to be an unsatisfactory state of affairs.”

The Associate Coroner recommended the Ministry of Transport consider changes to the Land Transport Act 1998 requiring health practitioners to mandatorily report to Waka Kotahi/NZ Transport Agency any patient deemed unfit to drive.

The ministry agreed the current system relied on a patient indicating they do not accept or intend to follow restrictions imposed by their health practitioner.

The ministry supported improving Waka Kotahi’s awareness of drivers medically unfit to drive for extended periods and advised it will consider the recommendation as part of its review of licence renewal requirements for drivers aged over 75.

Waka Kotahi acknowledged that Chapman was medically unfit to drive commercially when he resumed driving and expressed support for legislative change where this can be shown to improve road safety.

It advised it would assist the ministry with its review while considering potential implementation impacts.

The Beckenridge mystery: Mother believes her son is still alive – PI informed of possible new sighting

New Zealand Herald September 04, 2026

John Beckenridge and his stepson Mike Zhao-Beckenridge vanished on March 13, 2015, with a coroner ruling the case was a murder-suicide. But Mike's mum holds out hope her son is still alive. New Zealand Herald composite photo

The mother of a boy who vanished with his stepfather more than 11 years ago remains convinced he is alive.

The disappearance of Michael (Mike) Zhao-Beckenridge and his stepfather, John Beckenridge, in early 2015 has become one of New Zealand’s enduring mysteries.

His mother is still searching for answers — and refusing to believe her son is dead.

In March, Coroner Marcus Elliott ruled the case a murder-suicide, saying Beckenridge had driven the vehicle containing the pair off a cliff in Southland.

Elliott dismissed claims that Beckenridge, a Swedish-born helicopter pilot who lived in Queenstown, had staged his death and fled overseas with his stepson.

No bodies were ever recovered.

Before tomorrow night’s screening of a one-hour documentary into the case – Inside Operation Mike: The Beckenridge Mystery, to be shown on TVNZ – Mike’s mother, Fiona Lu, says she has never given up hope of finding her son.

Lu’s view is at odds with the coroner’s finding, and when the Herald approached her this week, she remained firmly convinced her son was alive.

“I believe Mike is alive,” Lu said.

Beckenridge met Lu while they were working in Afghanistan in 2006 — he was a pilot, and she was a waitress.

Lu had previously married a businessman in China and become pregnant with Mike. When Mike was a toddler, his father was convicted of fraud and sent to prison.

Desperate for work, Lu went to Afghanistan while her parents continued to raise Mike.

After meeting, the couple left Afghanistan, collected Mike from China and moved to Lake Hayes in Queenstown.

Lu is not the only person still holding out hope that Mike – who would now be 23 – might still be alive.

Private investigator Mark Templeman has spent many years trying to solve the pair’s mysterious disappearance.

He told the Herald this week he had been informed about a possible sighting of the pair just two months ago.

“We haven’t exhausted our inquiries,” Templeman said.

In March 2015, John Beckenridge picked up his then 11-year-old stepson from an Invercargill school in breach of a court order – and vanished.

His vehicle was later found in the surf off the Southland coast, but there was no sign of their bodies in the 4WD, and speculation grew that the pair had fled the country.

Three months after their disappearance, there was a possible sighting of them in Indonesia.

Inside Operation Mike: The Beckenridge Mystery revisits the case tomorrow night.

Originally commissioned as a Sunday special in 2017, the documentary was made following the police investigation into the pair’s disappearance. NZ On Air funded it, and Greenstone TV produced it.

Barbara Smith, a former Queenstown neighbour of Lu and Beckenridge, features in the documentary alongside Detective Sergeant Dave Kennelly and Beckenridge’s friend Roger Henricson, a pilot.

Smith said it was hard to believe more than 11 years had passed since the pair vanished.

“It’s hard to imagine Mike would be 23 now,” she said.

“Strangely, the police never contacted us for the coroner’s inquest. We were the last to hear from them, and I handed over all the texts, photos, emails and video clips from John. Our son Caleb was also involved in the search at the time.”

In 2018, a Herald on Sunday investigation into the pair’s disappearance unearthed the final texts and a video of Mike, who can be seen pleading with his stepfather before he went missing: “Dad, can you please come help me? I miss you ... please.

Beckenridge sent Smith another text on March 20, 2015 – the day the vehicle went off the cliff at Curio Bay – where he wrote the pair was being “chased by the Gestapo. Fiona f***ed up. No going back. My estate will pay back your money. Do not contact anyone, please. Regards, JB and MB”.

The artist, who now lives in Winton and was Mike’s babysitter, claimed that Beckenridge loved him like his own son.

Smith claimed the relationship between Beckenridge and Lu began to break down in 2014, when Lu started a hairdressing course in Invercargill and met Peter Russell, a retired farmer.

“John told me that Fiona kept it from him that she was seeing Peter Russell. He said that she came home with a new 4WD. She told him she had won the Lotto!

“That’s when John got suspicious,” Smith said.

Smith previously said she met Lu picking walnuts at Lake Hayes Estate.

Smith and her husband, Jack, cared for Mike when Beckenridge was working in Papua New Guinea, and Lu started working at the local dairy to improve her English.

Smith said Beckenridge was devoted to Mike. He would phone Mike every night to ask how his day at school had gone and whether he had done his homework.

When Beckenridge took his monthly break from Papua New Guinea, he and Mike would go ten-pin bowling and ice skating. They also shared a love of gaming.

Smith recently claimed that before the pair disappeared, Beckenridge told her Mike had pleaded with him to come and get him from Lu’s home.

Lu had been granted sole care of Mike after a Family Court hearing in February 2015.

Sixteen days later, Beckenridge took Mike from his Invercargill school in breach of the court orders.

On March 24, 2015, police found Beckenridge’s car after it had earlier gone off a cliff at Blue Cod Bay, southeast of Invercargill.

The family’s search for answers led them to employ Templeman.

This week Templeman told the Herald that every anniversary of the pair’s mysterious disappearance is difficult for the family.

Over the years, Templeman has forged a friendship with the couple and continued to work on the case pro bono because he believes it is “solvable”.

Lu and Russell now commute between Northland and Invercargill as they continue their search for answers.

Templeman still believes Beckenridge and Mike are somewhere in Asia.

“I understand how the coroner reached his conclusion, but it would not surprise me if they are still alive,” Templeman said.

“I’ve had about 10 to 15 people contact me over the years about sightings of Mike and Beckenridge.”

Russell had previously told the Herald he spent more than $150,000 on the search, including checking out a possible sighting of the pair on Gili Air Island, Indonesia.

Templeman explained that the police only interviewed the Gili Island witness by phone – something he described as “poor policing”.

In a statement obtained by the Herald, the witness claimed: “As I got closer to them, I recognised the man and boy as people I had seen in a media report. I knew they had gone missing, so the images of them were still fresh in my mind.”

She said the pair were in a “happy conversation”. The man appeared about 60-63 and was wearing a brimmed light-brown suede hat.

“He had a light grey, straggly beard. The boy looked a little bit more solid — he had put on weight.”

The witness called her father in New Zealand, who advised her to contact police.

The witness later met Templeman, Lu and Russell in December 2016.

Lu recognised Beckenridge’s hat from a missing-person poster created by the private investigator.

The witness also identified a physical characteristic of Beckenridge that, according to Templeman, only Lu would have known. Templeman declined to say what it was.

Police also monitored international gaming sites for clues to Mike’s whereabouts, as he was a keen online gamer.

The private investigator previously believed the pair had fled to Asia by sea, stating his inquiries had highlighted that Beckenridge was “intelligent, very resilient and adaptable”.

He said the police told him the divers who found Beckenridge’s vehicle in the water said both front seatbelts were engaged and the seats were pushed back because of the roof being compressed.

“It seems unlikely to me you would both put seatbelts on to drive over a cliff,” he said.

Neighbours had also told Templeman they had seen a satellite phone at Beckenridge’s Queenstown home, which has never been located.

The 64-year-old had four known aliases: John Locke, John Robert Lundh, Knut Goran Roland Lundh and John Bradford.

Templeman says he believed the only way the pair could have left New Zealand was “with fake passports or by getting a ride on an ocean-going vessel”.

After 12 years, his message to Mike and Beckenridge, if they were still alive, was simple.

“Michael, you haven’t broken the law. You can fly back to New Zealand tomorrow. Beckenridge is a different story. Just give yourself up.”

Barbara Smith says she often thinks of Mike when she sees her own grandson John. The pair are the same age.

“Every time I see a Chinese boy, I think of Mike with his floppy hair and wonder whether his eyes were open or not. He’s a man now, and I would be looking up at him,” she said.

“I don’t think I’ll hear from John again. If they are alive, New Zealand is the last place they will come near. Find somewhere where you and Mike can make a new life. I hope they have.”

Cold case timeline

2015

March 13: Mike Zhao-Beckenridge was picked up by his stepfather, John Beckenridge, at an Invercargill school, breaking a court order.

March 18: A farmer sees the pair sleeping in a vehicle and notifies police. Police seek help to find the pair, thought to be travelling in a dark blue Volkswagen Touareg.

March 20: Final texts sent by Beckenridge to Mike’s mother, Fiona Lu, lawyers and friends.

March 24: Police find car in Blue Cod Bay, southeast of Invercargill. Six days later confirm it belongs to Beckenridge.

April 8: Detective says “all the evidence” points to the pair being inside the car when it plunged off the cliff.

May 8: Divers and helicopter recover car. Ten days later, police say forensic examinations find “no signs of human remains” in car.

June: Possible sighting of Beckenridge and Mike in Indonesia.

2016

March: Police still treating the disappearance as a missing persons case.

April: John Beckenridge’s Queenstown home sells for $860,000. The funds are expected to be held in a trust until he is declared dead.

2017

July: International child abduction expert Col Chapman says after considering evidence, he believes the pair have left New Zealand.

2018

March: Herald on Sunday obtains a witness statement of a person who claims to have sighted a pair who looked like Beckenridge and Mike in Indonesia. Police say their inquiries are “ongoing and this remains an active investigation”.

2026:

March: Coroner Marcus Elliott rules the case a murder-suicide.

In his ruling, he states: “Mr Beckenridge’s willingness to use Mike as a weapon against Ms Lu reveals a callous disregard for the harm he was causing Mike. He did everything he could to turn Mike against, and incite hatred of, his mother and [Lu’s new partner Peter] Russell.

“The only conclusion one can draw from Mr Beckenridge’s indoctrination of Mike against his mother is that he was at least indifferent to the harm he was causing to Mike. He had become so vindictive towards Ms Lu and so self-obsessed and self-righteous that he was willing to harm Mike.”

A moderate magnitude 4.9 earthquake has rattled the lower North Island this morning.

Within 10 minutes of the quake, nearly 15,000 people had reported feeling it to GeoNet, including four who reported extreme shaking and 16 who described it as severe.

The quake struck about 30km northwest of Paraparaumu at 6.34am.

GeoNet said it was at a depth of 29km and classified the shaking as moderate.

It was centred 30km north-west of Paraparaumu on the Kapiti Coast, at a depth of 29km.

Thank you for joining our live updates this morning.

Barbara Houlding said she felt "very mild trembling" in her retirement village near Johnsonville.

Doreen Carter said the jolt woke her up. "The shaking was quite bad," the Paraparaumu resident said.

Herald readers have described being jolted awake by this morning’s earthquake.

Katie said her phone alarm woke her before she realised the quake was shaking her home.

“I jolted up and stood in my doorway whilst pictures were falling down,” she said.

Kate said she was woken by her bed shaking “quite violently”.

Another person in Wellington told the Herald the quake made their whole room shake.

"Seemed to wake quite a few people up in my hotel. Only lasted a couple of seconds but knocked over some stuff on the floor above me as there was a loud crash once it hit. My whole room was shaking."

Prue Jones said the earthquake felt much stronger than a "moderate" quake, saying it sounded like a train derailment and felt higher than a magnitude 5.

"My three Birmans ran for cover before the rattle arrived! First time feeling one at that strength. Eeeekkkk!!!"

More than 21,000 people have now reported feeling the earthquake, just 30 minutes after it struck.

GeoNet’s “Felt It” reports had climbed to 21,897 by shortly after 7am.

"Felt that earthquake pretty abruptly this morning, was brief but woke a lot of people up," a person in Wellington told the Herald.

The earthquake may have been felt across a wide area of the lower North Island and upper South Island.

GeoNet listed Wellington, Palmerston North, Whanganui, Paraparaumu, Levin, Masterton, Martinborough, Feilding, Eketāhuna and Hunterville among the areas where shaking may have been felt.

It may also have been felt across the Cook Strait in Blenheim, Picton, Seddon and surrounding areas.

The earthquake comes after a series of sizeable quakes around the country this week, including two moderate earthquakes near Milford Sound on Wednesday evening.

The first, a magnitude 5.5, struck about 40km northeast of Milford Sound at 6.13pm.

It was followed less than an hour later by a magnitude 5.6 quake about 35km northeast of Milford Sound.

Several smaller earthquakes were recorded in the same area afterwards.

Open-plan classrooms: A failed experiment or still the future of learning?

New Zealand Herald September 04, 2026

Pāpāmoa College principal Iva Ropati says the school’s open‑plan design was “an experiment that went terribly wrong”.

For some schools, open-plan classrooms were an experiment that failed. For others, they’re still the future.

In August, the Government announced a further $31.3 million to help nearly 90 schools create calmer, less disruptive learning spaces by modifying existing open-plan classrooms.

Open-plan classrooms, also known as modern or flexible learning environments, are large shared spaces designed for multiple teachers and classes to work together.

The funding will go towards creating practical changes to more than 600 classrooms, including installing internal walls to create more defined teaching spaces.

Eight schools in Tauranga and Pāpāmoa will receive the funding: Tauranga Girls’ College, Taumata School, Te Manawa o Pāpāmoa School, Pillans Point School, Tauranga Intermediate, Welcome Bay School, Pāpāmoa College and Tauranga Primary School.

These schools have welcomed the chance to add more defined classrooms, although some say flexible learning spaces can still work when the buildings, acoustics and teaching practices are designed to support them.

Education Minister Erica Stanford said the investment followed strong demand from schools wanting to move away from open-plan environments.

It builds on the $10m allocated to 40 schools last year after the Government announced new schools would no longer be designed as open-plan learning environments.

Pāpāmoa College was among the schools to receive funding in the first round and had begun converting its open-plan learning spaces back into single-cell classrooms.

Principal Iva Ropati said the college had been built as an open-plan school in 2011, when the approach was at its peak.

When he became principal about four years ago, staff identified the school’s design as one of the major barriers to student achievement.

The college’s open-plan blocks had no walls between classrooms, with up to 180 students and six teachers working in one space at a time.

Ropati said the environment had become “pretty chaotic”, with noise and students moving between spaces making it difficult for teachers and students to focus.

“There was just no environment at all that we thought was conducive to really good learning, or teaching for that matter.”

About three years ago, the college began reconfiguring its learning spaces, specifically focusing on moving senior students into buildings with individual classrooms.

Ropati said the move resulted in significant improvement in NCEA results.

“Over the last three years, our NCEA achievement has gone from below average and below national averages, and we’re now one of the highest-performing schools in NCEA in the Bay of Plenty.

“A lot of it we can attribute to moving out of these open-plan and into more privatised classrooms.”

Ropati said the latest Government funding would help schools, but converting existing buildings was expensive, so it would only go so far.

He said Pāpāmoa College had already received more than $200,000 to begin the first stage of the work, with the conversion of one block alone costing a similar amount.

“It was an experiment that I think went terribly wrong for Pāpāmoa College.”

Tauranga Girls’ College principal Tara Kanji said the school had been selected for the Government’s funding, and one of its buildings was due to be assessed in December for changes.

The school’s three-storey block was refurbished for earthquake strengthening and redesigned as a modern learning environment in 2018.

Kanji said the school was pleased with the result, and open-plan learning worked well in some parts of the building.

In other areas, however, a lack of acoustic treatment had created noise problems.

The school is seeking about four walls to reduce noise in specific areas, but did not want to convert every classroom into a single-cell space.

Kanji said open spaces worked well for subjects such as technology, where students needed to move around and collaborate.

More defined spaces, she said, were useful for assessments, films and other activities where noise could be distracting.

“You’ve got to have a choice. One size doesn’t meet the needs of everyone.”

Golden Sands principal Melanie Taylor said the school’s flexible learning model was working well and there were no plans to change it.

The school opened its doors to students in February 2011.

Its six learning community blocks were designed with acoustic treatment, defined teaching areas, quiet breakout spaces and areas for activities such as art.

Taylor said the model allowed teachers to work collaboratively, plan together and draw on each other’s strengths.

Students also benefited from building relationships with multiple teachers and a wider group of peers.

“Our teachers love the professional support of co-teaching, and our students consistently tell us they enjoy having multiple teachers who know them well.”

Taylor said Golden Sands had not experienced the same challenges of some open-plan environments because its buildings and teaching model were designed to support the approach.

“Our spaces provide the best of both worlds: quiet, focused environments for targeted instruction, alongside flexible areas for collaborative learning and creativity.”

Bay of Plenty MP Tom Rutherford said the Government’s decision reflected concerns he had heard from teachers, parents and school leaders about the challenges of open-plan classrooms.

He said more defined spaces could help reduce distractions and give students a better environment to focus and learn.

“Students learn best when they can focus, and teachers teach best when they have the environments that support effective learning.”

Rutherford said open-plan classrooms had been introduced with good intentions, but they did not work in every setting.

He said feedback after the Government’s announcement had been strongly positive, particularly from local parents.

“People are saying, ‘Thank you, this is just great. This is what we’ve been asking for’.”

Zoe Blake is a multimedia journalist at the Bay of Plenty Times and Rotorua Daily Post.

Not buying it: Melbourne’s build-to-rent boom comes at a high price

Sydney Morning Herald September 05, 2026

Build-to-rent projects are outpacing conventional apartments in Melbourne. But are these luxury towers an answer to the rental squeeze and affordability crisis, or a costly distraction?

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Travis Fein’s St Kilda Junction apartment has one of the most seductive views of Melbourne that money can buy.

On an upper floor in one of St Kilda’s tallest towers, his unit’s floor-to-ceiling windows give an uninterrupted view of the patchwork of open spaces around Albert Park Lake, Middle Park’s multimillion-dollar cottages far below and the curved shoreline of Port Phillip Bay beyond.

But Fein didn’t buy the view; he leased it.

The 28-year-old property investor and social media identity sold his apartment and moved into a two-bedroom pad in Beach House, a 297-unit build-to-rent development that towers over St Kilda’s northern gateway.

Fein pays $1275 a week for his luxe apartment, virtually double St Kilda’s $650 median price for a two-bedroom unit.

“But for context on that – because that’s a big number – it’s a beautiful apartment,” he says. “I have Albert Park views, beach views, city views, so it’s one of the top-tier apartments.”

Built by Melbourne developer Gurner Group for $300 million, Beach House bills itself as a place to “live like a millionaire, mortgage free”.

Its amenities would not be out of place on a cruise ship: a heated pool lined with banana lounges, dimly lit billiards room, 10-pin bowling alley, cinema, plush private bar with city views, day spa, pet spa.

The opulent complex is part of Melbourne’s first wave of build-to-rent developments, inner-city buildings marketed at lifestyle-conscious renters happy to pay over the odds for a central pad with perks.

“To be able to just use a sauna, ice bath and the whole wellness area and then go home to sleep, you’d need to spend $30,000 to $40,000 to have that at home privately,” Fein says. “You’re not paying for a normal rental. You’re paying for a nice lifestyle, which would cost a shit-ton of money otherwise.”

Footloose, financially flush and renting because he wants to, Fein could be a poster child for Melbourne’s burgeoning build-to-rent housing market, which has burst out of the ground and into the city’s skyline with a promise to make renting simultaneously more glamorous and more secure.

Governments desperate for solutions to the housing crisis have laid out the welcome mat for some of Australia’s biggest builders, including Lendlease, Mirvac, Grocon and Salta, along with operators from the US, Japan and Singapore.

But some experts say the influx of high-priced housing is doing nothing to ease Melbourne’s rental affordability crisis.

An analysis by The Age of 12 months of rental data from hundreds of listings at 14 completed build-to-rent developments bears out this criticism: they are 20 to 70 per cent more expensive on average than other nearby rental homes.

Meanwhile, some tenants interviewed for this story have said the experience does not live up to the glamorous sales pitch, or justify the high-end rents.

Build-to-rent isn’t mainstream housing. It’s pitched at a select cohort with money to spare.

But the model is muscling in on Melbourne’s struggling apartment sector so rapidly that some property analysts predict it will soon grow to be a major player in the rental market.

One set of numbers, calculated by property advisory firm Charter Keck Cramer, captures the seismic shift under way.

In 2021, an estimated 14,000 new apartments were built in Melbourne. Not one was a build-to-rent unit.

In the 12 months to July 2026, an estimated 8200 new apartments were built in Melbourne. More than half of them, 4400, were build-to-rent.

It’s the first time the incipient housing model has overtaken the delivery of conventional (or build-to-sell) apartments in Melbourne, or any other Australian city.

Build-to-rent towers have sprung up around Docklands, South Melbourne and Southbank, near train stations and tram lines in Kensington and Brunswick, and along the city’s hippest high streets in Fitzroy and Collingwood.

Several thousand more are in the pipeline, funded by a mix of domestic and foreign institutional capital that is swooping in to take advantage of federal and state tax breaks and friendly planning laws aimed at buoying investment in build-to-rent (BTR) housing.

Projects that had previously stalled are being revived and repurposed as build-to-rent: Southbank’s STHBNK, conceived and sold off-the-plan as Australia’s tallest apartment building, were altered last month to a smaller build-to-rent tower.

Plans for a 39-storey CBD office tower on Lonsdale Street were also dumped in August in favour of build-to-rent. Multiple BTR high-rises have just been approved around Arden underground station.

It’s a remarkable rise for a sector that barely existed in Australia five years ago.

But housing analysts warn the boom is a symptom of a dysfunctional housing market in which the annual number of new apartments being built in Melbourne has shrunk to lows last seen in the global financial crisis, while the city absorbs well over 100,000 new residents each year.

“I remember the good old days in 2016 and 2017, when we did 19,000 [new apartments a year]; that’s really the level that we should be building to bring Melbourne back into balance,” Charter Keck Cramer national executive director Richard Temlett says.

“People still need a place to live, and a lot more of them are just being forced to rent.”

“We drive to a house in PrestonWe see police arrestingA man with his hand in a bagHow’s that for first impressions?This place seems depressingIt’s a California bungalow in a cul-de-sac.”

Melbourne singer-songwriter Courtney Barnett’s 2015 tune Depreston was a forlorn indie anthem for a generation who believed ever-escalating property prices – up more than 400 per cent in Melbourne since 2000 – had denied them the Australian dream.

Renting has historically been a transitional form of housing for most Australians, Dr Tom Alves, acting managing director of the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute, says. But in the 21st century, a growing cohort of lifelong renters has emerged.

This is particularly so among younger adults. In two generations, Australians aged 25 to 34 have changed from mostly home owners to mostly renters. Ownership rates have also fallen below 50 per cent among low-income Australians aged over 45.

“There obviously always were a bunch of people who were renting for their whole lives, but that was a small group, whereas now it’s become fairly mainstream and not necessarily by choice,” Alves says.

Australia’s steadily declining home ownership rate has “prepared the ground” for the recent boom in BTR housing, Alves says. As home ownership falls out of reach for more people, it offers those on good incomes an opportunity to lease a style of housing they could not afford to buy.

The new wave of BTR accommodation, overwhelmingly leased at a premium, has also emerged at a time when rental affordability is the worst on record, according to federal government advisory body, the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council.

An analysis by The Age of 1223 listings in 14 operational BTR developments, between July 2025 and June 2026, found that median rental rates in those buildings are 20 per cent to 70 per cent more expensive than other apartments in the same suburb.

Beach House, in St Kilda, listed its units at 66 to 70 per cent above St Kilda’s median. Realm in Caulfield North is similarly high-priced, leasing some of its one-bedroom apartments for more than double the suburb’s $455 weekly median.

Even Local, an operator that has sought to differentiate itself as a rare provider of affordable build-to-rent accommodation, listed units in Kensington at 37 to 48 per cent above median for the suburb.

Only one development, Spotswood’s Union Quarter, offered rental accommodation in line with the suburb’s median.

“What’s this doing in terms of affordability? I think very little is the answer. If anything,” Alves says.

Victoria’s Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny visited Preston in late April to officially launch the maiden Melbourne apartment building for BTR brand, WeAreLiving.

Standing on a 16th-storey rooftop BBQ area with a view of the CBD skyline behind her, Kilkenny gushed about the building to an audience of property and superannuation stakeholders being served finger sandwiches, Portuguese tarts and developer-branded cans of carbonated water.

“What a beautiful building it is. The bold red brick as you enter downstairs, I must say it’s one of my favourites,” Kilkenny told the crowd before helping to cut the ceremonial ribbon.

“This is exactly the type of development we want to see: great homes, well-built, secure, in fabulous locations, offering choice and diversity.”

Melbourne’s worsening housing affordability challenge “can only be met by boosting supply”, Kilkenny said, before listing the planning and tax changes she has steered through parliament to stimulate housing development.

“We’re also, of course, really proud to be the nation-leading build-to-rent capital, and we’re going to continue to support build-to-rent developments with 50 per cent reduction on land tax and, of course, the exemption from absentee surcharge.”

The absentee land tax surcharge is blamed by the property industry for driving foreign investors away from Melbourne’s apartment market. BTR buildings are exempt.

WeAreLiving ticks all the high-amenity boxes of Melbourne’s BTR boom. The building’s handsome red brick ground floor and basement levels include a gym, sauna, steam room and cold plunge pool, and a bookable dining room.

The building adds a splash of style to the cluster of grey high-rise apartment buildings that have been wedged into the narrow triangle of land between gentrifying High Street and the route 86 tram corridor on Plenty Road.

Rental units range from $545 a week for a studio apartment to $1390 for a three-bedroom townhouse, putting the development at the top of the range for Preston.

The building does not include any affordable housing.

This omission was a calculated decision. To do so would jeopardise the returns of the 1.2 million Aware Super members who have financed the project, one of its developers said.

“Our starting position here was a return for Aware and return for their members,” Barings Real Estate Head of Residential Warwick Dowler said. “So, from our perspective, that’s number one. To hit that minimum return hurdle here it had to be market rent.”

The project was financed with the assistance of a 50 per cent concession on land tax.

The government has established a four-month, accelerated approvals timeline for projects that include at least 10 per cent affordable housing. But Dowler said this inducement would do little to tackle the level of unmet need for lower-cost rental housing.

“Quite honestly ... if [the government] want to see more affordable product, they need to look at subsidy programs,” he said.

Monday afternoon is Sasha Sheko’s rostered time to feed and water the four resident hens at 15 Thompson Street, a 197-room build-to-rent development run by Assemble in Kensington.

“I’m so inner-north I’m blanching kale stems to take to my chickens,” Sheko says.

Sheko moved into a two-bedroom apartment in Thompson Street last year, saying a wistful goodbye to their old CBD apartment, where they paid a private landlord bargain-basement rent of $440 a week.

The new home is no bigger but is more modern and has communal amenities: including a common room where new friendships have been made, and a rooftop basketball court they almost never use. It costs $605 a week.

Sheko says it’s decent value for the area, although they have been so underwhelmed by the standard of maintenance that they expect to move out within a year.

“Just the whole Assemble model, ‘we’re ethical, we’re sustainable, blah blah blah’, I think it maybe raised my expectations in terms of what it would be like dealing with property management.

“I’m at the point where if I have any more issues I will ignore them and probably won’t be there in six months, which is a shame because the community is really lovely.”

Assemble is positioned at the affordable end of the build-to-rent market, with fewer amenities than most other BTR developers offer. It has also bought heavily into federal and state government schemes to deliver subsidised affordable housing.

Even so, Sheko’s weekly rent is more expensive than the $550 weekly median price for a two-bedder in Kensington.

University of Melbourne Professor of Property Piyush Tiwari has researched Melbourne’s first wave of BTR developments, and says the financial feasibility of the sector “hinges on the ability of units to be leased at higher than market rents”.

Communal amenities such as wellness rooms, swimming pools, gyms and cinemas have been included to attract tenants willing to pay the steeper rents necessary to make a profit.

“The original proposition was that BTR provides a higher end rental offering, including amenities, so the rents would be higher,” Tiwari says.

“Generally, the providers were expecting a rent to be 20 to 25 per cent above the market.”

Build-to-rent housing is mainstream in parts of Europe and in the US, where it accounts for roughly 4 per cent of the housing market, and caters more for lifelong renting families.

Tiwari says that if Australia follows these countries, mid-market build-to-rent housing will emerge. But two years after his research paper was published, most BTR buildings in Melbourne are even more expensive than the 20 to 25 per cent premium the first wave was financed on.

The Age calculated rental rates for Melbourne’s BTR developments using Homer, a property app that tracks the prices over time of all Australian properties on the market.

Homer chief executive Henry Pedersen had personal experience with Melbourne’s premium-priced BTR sector while looking for a rental home for his family of three in 2024.

Pedersen and his wife considered leasing a three-bedroom apartment at Home in Richmond, but baulked when they found a modern four-bedroom townhouse in the same suburb for $250 a week less.

“The amenities of those things are really cool and that somewhat inflates the value, but at the same time I didn’t think it was worth that much of a difference in price personally; maybe if money was a bit looser,” Pedersen said.

He suspects many renters, aspiring to own a home one day, would make the same calculation.

“Paying 10 to 20 per cent more doesn’t help you save to enter the property market.”

Edward McAuliffe is director of BTR operations at Salta, which operates Fitzroy and Co, a boutique BTR in Fitzroy North, and has two large projects in development in Richmond and Docklands.

Median rental rates at Fitzroy and Co exceed the median rental in Fitzroy North by about 50 per cent, The Age and Homer’s analysis found.

McAuliffe agreed that most BTR housing in Melbourne is relatively expensive to rent, but said that was the only way to make the developments stack up financially.

“You know, we’re creating housing,” he said. “Yes, some of it’s at the premium end at the moment, but that’s a function of what you need to do to get a project to become viable, get the funding you need to build it and get it operating.”

Where younger renters have baulked at BTR, some operators have turned to international students to fill their new buildings, satisfying their financiers but undermining the premium rental experience.

The first few months living in Mirvac’s LIV Aston building in Docklands were pleasant for David Powlett. The apartment was comfortable, the neighbours were friendly and the address on the Yarra’s north bank was convenient.

The rent was high compared to other places he’d considered, but the single father and IT service designer needed a spacious and well-built apartment for himself and his two children, and was prepared to pay a premium for it.

“I was a bit fussy about cupboards that don’t open and noise levels and things like that, and the Mirvac apartment was actually very quiet, very comfortable, the build quality was very high,” he says of the three-bedroom unit he rented, initially for $1270 a week.

Powlett was one of the building’s first tenants.

“I was almost the only person on my floor,” he says. Even so, the small community of residents were socially lubricated by regular, catered gatherings thrown by management in one of the building’s common areas.

But six months in, the community in LIV Aston changed dramatically as scores of vacant units were filled with international students, seemingly within a matter of days.

“It really changed the whole atmosphere … I know quite a few people left because they felt the vibe had changed a bit too much. It just didn’t feel like premium accommodation, it felt like a student campus,” Powlett says.

Amenities such as the building’s cinema room, media room and dining spaces were booked out, sometimes for months.

“We didn’t use the amenities anywhere near as much as we thought we would … People just had them constantly booked, so it was just a nightmare to try and get in there,” Powlett says.

He stayed until the end of his 12-month lease, but left when the company sought to increase his rent by more than $300 a week.

On the other side of the CBD, in Mirvac’s LIV Munro building, Alaisdair Leith’s experience was almost the same: a luxurious lifestyle in a near empty building soured after the building rapidly filled up with overseas students.

Leith and his partner moved into a two-bedroom apartment facing Queen Victoria Market just three months after it had opened, paying $700 a week.

“The first six months there was incredible; no issues,” Leith says. “There was a really good blend of tenants; people in their 30s, retirees.”

But the building was clearly well below capacity until it was filled with international students, leading Leith to question the value in his premium accommodation.

“It was near impossible to book anything because they would book six months in advance. So it was like, well, I can’t use the amenities. So why am I paying this?”

They moved out earlier this year.

Melbourne University’s Tiwari says that international students are an easy market for BTR operators to tap.

But he says the fact they are doing so is also an indication that one of the key selling points for the BTR sector – the offer of long-term, multi-year leases instead of standard, 12-month leases – is attracting relatively few takers.

A Mirvac spokesperson said its BTR buildings attract different resident profiles depending on location, with some drawing in more students, others appealing to professionals, families, key workers or downsizers.

Mirvac is pursuing legal action against Victoria’s valuer-general in the planning tribunal, arguing that LIV Munro’s land value for tax purposes should be slashed by more than $32 million, due to “the deterioration in property market conditions and economic uncertainty over the past 12 months”.

But its 2026 annual report, published in August, presents a more bullish position about its build-to-rent growth strategy, telling investors that Australia’s housing crunch is fertile ground.

Low housing supply, historically low rental vacancy, increased migration and population growth, all support the company’s BTR expansion strategy, the report noted.

Charter Keck Cramer’s Temlett says the BTR boom is delivering desperately needed housing for Melbourne at a time when far too few conventional apartment developments are being built.

“We’ve got the fastest growing population other than WA, we’ve got a chronic shortage of rental stock, so that all points to the fact that rents will continue to rise.”

But in chasing the upper tiers of the market, Melbourne’s BTR boom has left the renters most in need of an affordable place to live out in the cold, Tiwari says.

“At the end of the day, millennials are budget conscious, and their experiences are very different. They are not necessarily looking for all those amenities, they’re looking for a decent home.”
