He was the ‘Baron of Blacktown’ – then his empire fell apart

Sydney Morning Herald September 05, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Five years ago, he was lauded as the “Baron of Blacktown”. Bathla Group founder Bhart Bhushan’s irresistible migrant success story – from a taxi driver to reclusive multimillion-dollar property developer – was celebrated across western Sydney.

His company was credited with changing the face of the region by building thousands of properties at prices that appealed to first home buyers.

Bathla became a major sponsor of the Western Sydney Wanderers soccer club, while family members set about building a palatial spread in the city’s rural north-west. The red Bathla logo became omnipresent on fences, signage and cranes at sites from Box Hill and Marsden Park to Schofields, Castle Hill and beyond.

Today, however, all of it – his reputation, the fortunes of Bathla Group, and his family members’ dream home – lies in tatters.

The company went into voluntary administration with $3.4 billion of debt last week. It was the news many had dreaded, but expected, for weeks. The collapse leaves thousands of victims, including buyers with money tied up in unfinished developments, residents of homes with defects, as well as unpaid subcontractors, tradies, suppliers and staff, with little to no recourse.

“We’ll be left in the dust,” said McDonald’s restaurant manager Harris Mazoudier, who has a Bathla apartment in Schofields that he says is riddled with defects.

The scale of Bathla’s debt is so extraordinary – equivalent to the cost of 17 of Australia’s futuristic F-35 fighter jets and their support systems, training, weapons, and infrastructure – that it poses the question: how did it come to this?

Indian-born Bhushan and his brother Rajinder Mohan founded the Universal Property Group, now known as Bathla, in 1997.

It was good timing. Western Sydney was undergoing rapid population growth, inflation was low, interest rates were falling and a new generation of migrant families was looking to buy.

While his formal qualifications are unknown, the then-33-year-old Bhushan was ambitious, shrewd, charismatic and a skilled negotiator. He took the lead while the quieter Mohan was said to be content to work behind the scenes.

The following year, they celebrated their first development of five red-brick townhouses in Girraween, the multicultural western suburb where their company headquarters is based.

Located around the corner from the highly ranked and then soon-to-be-selective Girraween High School, it was a smart move to attract the aspirational migrant buyers and members of the Indian diaspora they were targeting for sales.

Over the next decade, the brothers transformed the family business into an aggressive and fast-paced development machine, buying up swaths of land and completing 1000 townhouses, duplexes and houses before turning their attention to apartments.

Key to their success was value in a price-conscious market. “They gave people opportunities in the cheaper end of the market,” said Blacktown MP Stephen Bali, whose electorate is home to many of Bathla’s developments. “Low-cost housing has a role and people pay what they can afford.”

Now aged 62, Bhushan is described as “an enigma”. He never gives interviews, there’s only one official photo of him online, and he kept a low profile even when it came to his involvement with the Western Sydney Wanderers, which was terminated last week.

Bathla is also a long-term platinum sponsor of the Sydney Sikhs Sports Club, with an untagged Facebook photo from 2022 depicting Bhushan holding up a poster for an awards night.

“He’s reasonable to deal with, and he supported charitable organisations, which makes him human,” said Bali, who met with him several times. “But as a businessman, he was ruthless.”

Those who know him say he dreamt of a legacy family business and that he aspired to elevate the status of his company, moving into higher-quality homes.

But with a business model that was too risky for the banks, Bhushan financed his operations with loans from a string of private lenders that charge notoriously high interest rates. They included Ray White Capital, which reportedly lent Bathla $240 million, Centuria Capital and La Trobe Financial.

So what went wrong? Bhushan would describe “a perfect storm” of softening sales, the federal government’s May budget and the falling confidence of key markets. Spiralling construction costs also played a role.

Western Sydney Leadership Dialogue chief executive officer Adam Leto says he’s not alone. Many developers in the area are struggling with tightening margins amid rising costs and falling demand.

“It’s a lot easier to sell a $1.5 million apartment east of Sydney Olympic Park than it is west of Sydney Olympic Park,” he says. “That’s the grim reality of it.”

In truth, there had been warning signs about Bathla for years. Growing debt. Unpaid contractors. A chorus of buyers disgruntled over unfixed defects. Court cases and tribunals.

When the end came, it came very suddenly. On August 25, the company made an announcement on its website and on social media titled “Bathla seeks orderly restructure of business”, and entered voluntary administration.

In its second decade, the company really hit its straps: by 2008, it had built 1000 homes; 10 years later, that figure had ballooned to 5000. Insiders say Bhushan was a master of efficiency and frugality in those years, keeping as much skilled work in-house as possible to control costs and driving a hard bargain on everything else.

Many of his staff were family, including his children and nephews, or foreign workers on working visas.

He was said to work 18-hour days; to be a micromanager who maintained a tight grip on control of all aspects of the business; and yet who dressed more like a labourer than a senior executive. And he loved to make a deal.

But the business was not without controversy. An investigation by corporate regulator ASIC raised flags over vendor finance Bhushan was offering to vulnerable buyers, many of whom were immigrants from non-English-speaking backgrounds, between 2004 and 2009.

In 2011, Bhushan and UPG agreed to an enforceable undertaking that meant borrowers could seek compensation if they believed they were the victims of unconscionable conduct.

The company was fined $135,000 by SafeWork NSW and it expressed remorse in 2018 after a surveyor’s assistant was seriously injured when he fell four metres and became impaled on concrete bars at a site in Doonside.

Concerns were also being raised over the quality of Bathla’s building work, described by some as “shonky” and prone to the results of cutting corners. Bhushan wanted to improve, according to those who knew him, but this seemed incompatible with his business model.

Former NSW Building Commission chief David Chandler, who blames non-bank lenders for the Bathla crisis, recounts meeting Bhushan briefly at an event.

“My message was to him, you would look a whole lot better in my eyes if you had an [Independent Construction Industry Rating Tool] rating,” he says. “But it didn’t happen.”

To get an ICIRT rating, a company has to undergo an independent assessment, including on financial viability, regulatory compliance, integrity and risk management.

As Bathla charged on in a seemingly unstoppable trajectory, Bhushan was increasingly locking horns over development with councils, often contesting decisions in the Land and Environment Court.

Bali, who was mayor of Blacktown at the time, said the council would refuse Bathla’s plans on the grounds of overdevelopment and inadequate amenity. “We would try and reduce [the number of homes in the development]. They didn’t like it and would take it to court to try and get it overruled,” he says. “The bill was over $1 million a year in legal costs.”

Schofields resident Mazoudier, who says there isn’t a single area of the Bathla apartment he bought off the plan that is unaffected by defects, was also pursuing legal action.

“The biggest one is the flooring, which needs to be pulled up and relaid,” he says. “The mixers in the shower are scratched; the kitchen cabinet has laminate peeling off; and the silicone in the bathrooms is poor and coming off.”

Residents of his building have raised the issues with Bathla representatives, he says, to no avail. “They didn’t seem to know what they were doing.”

By 2020, Bathla was expanding into regional NSW and to South Australia and Victoria. Two years later, it had started development on 2000 apartments and 1000 homes.

The Parramatta Advertiser crowned Bhushan the “Baron of Blacktown” in an article featuring the 50 most powerful and influential people in western Sydney.

On the surface, it looked like Bathla had made the big time and that he was flush with cash. At a series of formal “lucky draw” events for buyers of its Pinnacle Schofields apartment developments between 2021 and 2024, Bathla staff handed oversized cheques of between $20,000 and $500,000 to delighted prizewinners.

In events held in a function room at a leagues club and professionally filmed, guests were greeted with celebrity MCs, music, balloons, and a Bathla media wall for photographs and celebrations.

But even as the champagne flowed and Bhushan’s fame and business empire grew, cracks were starting to show.

Cashflow became a recurring issue: contractors were complaining of problems and delays in getting paid. Hoxton Park excavator Sanjay Sewak was among those chasing unpaid invoices.

“Getting my money was a real struggle,” he says. “I had to make several visits to their office in Girraween. It was very different from other customers that we deal with. It was always chopping and changing.”

Fed up, Sewak said he accepted several thousand dollars less than he was owed in order to get paid. The firm seemed “fairly inexperienced” with earthworks, he said.

He’s one of the lucky ones: a subcontractor told the Herald last week Bathla hadn’t paid him for between $700,000 and $800,000 worth of work, causing his own business to collapse from debts he was unable to pay off.

More signs emerged: developments were delayed, sites increasingly came under scrutiny from Building Commission NSW inspectors, and private lenders began warning investors of issues with Bathla.

Work stopped on the extravagant $5.5 million family estate, Sierra Morena in Dural, which was planned to include a tennis court, swimming pools and a basketball court.

The trophy estate now sits in limbo alongside 2500 partially built Bathla properties, plus another 14,000 proposed homes that may never be completed.

Bathla was a house of cards that should have been exposed earlier, according to Environa Studio architect Tone Wheeler. He believes there were missed opportunities for regulators to intervene over building quality, site conditions and financing. “It is going to take down a huge part of this industry,” he says.

Lifting the bonnet of Bathla further reveals a web of hundreds of subsidiaries, each linked to separate developments. Some in the industry are suspicious, likening it to a Ponzi scheme and saying this could leave buyers without recourse if issues arise after subsidiaries are wound up.

There’s also reported to be some reluctance to complete partially built Bathla projects because of fears new developers may not be adequately indemnified for potentially substandard work.

It’s a very different picture to what Bhushan envisioned for his company almost 30 years ago.

“Was he good for Blacktown?” says Bali. “To me, no. He has left the legacy of overdevelopment and issues for the community. You need parks, reserves and amenity, not just jamming as many small units in as you can.”

With Ellie Busby and Anthony Segaert

‘Caught in a trap’: The most expensive regions for insurance on Australia’s east coast revealed

Sydney Morning Herald September 05, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Megan Vicary is among the growing ranks of Australians who do not carry full home insurance.

The 52-year-old moved to her 10-hectare property in Yarramundi in the Hawkesbury region nine years ago and had an insurance policy that cost her about $6000 a year. After four floods in 2022, it went up to $35,000 a year, and she could no longer justify the expense.

Now, the quotes are as high as $50,000 a year, and many insurers won’t offer flood coverage at all, based on her postcode. She still has a policy but it doesn’t cover flood.

“No one’s insuring for flood,” Vicary says. “If we have a major flood, it is going to be a crisis because none of us can afford it. All the way down the riverbank, none of us are flood-covered.”

The same crisis is playing out nationally as mounting climate disasters drive up insurance risk, and consumers drop their coverage, preferring to self insure or hope for a government bailout. As the United Nations reports that the goal of curbing global warming to 1.5 degrees has failed, the task of climate adaptation grows more important. Insurance is at the heart of the challenge.

Across Australia, the regions with the highest insurance premiums are those with the most flood risk, and this is particularly true on the east coast, according to analysis prepared exclusively for this masthead by actuarial firm Finity. Bushfires are a factor, too, but flood is the overwhelming driver.

The most expensive insurance on the east coast is in the Richmond-Tweed region in the NSW Northern Rivers, when comparing large sub-state regions defined by the Australian Bureau of Statistics as statistical area 4 (SA4).

In Richmond-Tweed, near the Queensland border, premiums have risen by 81 per cent since January 2021. The average quote for a new policy in the region, which includes Lismore, Tweed Heads, Murwillumbah, Byron Bay and Ballina, is now $8836 a year.

The most expensive insurance in Victoria by SA4 is in the Shepparton region along the Murray River, where the average quote is $4871 a year, up 77 per cent. The highest in Queensland is in the west of Brisbane, where home owners now pay an average of $6173, up 74 per cent.

What all three regions have in common is that they were hit by devastating floods, sometimes multiple times, over the past decade, and most especially in 2022. NSW premiums are particularly high because they include the emergency services levy of between 15 per cent and 18 per cent, which is not funded through insurance in other states. The NSW government is considering reforms.

Premiums in the Cairns SA4 region have gone down over the past five years and are now an average $3985 a year. Finity principal Stephen Lau says this is because the federal government created a cyclone reinsurance pool in northern Australia to make insurance more affordable in cyclone-prone areas. The program is monitored by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission.

In some locations, it is possible to zoom in even closer to clusters of individual suburbs. Breaking down the Blue Mountains and Outer West sub-state region into three SA3 sub-regions reveals that the Richmond-Windsor area – where Yarramundi is located – has average premiums of $12,606 a year, a rise of 91 per cent over five years. Again, the main reason is flood risk.

But in Victoria, the most expensive of these smaller regions is the Yarra Ranges, east of Melbourne, which has an average premium of $5183 a year, an 81 per cent rise mainly because of fire risk.

Analysis used by the Insurance Council of Australia suggests that the most vulnerable people and communities in Australia have the highest flood risk but the lowest financial and social capacity to protect their properties and families and to recover from disaster.

Council chief executive Andrew Hall is hugely concerned by this trend.

“When the worst happens to them, and most of the time I’m talking flooding, they just go backwards, and [that] creates this intergenerational cycle of poverty because they’re caught in a trap that they can’t get out of,” Hall says.

“They can’t sell their home [because] no one buys it back. It gets rebuilt in the location it was in, or they’ve just got no money and they’re stuck trying to put together what they’ve got left. That is the big picture.”

About 1.4 million properties nationally face some risk of flooding, including almost 300,000 properties that face a severe-to-extreme annual flooding risk, largely in NSW, Queensland and Victoria, says the Insurance Council.

The cost of dealing with natural disasters without insurance is high.

Vicary’s home was built in the past nine years and sits about five metres above what is commonly referred to as the one-in-100-year flood line – though more accurately, that means there is a 1 per cent chance of flooding in any given year. The water has never risen as high as her house but the clean-up is still a big task.

“Even if you don’t get floodwater in your home, when that river comes up, you’ve got all the animals that come out of everywhere – the mice, the snakes, the bugs,” Vicary says. “Mildew starts to grow in your house – I literally for weeks had to turn my air-conditioner on to get the humidity out of my house, so I didn’t have mould growing.”

Her lower paddocks front the river, so she has to evacuate animals including alpacas, sheep and horses, and then clean up for their safe return. She has spent $65,000 of her savings on replacing fences, cleaning out low-lying sheds and disposing of the debris dumped by the river, including a washing machine and half a speedboat.

Australia remains a relatively well-insured nation but the protection gap is growing. The Insurance Council’s Alix Pearce wrote in a Churchill fellowship report Insuring Australia Tomorrow in January that, of Australia’s $US37 billion ($51.7 billion) in losses from extreme weather over the past decade, $US12 billion, or about a third, was not insured.

Between 1987 and 2015, the number of properties exposed to high flood risk grew by more than 65 per cent both because of more homes being built and also climate change increasing the physical risk.

The average cost to build a new house in Australia has increased by 30 per cent since 2021, faster than the cumulative inflation rate of 24 per cent over the same time frame, the Insurance Council reported this week.

When damaged properties are repaired under insurance, they are held to outdated building standards, which means they will not be resilient to worsening weather. People who can afford it are taking matters into their own hands and are disaster-proofing their homes.

Sarah Thomson, 53, and Bec Nicoll, 56, moved into their newly rebuilt home in Kialla near Shepparton a week ago, more than four years after they were flooded by Seven Creeks, a tributary of the Murray.

They are relieved and delighted, after first living in a caravan for nine months and then in a 36-square-metre shed for more than three years. They have built back better, putting in about $500,000 of their own money on top of the insurance payout.

First, they had to battle with their insurance company, Allianz, for 12 months to be allowed to demolish and rebuild. “They said that it was repairable but the slab was still wet after nearly 12 months and we didn’t want to be putting floorboards on top of a wet slab,” Thomson says. “Negotiating with the insurer was a long, tedious, irritating process. That’s not available to a lot of people. We’ve got the ability to actually negotiate and to be able to fight for a good outcome.”

Nicoll says Emergency Recovery Victoria provided teams of engineers and hygienists who recommended demolition but Allianz “completely disregarded” the report as too generic. Eventually, the couple engaged a private engineer and researched insurance law to force the issue.

Allianz chief claims officer Luke Whenman apologised if Thomson and Nicoll had had a bad experience. He said the company always looked for the best way to build back within the funding envelope, and that it could provide an extra $20,000 to boost resilience. Cash settlement was not a good option for most customers because they would be unable to find tradespeople after a disaster, he said.

Thomson and Nicoll’s new house is raised on stumps and is also on a hillside, making it 1.25 metres higher than their old home and above the one-in-100-year flood level, with a buffer for climate change. They have also adhered to Passivhaus principles for temperature control and relevant bushfire codes.

None of this has made a difference to their new insurance premiums. Before the flood, they were paying between $2000 and $2500. They have now found insurance for $6100 a year, having fielded some quotes as high as $18,000 a year.

When shopping around, the couple found there was nowhere to disclose any of the resilience features of their new home. “When I said to a sales agent that we’ve actually rebuilt well above the mandated height for flooding in our area, he said, ‘that’s nice, I’m happy for you, but that doesn’t alter the policy’,” Nicoll says.

It was a similar story for home owners in northern NSW who flood-proofed their dwellings after being inundated in 2022. Virginia Jones and her husband Tim Lawson in Bogangar, near Cabarita Beach, put their home on stilts, raising it so high a full-size netball hoop stand could fit underneath. Their next-door neighbour Bernie Zietlow rebuilt his home with materials that mean it could be hosed out after a flood.

Jones says her insurance premiums have more than doubled to about $6000 a year, despite the lower flood risk because of raising the property. Zietlow’s insurance premiums have gone up from $1000 to $4000 a year for a small home. He has priced insurance with and without the improvements and it made no difference.

This is a problem that the Housing Resilience Action Plan aims to solve. A collaboration between Finity, the Resilient Building Council, Monash University and consumer advocacy groups, the proposal is to develop a rating system for every home in Australia that insurers use when pricing premiums.

Finity principal Sharanjit Paddam says the rating for each type of natural disaster would incorporate the risk profile of the area and the resilience of the actual home. “The idea … is to have a common language, so that consumers understand what the resilience of their home is to different disasters, insurers use that information to price insurance contracts, and then banks lend people money so that they can get the house to a different resilience level,” Paddam says.

“When you get your renewal notice, they’ll say, ‘OK, you are three-star-rated against flood, and that has led to this pricing for your insurance premium, but if you were four-star-rated, this is what your premium would be’. Including signals like that can empower consumers to make decisions.”

Scott Hawkins, managing director for Australasia at global reinsurance company Munich RE, says lowering the risk of events that occur every three to five years won’t significantly reduce premiums. It’s mitigating the risk of more extreme events that occur every few decades that would make the difference, he says.

“Some things people can do at the home level but some things need to be done at the community level,” Hawkins says.

The Insurance Council has called for a 10-year $30 billion flood defence fund to bolster infrastructure in 24 priority catchments nationally. The catchments were chosen because of flood risk and insurance affordability pressure. They are all in the eastern states.

Hall says the government has the right idea with the Hazards Insurance Partnership, which is designed to fund community and household infrastructure that can reduce risk and put downward pressure on premiums.

That is world-leading, Hall says, because the government persuaded insurance companies to provide information into the program, whereas in other developed jurisdictions such as the United States, governments had to sue to get access to the commercially sensitive data.

The government also created the Disaster Ready Fund, which was $200 million a year, though it has recently been reduced to $142.4 million.

“Again, huge tick, very smart idea,” Hall says. “The problem with it is that … so far… they’re programs like teaching people about bushfire awareness or building cyclone shelters.”

Hall says there would be more downward pressure on premiums if the money was spent on hard infrastructure and community-level defences, such as flood levees.

With Gay Alcorn

It took two Aussie entrepreneurs six years to build a cult sunscreen brand. Then it came crashing down

Sydney Morning Herald September 05, 2026

How Ultra Violette founders Ava Chandler-Matthews and Bec Jefferd found themselves at the centre of “SunscreenGate”.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

In every dramatic fall from grace, there is a before, and there is an after.

For Ava Chandler-Matthews, one half of the duo behind Australian suncare brand Ultra Violette, what preceded the fall that would plague her company was the stuff of bucket lists: a private dinner with billionaire beauty founder Hailey Bieber. What came after would throw this high into sharp relief.

It’s been more than a year since consumer advocacy group Choice published that investigation into sunscreen that would upend the industry. On June 12, 2025, Choice reported that 16 out of 20 Australian sunscreens failed to meet their SPF claims of 50 or more, implicating plenty of household names including Banana Boat, Invisible Zinc, Neutrogena and the Cancer Council. Among them, none suffered the kind of fallout that cult favourite brand Ultra Violette did: its “Lean Screen” product, a mineral zinc sunscreen and one of the most premium products in the cohort (a 75ml tube retailed for $52), trailed the pack with a woeful SPF score of 4 – the only one to score in the single digits.

Nine months since co-founders Chandler-Matthews, 40, and Bec Jefferd, 50, first agreed to this interview – after cancelling and rescheduling twice – the Melbourne-based friends turned business founders have flown to Sydney for the day for their first sit-down media interview since the story broke. They arrive at a North Sydney cafe in late July bearing a selection of designer tarts from Melbourne – a peace offering after the rescheduling – ready to talk about how they found themselves in the eye of the storm and how they climbed out of it.

“A trust rebuild is not an interesting story,” says Chandler-Matthews. “It’s not as interesting as a sunscreen scandal where there are interesting players. It became us versus Choice.”

Choice’s initial investigation morphed into a kind of national sunscreen scandal, sowing doubt about the efficacy of sunscreen altogether in the country with the highest rates of skin cancer in the world.

Dubbed “SunscreenGate”, the entire affair made global headlines as sunscreen experts, scientists and skincare girlies picked apart the merits of sunscreen testing, the role of medicine regulator the Therapeutic Goods Administration and the validity of Choice’s SPF results, not to mention Ultra Violette’s defiant initial response – quickly followed by a sudden volte-face – and then whether it was worth wearing sunscreen at all.

The fallout is ongoing: the TGA’s investigation into the other 15 sunscreens that failed Choice’s testing is yet to wrap, and in March, it opened up consultation for how sunscreen is regulated in Australia, the results of which are expected to be published by the end of the year.

The pair will tell you the past 14 months have been “triggering” and “traumatic”. Chandler-Mathers puts it more bluntly: “It’s been the hardest year of my life. So often I would come home and I was mute. I couldn’t talk to my husband. I couldn’t talk to my best friends. I couldn’t talk to my mum.”

Of all 16 sunscreens that failed Choice’s testing, the fall of Ultra Violette was the steepest. In the six years between launching the brand in 2019 and the Choice investigation in 2025, its sunscreens had become a darling of the Australian beauty industry – a cult favourite among young women for its pastel-hued packaging and its lightweight, tinted formulas that felt more at home in an upmarket beauty retailer than a chemist. (The Australian Financial Review credited the brand with “making sunscreen sexy”.)

Chandler-Matthews and Jefferd, alumni of household names like L’Oreal and Napoleon Perdis, met while working at beauty retailer MECCA – Jefferd as head of product development, Chandler-Matthews as brand manager – and they departed in 2017 to build what would eventually become Ultra Violette.

Neither are scientists – they enlisted a force of product developers, in-house regulators and chemists to build Ultra Violette – but their marketing backgrounds were pivotal in the brand’s sharp rise, enlisting influencers like Gen Z-favourite Sophia Begg (@sophadophaa to her 1.5 million TikTok followers).

Doors opened for them with financial injections from private equity and the support of beauty retailers such as Adore Beauty, Sephora, Net-A-Porter and Harrods. They had just launched in the US market when Choice’s report forced them to focus not on thriving, but simply surviving.

What the saga partially succeeded in doing was exposing the public’s limited understanding of how sunscreen works – and just how volatile the testing process can be.

Acknowledged by the TGA and the sunscreen industry, the current standard for SPF testing in Australia and internationally is inherently variable. This method (in vivo) involves applying sunscreen to 10 to 20 human subjects, who are then exposed to UV light. A trained tester observes this process, noting the time it takes for skin to redden (an assessment procedure which is itself prone to error), to determine the product’s SPF.

In Australia, most non-cosmetic sunscreens are regulated as medicines, meaning to get on the market they need TGA approval. To do so, brands send a product to a laboratory of their choosing to be tested according to the Australian and International standard. If approved, this is typically the first and only time in a product’s lifecycle it is tested.

And because the TGA doesn’t conduct its own testing (except in select circumstances), Choice has historically been the only body in Australia to conduct testing independent of brands. Its last report on Australian sunscreen, published in 2015, found four out of six products tested failed to meet their advertised SPF level.

When the worst year of her life began, Chandler-Matthews was in California’s Napa Valley, dining with beauty mogul Hailey Bieber, having just spoken at The Business of Fashion’s global beauty forum, headlined by the influencer.

Choice released its report at midnight AEST, and although Chandler-Matthews and Jefferd had known it was coming, they hadn’t been told exactly when. The advocacy group had alerted Ultra Violette about its test results in March, three months prior to its public release, prompting Chandler-Matthews and Jefferd to order additional testing on every batch of Lean Screen then on the market. They revisited manufacturing records and asked Choice for more detail on its testing methods.

The SPF figure that Choice’s testing (conducted at Eurofins Dermatest in Sydney) arrived at – 4 – was incomprehensible to them. “We genuinely could not understand how that result was even possible,” says Jefferd. ” ‘Is this true? Have we been damaging our customers?’. That was our first response. Like, ‘That can’t be right. Have we had any cases of people being sunburnt?’.” Choice was confused, too. When it sent a different batch of Lean Screen to a lab in Germany, it returned a score of 5.

Meanwhile, Ultra Violette had received the results of two of its additional SPF tests – sent to Princeton Consumer Research, an SPF certification lab based overseas founded by two British reality TV stars, with no connection to Princeton University – with scores of 61 and 64. Ultra Violette shared these numbers with Choice, to little effect. “We asked a few questions, but we weren’t engaged,” says Chandler-Matthews. “It was not like we were talking every day.”

After dinner, Chandler-Matthews returned to her hotel room to tackle customer service queries until the early hours. The next day, she mentally parked everything for a meeting with Sephora US before filming a video to respond to the Choice report and flying home. Fielding calls and messages from retail partners, brand ambassadors, customers and the media over questions the pair didn’t have the answers to, they were shocked to see 15 other brands had also failed their SPF claims.

On paper, though, they were less incredulous and more recalcitrant. Ultra Violette engaged a reputation and crisis management consultant to distribute a forceful statement condemning Choice’s results as “not even remotely accurate” and “scientifically impossible”, suggesting that what was most likely to have happened was “human error and the mix-up of samples”. The way the product was decanted, their statement said, may have led to destabilisation (Choice later published all its SPF tests and stood by the validity of the test results).

Chandler-Matthews doubled down the following day. In an eight-minute video uploaded to TikTok and Instagram, she pointed to Ultra Violette’s own SPF test results of 60-plus from the same batch Choice tested. “What we do know about Choice is they’re not a regulator. They are not the ACCC. They are not the TGA. They are not the ones who approve sunscreens,” she said to her iPhone camera in the video filmed in her US hotel room. “We stand by the tests we’ve done.”

It did little to assuage public concerns. Some looked at Ultra Violette’s distinct blue and purple colour scheme and concluded that the entire range must also be similarly defective (the pair later retested the entire range and said they found no issues beyond Lean Screen). Others accused Jefferd and Chandler-Matthews, who couldn’t help but read every comment on social media, of diluting their product to squeeze more out of their customers.

Meanwhile, additional test results returned with figures below 50 – and then another, and another (in Australia, products advertising SPF50+ must actually test at 60 or above). On August 22, the company apologised to customers and announced a voluntary recall of Lean Screen. It looked like a total capitulation – because it was. “We are deeply sorry that one of our products has fallen short of the standards we pride ourselves on and that you have come to expect of us,” their statement read. The next slide on the carousel was a chart of eight test results, returning SPF levels of 64, 61, 60, 33, 26, 21, 10, 4.

“We did a full 180,” says Chandler-Matthews. “There was no choice,” Jefferd says. “The product was not safe to keep on the market.”

While the recall was announced in late August, Ultra Violette had started refunding customers after Choice published its report. Some sunscreen brands tarred by the same investigation reached out to Chandler-Matthews and Jefferd for advice on how to handle the recall process (one copied their statement so closely that it still contained Ultra Violette’s specific product number). About $1 million evaporated, squeezing cash flow at a time when the company was trying to fund its US expansion. Its chief financial officer, alarmed at the amount of money going out the door, tried to put some limits on the refunds, but the founders say they were refunding just about anyone who asked. “It was absolutely in doubt,” Chandler-Matthews said of the business’ financial viability at the time.

So what actually went wrong with Lean Screen? Why were the results that low?

Unlike other sunscreens in Ultra Violette’s range, Lean Screen was the only product not developed in-house. The zinc sunscreen used a base formula made by Wild Child Laboratories, a formula which, ABC investigations revealed, was shared by 20 other Australian sunscreens that were all recalled, paused or under TGA review. The TGA would later find that this base formulation was “unlikely to have an SPF greater than 21”, triggering a domino effect of product recalls by brands that hadn’t been called out by Choice’s report.

Further ABC investigations cast a shadow on the integrity of the whole sunscreen industry. Sunscreen experts and whistleblowers called into question the data emerging from Princeton Consumer Research, which had tested and certified three of Ultra Violette’s SPF results – the ones they presented to Choice to counter its 4 – and at least seven other sunscreens in Choice’s report. Former employees said they resigned over the lab’s “tendency to cut corners”. In late September, the TGA said it found “significant concerns about the reliability” of Princeton’s SPF testing, and urged sunscreen brands to get their products tested elsewhere.

While there’s no suggestion it occurred in this case, fraudulent testing isn’t unheard of. In 2019, the regulator began reviewing sunscreens tested by American lab AMA, whose owner was arrested by US authorities for a scheme involving fabricated test results.

Perhaps no business suffered more from the saga than Wild Child. Ultimately, a TGA investigation didn’t find any manufacturing deficiencies that explained why the formula could only ever achieve an SPF of 21 and it pointed to variability in SPF testing as the potential cause. “Our investigation did demonstrate that materially different SPF results were generated when the formulation was tested by different laboratories,” says Wild Child chief executive Tom Curnow.

But the negative attention sparked by Choice’s investigation had done its damage; the Perth manufacturer collapsed, was acquired by a group of investors, and rebranded to Heliora. “The publicity, recalls and resulting loss of customer and market confidence in SPF testing caused significant commercial damage,” said Heliora chair Paul Waldren.

Ultra Violette stopped working with Heliora, which has ceased production of the recalled base formula, but the manufacturer managed to retain all 20 brands subject to recalls as clients and kept all 70 of its staff employed.

Chandler-Matthews and Jefferd accept responsibility for what they put out on the market, but they aren’t keen to say much more about what went wrong with the product. “We still don’t know. It wasn’t our formulation,” says Jefferd. “It’s a manufacturer’s formula. It’s up to them,” says Chandler-Matthews.

Princeton Consumer Research did not respond to multiple requests for comment from Good Weekend.

Fair or not, Ultra Violette’s tarnished brand became synonymous with faltering trust in Australian sunscreen as a whole, a $270 million-plus market that had been regarded highly by international consumers whose own regulators (like the US’s Food and Drug Administration) are less stringent than the TGA’s.

It didn’t help that this came at a time when the sunscreen “scepticism” movement, popularised by right-wing figures like RFK Jr and Joe Rogan who claim sunscreen contains “toxic” ingredients and prevents vitamin D generation, had been gaining traction on social media, alongside tanning culture.

“Regardless of whether people buy Ultra Violette or not, the fact that trust in sunscreen in general was shaken was really disastrous,” says Jefferd.

Chandler-Matthews hopes they can win back as many customers as possible, but she says some have turned their back for good. “For some people, it may take longer,” she says. “For some people, not at all.”

Chemist Dr Michelle Wong, a science educator known to her social media followers as @labmuffinbeautyscience, has followed the scandal closely. The founders’ approach – which took aim at the validity of Choice’s results – worked against, not for them, Wong believes. “I think a lot of the lack of trust actually came from Ultra Violette themselves and how they responded,” she says. Their claim that Choice’s results were “scientifically impossible” turned out to be untrue.

“If you compare Ultra Violette’s response to every other brand in the original Choice article, theirs was just out of line,” says Wong, who was paid to copywrite for the brand in 2021. “While I think a lot of what they did behind the scenes to sort out the issue was commendable, publicly it seemed like they were trying to influence their way out of this situation.”

Swathes of social media users have expressed that waning confidence in the brand was less because of Lean Screen’s failure in Choice’s report, and more because of their subsequent handling of it, which they claim included deleting unsavoury comments, blocking users and enlisting influencer friends to rage against Choice.

How Ultra Violette handled (or mishandled) its response became a PR lesson on how not to handle a crisis, inspiring multiple think pieces and LinkedIn posts on the topic. (It’s normally an excellent strategy to mobilise people in your network to defend you, opined crisis management consultant Sally Branson, but in this instance, Ultra Violette’s ecosystem of beauty influencers and TikTok creators were doing so “without bulletproof information to support it”.)

By speaking to customers in a video on social media, Chandler-Matthews had wanted to address customers directly and personally. Given the chance, they’d “absolutely” do things differently, they say now. “There’s a lot to be said for that classic PR response,” says Chandler-Matthews. “By doing that video, did I think I would become the face of a global sunscreen scandal? No, I didn’t. It was defensive.”

“We wouldn’t have operated on a platform of as much certainty,” says Jefferd. “We felt we were on really solid footing, and what turned out is that we weren’t.”

But while hindsight may offer the gift of perspective, both are emphatic they acted in good faith as passionate founders doing the best with the information they had. “This is not our business,” says Jefferd. “This is our life, and we care deeply about this.”

Despite the wreckage to Ultra Violette’s reputation, its cash flow crisis and its social licence to operate, Chandler-Matthews and Jefferd don’t regret the changes catalysed by Choice’s SPF testing. “I think [Choice] shone a light on an important area that needed to be talked about. We wouldn’t be having this discussion about regulatory change if they hadn’t,” says Jefferd.

The scale of the problems across the supply chain led the TGA itself to the conclusion that there were broader issues with the current regulatory framework for sunscreens, rather than isolated product failures. A TGA spokesman said this includes addressing known limitations in SPF testing reproducibility, laboratory oversight, and life-cycle quality assurance.

In March, the TGA opened up a consultation group seeking feedback on proposed regulatory changes – before its investigation into sunscreens that failed Choice’s testing has been published, which it said would be online “before the end of the year”. The public, and politicians, are getting impatient. When independent senator David Pocock tried to press for answers from a TGA official at a Senate Estimates hearing in June (he was not the first to do so), he was told the investigation was “nearing completion”.

Wong, who is part of the TGA’s consultation group, says industry insiders had been raising the alarm on issues with SPF testing with the regulator for years, without much progress. Choice’s investigation made the problems too big to ignore. “I think Choice felt like they needed to stir up some attention to get the TGA to act,” she says, “which, I think, is kind of justified.”

The consumer advocacy group, formed in 1959 at a Sydney Town Hall meeting, enjoyed a level of national exposure and attention it hadn’t had in years. For the first time, Choice was nominated for a Walkley Award, typically reserved for journalism, for its sunscreen investigation.

Without it, defective sunscreens would have stayed on the market and regulatory reform may have never happened, said Matt Steen, Choice’s director of reviews and testing. “The existing regulatory system, which relies heavily on companies certifying their own compliance, is clearly not working and cannot continue.”

One industry group that had been lobbying for regulatory change is Accord, representing the hygiene, cosmetic and personal care industry, of which Ultra Violette is a member. The organisation would like to see the TGA adopt in vitro [lab-based] test methods to validate results, particularly given many labs operate overseas under different regulatory frameworks. In vitro testing has since been approved for use in Australia, but it has yet to be implemented across the industry. Early analysis shows it is at least as reliable as in vivo testing, says Accord executive director Damien Mitsch, and it is a preferable alternative as it’s cheaper and faster (machines don’t need to be recruited and paid to have their skin burned).

Mitsch describes the way Choice handled its publication as “sensationalistic”. “Getting the sunscreen conversation into the public domain was in some ways helpful,” he says. “But at the same time, to throw it out into the ether and watch the chaos ensue is probably not the best way to manage a significant public health issue.”

All stakeholders Good Weekend spoke to agree the regulator needs to do more – particularly around eliminating issues with testing variability – but opinions diverge on the nitty gritty about exactly how this might play out.

Ultra Violette has come full circle. In mid-August, 361 days after the company pulled Lean Screen from shelves, it released Velvet Screen, a mineral zinc sunscreen that has gone through two rounds of testing from separate laboratories and is manufactured at a different, TGA-approved third-party manufacturer.

The number on the bottle has been lowered to 40 – unlike its predecessor’s SPF 60 claim – a decision Jefferd says was made in the hope consumers take a little extra time in applying sunscreen properly (mineral sunscreens are heavier, meaning users are more likely to apply insufficient amounts), and despite testing returning results in the high 40s and 50s. Velvet Screen’s development has heralded broader changes across the brand, aimed at reducing SPF testing’s inherent variability.

They have also engaged French photobiologist Sebastien Miksa, whose job it is to review the validity of test results through his company Suncert and identify potential anomalies. Ultra Violette is pushing for the TGA to have someone perform this role in-house.

“The trust in the rest of the range should probably be stronger than ever, because we’ve implemented all of those changes,” says Jefferd.

Chandler-Matthews hopes these changes will help Ultra Violette rebuild as a leader in the sunscreen industry and rehabilitate the reputation of Australian sunscreens. “It’s actions and not words at this point,” she says. “It’s just consistency. I think we’ve done the work.”

The drama has bruised, but not hamstrung, Ultra Violette’s ambitions to expand across the globe. Despite the public tumult, Ultra Violette didn’t lose any retail partners, and new US investors had come on board some weeks before Good Weekend sat down with the pair. The day after Choice’s investigation came out, Chandler-Matthews met with Sephora US, which renewed its deal and gave them four times more shelf space.

This time last year, they were asking themselves why they had bothered to make sunscreens at all.

“We could have made a blush,” says Jefferd. “We could have made a f---ing fantastic moisturiser.”

She didn’t start painting until her 60s. Now she’s considered our most important artist

Sydney Morning Herald September 05, 2026

She came to painting late and acrylics even later – but this artist’s prolific legacy had repercussions beyond popularising Aboriginal art.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Warning: This story contains the name and images of an Indigenous person who has died.

Thirty-eight years ago, 11 tall ships from Britain swept into Sydney Harbour for the 1988 Bicentennial re-enactment of the First Fleet’s arrival, and in that historic moment, artist and gallerist Christopher Hodges was struck by a terrible sense of unease.

Watching the celebratory scene with a glass of champagne, Hodges immediately realised that one crucial element was missing: the involvement of Aboriginal Australians who were, instead, in another part of the city, marching through Sydney in protest.

“Looking back, how the hell did Australians think the ships coming in was an appropriate event to celebrate 200 years of settlement?” he asks today, standing in Utopia Art Sydney, the gallery he founded that same year with the goal of championing Indigenous artists. “People were there from around the world, but there was no Aboriginal presence at all. I can clearly remember my chagrin. I knew I was in the wrong place. I should have been in La Perouse with all those First Nations people.”

In the wake of the commemorative event, Hodges decided to act. First, he persuaded prominent Sydney gallerist Chandler Coventry and James Mollison, the founding director of the Australian National Gallery (later to become the National Gallery of Australia), to accompany him to Alice Springs. Hodges wanted to look at some of the art that had begun coming out of the remote Utopia community, 250 kilometres to the north-east.

There they were shown the work of an Indigenous elder and Central Desert law woman in her late 70s, who had just started painting on canvas that year. Her name was Emily Kame Kngwarreye. Mollison, who’d come to prominence by buying Jackson Pollock’s Blue Poles, immediately bought one of her paintings, only the third Kngwarreye had ever produced, for the national collection. She was, he said, “one of the finest abstract expressionists” he had ever encountered.

It was the moment of professional discovery – one that launched Kngwarreye into the Australian art world, providing the impetus for a number of landmark exhibitions. Her abstract paintings hit the mainstream, then ended up being exhibited around the world – an unexpected yet undisputed critical, commercial and cultural success. Her rise to prominence was stratospheric and coincided with a period of profound change in Australia when it came to Indigenous culture, says Andrew Bailey, the author of a major new book, Emily: Emily Kame Kngwarreye, the Artist Who Changed Australia.

Between 1988 and 2000, a series of key events occurred, notes Bailey, from the Mabo decision in 1992 to the Native Title Act 1993, the Wik decision in 1996 and the Bringing Them Home Report the next year, followed by the first National Sorry Day in 1998. Against that backdrop, there was the rise of other notable Indigenous artists, such as Clifford Possum Tjapaltjarri, Rover Thomas, Gordon Bennett, Tracey Moffatt and Sally Morgan.

“But the main factor was the emergence of Emily Kame Kngwarreye,” Bailey argues. “She changed the art world so much, both Indigenous and mainstream, and then became a catalyst for profound national cultural change as well.

“By 1998, a new idea was forming: mainstream Australians had begun to consider that Indigenous art provided a visual representation of the nation, themselves included. It seemed to articulate a visual identity that all Australians could feel was authentic – something they had wanted for a long time.”

Celebrated Ngan’gikurrungurr artist Regina Pilawuk Wilson, whose paintings are held in major state and national collections and have been exhibited internationally, including at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art, agrees. “Emily opened the eyes of the world to Indigenous painting,” she says. “Today I paint my weaving designs, and my paintings are shown around the world. Emily started this.”

Emily Kame Kngwarreye only started painting late in life at Alhalker, a rock hole in south-western Utopia, an isolated 2000-square-kilometre area belonging to the Anmatyerr and Alyawarre people, where she worked on cattle stations, mustering, looking after camels and doing housework. She began painting in batik in the 1970s, but after being introduced to acrylics became absolutely prolific. She is believed to have produced more than 3000 paintings over her eight years as an artist until her death in 1996. Her first solo exhibition was held at Utopia Art Sydney in 1990, and her artworks went on to represent Australia at the 1997 and 2015 Venice Biennales, and have been shown in France, Tokyo, New York, Switzerland and at the Tate Modern in London.

Starting as a dot painter, using the familiar technique to underpin representations of Country, Kngwarreye later moved on to larger dots or blobs in luminous colour, then to stripe compositions and linear “yam dreaming” paintings and, in the final year of her life, complex arrangements of abstract blocks. She’s now regularly referred to as perhaps Australia’s most significant, and celebrated, artist.

“Emily created work that people with no kind of Indigenous art knowledge could understand, to some degree, and appreciate,” says Mirri Leven, the managing director and owner of Art Leven, formerly Cooee Art, Australia’s oldest exhibiting Indigenous-focused fine-art gallery. “Obviously, they can’t get the full cultural meaning and understand that those dots and snakes on the canvas are the blood that runs through people’s veins. Her art somehow transcended contemporary modern abstract art even though it wasn’t modern or contemporary at all. But it crossed into that for ‘white eyes’. It was less ethnographic and had a soul that everyone can see.”

Andrew Bailey is a perhaps surprising person to have written Kngwarreye’s biography. A neat, lean, precisely spoken, non-Indigenous man, he looks in every way the retired economist and business executive he is, with roles at the federal treasury, management consultants McKinsey & Company and Optus among others. He describes himself as “no art expert” and has no professional background in art, although he does publish the weekly art newsletter The Easel.

Long an admirer of Kngwarreye’s work, he was, however, amazed to discover that there had never been a full biography written, and decided to tackle it himself. Three-and-a-half years into the writing, however, he felt he had hit a brick wall. Despite conducting a marathon of about 50 interviews with people from the art world and beyond, no one could explain exactly how she became so prominent.

“I would be asking, ‘What actually happened?’ and nobody could give a straight answer,” says Bailey, now 74. He, too, saw the conspicuous absence of any Aboriginal iconography at the Bicentennial in 1988, and yet 12 years later, he could see that very imagery everywhere at the opening of the 2000 Sydney Olympics – including a Kngwarreye-inspired artwork displayed on the stadium floor for the opening ceremony – but it was hard to tell if there was a link.

“As I continued interviewing and writing, I had no sense I was getting any closer to an answer,” he says. “I recall being immensely frustrated that no one could tell me exactly the events that took Emily from being an unknown to being famous. Getting clear about that is what led me to going down a rabbit hole.”

That rabbit hole was completely untraversed ground. With no reliable records of art exhibitions throughout the country featuring Indigenous work, Bailey set himself the task of trawling through the ephemera boxes – archived jumbles of cards, letters, pamphlets and photocopied sheets advertising exhibitions – of 26 of the main commercial galleries operating in Sydney and Melbourne. From the details of their 4983 commercial exhibitions, Bailey assembled a database of activity over the two decades to 2000.

To provide context, he also collected data on the exhibition activity of four major public art galleries, Queensland Art Gallery, the Art Gallery of NSW, the National Gallery of Victoria and the National Gallery of Australia. They’d held 1418 exhibitions. The whole operation was a laborious five-month process that no one had ever attempted before, with every one of the more than 6000 exhibitions compiled and analysed by hand. Perhaps an economist was, after all, the ideal match for the task.

What Bailey discovered from that exercise stunned him. Between 1980 and 1988, Indigenous art featured in barely 2 per cent of Sydney and Melbourne commercial gallery shows. Public gallery activity was similarly modest, at 3 per cent. But between 1989 and 1996 – “the Emily years” – the number of Indigenous commercial exhibitions skyrocketed, from just one in 1980 to 86 in 1989 and 1990 alone. In the four major public galleries, Indigenous shows as a portion of total shows went from 2 per cent in 1985 to 12 per cent in 2000.

As a result, Bailey argues that the art world’s recognition of Kngwarreye’s work became the catalyst for the modern Aboriginal art movement. Before her, Aboriginal art was largely considered ethnographic and belonging in a museum or a tourist souvenir shop. Her art was the first to be perceived as modern abstract art, rightfully belonging in an art gallery and, with that shift, First Nations art became so successful that it’s now a major part of the Australian art market and a consistent attraction for overseas tourists.

“Up until the late 1980s,” he points out, “there were almost no Indigenous exhibitions. Then there was an absolute explosion, a bonfire, that’s kept on growing. The emergence of Indigenous art was not – as I’d repeatedly been told – gradual. It was sudden. Explosively sudden. I can’t exaggerate how surprised I was by those figures, and how profound that change was. And Emily was demonstrably the catalyst, because she was, by orders of magnitude, more prominent than any other Indigenous artist of the period.”

If he’s being honest, he completely mistook what the data would show. It had answered his question about Kngwarreye’s rise to fame, but the real surprise was what it revealed about mainstream Australia – where it had come from in the early 1980s, and how it changed during the time she was painting and why. “The phrase that comes to mind,” he says, “is that I went fishing for a sardine and caught a whale.”

Tracking the commentary in newspapers through those two decades revealed another surprise – the seeming search for national identity that was well underway. Up until then, the Great Australian Silence – a term coined by anthropologist W. E. H. (Bill) Stanner in his 1968 Boyer lecture to describe the omission of Indigenous Australians from national history – still seemed to rule.

Nicolas Peterson, emeritus professor of anthropology at Australian National University, says the only real attention being paid to Aboriginal Australians was from fellow anthropologists in writings never intended for mainstream consumption. Kngwarreye helped change all that. “When Qantas starts painting its planes with dot paintings, we know that Aboriginal art has become mainstream,” Peterson says. “Now, the whole profile of Aboriginal Australia has been magnified through Aboriginal art and has become part of the national imagination.”

Beyond the many social and political events that contributed to the rise of Indigenous art, there was a broader social and demographic shift underway, too. One small measure: in the 2021 Australian census, 25 per cent more people identified as Indigenous (3.2 per cent) than in the previous national survey in 2016 (2.8 per cent).

“I would frame Kngwarray not as the sole cause, but as a crucial catalyst within a much larger transformation in the Indigenous art sector, including the increasing visibility of Indigenous artists, major exhibitions, collecting by public institutions, galleries and private collectors, and growing international attention,” says curator Kelli Cole, a Warumungu and Luritja woman from Central Australia, who worked with Hetti Perkins on the 4th National Indigenous Art Triennial: Ceremony.

Cole also co-curated the major exhibition Emily Kam Kngwarray (Cole’s spelling of the name is different, on her family’s wishes) for the National Gallery of Australia, which subsequently toured to the Tate Modern in London and Fondation Opale in Switzerland, and says Kngwarray’s success coincided with – and helped accelerate – a wider conversion in which Aboriginal art moved from the margins of Australia’s cultural institutions into the centre of its national vision.

“Kngwarray’s work became particularly significant,” Cole says, “because it enabled non-Indigenous Australia to embrace Indigenous art as an expression of cultural identity, even as the paintings themselves asserted radically different understandings of Country, knowledge and belonging.”

Bailey sees it differently, asserting that Kngwarreye was “the spark” that led to change. “I am fully aware that is incautious language,” he says. “Yet, there is simply no other way to fairly represent the evidence. That’s the meta-narrative: Emily, as our most important artist ever, changed Australia.”

Certainly, Indigenous art has never been more popular. This year’s National Indigenous Art Fair, held on July 3-5, generated more than $1.2 million for exhibitors, a record $450,000 more than the previous year. “None of us was expecting this kind of increase in sales in these hard economic times,” says Sarah Martin, the founder and general manager. “It shows there is such an appetite for Indigenous art, and a genuine interest in learning about the artists and their stories.”

The four-day Sydney Contemporary, which concludes September 6 with a line-up of more than 100 galleries and its celebrated component of First Nations art, now has its largest-ever public art and city-wide installation program.

First Nations APY Lands artist and cultural consultant Sally Scales says Indigenous artists owe a huge amount to Kngwarreye. “She absolutely made such a difference for us,” she says. “She was a superstar, and one of the most important artists for all Australians, as well as for First Nations artists. She’d lived a full life then painted her story, her lore and her culture later in life and in multitudes of ways. The doors she opened for us, and I’m getting teary even thinking about it, made an incredible difference for everyone who followed. It’s an amazing legacy.”

Wiradjuri artist Brett Groves says Kngwarreye was deeply inspirational, living her traditional life and being inspired by Country, and ceremony and family. “I run workshops and many people say they’re put off creating art as they feel they need to go to university,” he says. “But she was a stirring example of painting from the heart and letting the paint on the canvas speak for her. But while so many more people are now interested in Indigenous art, we still encounter racism about our art.”

Kngwarreye holds the record for an Australian female artist with her 1994 masterpiece Earth’s Creation, which sold through Art Leven for $2.1 million in 2017. It was also the second-highest price ever paid for an Indigenous work after Clifford Possum Tjapaltjarri’s 1977 Warlugulong which, with its 25 per cent buyers’ premium, came to $2.4 million in 2007.

Her enduring significance is clear to social anthropologist Dr Peter Sutton. “She got to people through beauty, reaching even people who don’t know the narrative or spiritual meaning of her work,” he says. “Her use of colour tones and arrangement of forms are very satisfying. People sometimes hate to admit they like beauty, but most people do. Emily had a fantastic run in a very good market.”

Toby Meagher, director of Michael Reid Sydney + Berlin, the galleries that represent contemporary Australian and New Zealand artists (with half of their artists being First Nations), says that Kngwarreye, even posthumously, continues to wield huge power and influence. “We certainly watch closely the global response to Emily because, in lots of ways, she is iconic and her success is a window into First Nations contemporary art today,” Meagher says. “She really opened the doors to others, like Regina Pilawuk Wilson, who’s our most important senior woman artist.”

He wouldn’t say Kngwarreye was the only influential First Nations artist, but her practices and energy and art-making propelled her to another level, generating a momentum that made her symbolic of something larger. “With Emily, there’s a depth to her work and a beauty and a story-telling that really resonates and builds an emotional connection,” he says. “In a lot of ways, Emily has become emblematic of the shift that happened with First Nations art over that period.”

Bailey makes the case, of course, that Kngwarreye is Australia’s greatest artist ever, and even though Brett Whiteley is a contender for the title, the strength of his rivalry ebbs when their solo shows and retrospectives are compared, especially on the international stage. At least by the numbers.

In 2008, Kngwarreye had her Tokyo retrospective, and then the Venice Biennale again in 2015, but Bailey says it was with her 2025 retrospective at the Tate Modern – the first major exhibition there for any Australian artist – that she left Whiteley behind.

“Of course, Whiteley was a tremendous artist, no question, but Emily, having a solo show at one of the four to five most influential contemporary art galleries in the world, that puts her in the pantheon of internationally important artists like Van Gogh, Picasso, Mondrian and Jackson Pollock,” he says. “If you ask people who’s our most important artist … not a lot of people would say Emily. But she’s someone who changed our view of Indigenous art, of Australian art and, along the way, transformed the Australian national identity.”

Christopher Hodges, the man who sat watching those tall ships and wishing he was elsewhere, and who played a role in introducing so much of the outside world to Kngwarreye’s work, has little doubt, either.

“Emily’s work is so aesthetically pleasing, beautiful and appealing, and people react to it with an almost back-of-brain response,” he says. “Her work insinuates itself inside, it seeps in, and it beats all the filters. Even people who say they don’t like modern art are drawn to hers. It has such a charismatic quality, just like Emily herself, and has left an enduring legacy.”

Emily: Emily Kame Kngwarreye, the Artist Who Changed Australia by Andrew Bailey (Allen & Unwin, $50) is published on September 29.

Suzie Miller thought footy was just for blokes. Then one game blew her away

Sydney Morning Herald September 05, 2026

The acclaimed playwright makes women’s toughest fights into stories the world can’t get enough of. Her inspiring new play about the birth of AFLW is just one of her projects launching this month.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

A popular musician is said to be in their imperial phase when everything they release becomes a hit, like Elton John in the early 1970s, Madonna in the late 1980s or Lady Gaga at the end of the noughties. It describes an artist at the top of their game when they seem to be everywhere, to dominate the medium they work in and to make an indelible mark on the culture.

If September 2026 is any indication then Suzie Miller is surely experiencing her imperial phase. She has a new novel out, Inter Alia (Picador), based on her own award-winning play, which had a sellout season at the National Theatre in London last year.

She has a movie, Prima Facie, having its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival – a major Oscars launch pad – with an A-list star, Cynthia Erivo, in the lead.

And she has a new play, Strong Is the New Pretty, opening at Brisbane Festival ahead of a national tour – which is what brings her to a chilly rehearsal room at the Wharf Theatres in Sydney on a crisp and sunny Friday.

The play is the story of the birth of the AFLW, and features a cast of eight women led by Tara Morice (Strictly Ballroom), Lucy Bell and Amy Ingram.

Miller has been mulling over the idea for the play since witnessing the inaugural AFL Women’s grand final at the former Metricon Stadium on the Gold Coast in March 2017, when the Adelaide Crows defeated the Brisbane Lions.

“I grew up in Melbourne, so you’d think I’d be a massive AFL fan,” Miller says. “But as a young girl I thought: how come it’s just boys? So I didn’t really invest in it the way other people did.

“It didn’t even occur to me that maybe girls could play AFL. So I was blown away when the AFLW came to pass. I thought, how many other areas in the world do we not envisage that this is a possible place to have equality until we actually see it happen before us?”

Miller rolled up her sleeves and interviewed players, coaches, commissioners, people involved at the grassroots – “everyone you could imagine”.

Columnist and author

“They had to get over all the hurdles of ‘how are we going to get sponsorship?’ ‘How are we going to get media on board?’ Because every single person had the same view: ‘Oh, no, women don’t play football’.”

Aussie Rules is now the second-most played code among women and girls in Australia (after soccer). The AFLW season attracted more than 317,000 spectators in 2025.

As Miller’s research progressed, she became aware that the competition came about not through the work of one individual but through collaboration and the passing of the baton.

Sarah Giles, who stepped in to direct Strong Is the New Pretty at short notice when Lee Lewis had to withdraw for family reasons, describes it as “a very clever play”. “Much like Suzie’s other work, she smuggles in the politics. She’s using football as a vehicle to talk about equality on a much bigger level. So the play becomes this very inspiring example of how many, many women over time fought for the right to be treated as equals, and succeeded.”

Like her acclaimed earlier plays, Strong Is the New Pretty celebrates a particularly Australian brand of female grit. “There is something remarkable about Australian women and I just wanted to write this for them,” she says.

Brisbane-based actor Ingram, who plays several of the play’s more than 50 characters, says Miller is extremely open and collaborative for a playwright the whole world is watching right now.

“We have a lot of big, open discussions about things. She’s a font of knowledge and she pours all of that into her work. We’re really lucky to have her in the room with us so we can ask questions.”

Giles says Miller’s women “have this incredible ability to hold court … and I don’t just mean that in a lawyer sense. She has this way of connecting an audience to a female character that’s so authentic and immediate and present.”

Trained in science and law, Miller didn’t see a professional play until she was in her early 20s; she learnt her craft at UNSW and NIDA while working as a human rights and youth lawyer.

She famously had to choose (in 2009) between becoming a magistrate and accepting a writing residency at the National Theatre in London. London won out, and she moved over with her two young children and her husband, barrister (now High Court judge) Robert Beech-Jones.

“I gave up my whole legal profession to be a playwright. That doesn’t mean I knew I’d get there because I didn’t. I worked like an absolute dog. But, you know, I always dreamt that maybe, you never know.”

She had already written about 30 plays when Prima Facie premiered at Sydney’s 105-seat Stables Theatre in the Griffin Theatre Company production starring Sheridan Harbridge and directed by Lee Lewis.

Prima Facie homes in on a criminal barrister, Tessa, who defends people accused of sexual assault. When Tessa is herself raped she experiences the way the legal process puts victims on trial. Giles recalls being “knocked for six” by it.

“What I found extraordinary was how Suzie and Lee and Sheridan placed the audience on a particular side of the argument and put us in a warm, comfortable bath that we all knew,” the director says. “And then, through the shifting experience of that central character, we were pushed to the other side of that argument.”

The production toured the country, and Harbridge has just wrapped encore seasons in Melbourne and Sydney.

When the play opened in London, with Killing Eve’s Jodie Comer in the lead, it inspired barristers and judges to set up TESSA (The Examination of Serious Sexual Assault) to spearhead legislative changes. The National Theatre’s filmed version is now mandatory viewing for high court judges in Northern Ireland.

Prima Facie has been staged in more than 50 countries and translated into more than 30 languages. Miller has seen it performed in Greek, Italian, Norwegian, German and Mandarin (“which was magnificent”).

Comer won the 2023 Olivier Award for best actress, and Miller won for best new play over such household names as Aaron Sorkin (The West Wing) and Peter Morgan (The Crown). It was a night Miller won’t forget in a hurry.

“Someone did say to me, just remember that when they make the announcement, the camera is still on you. One time a very famous playwright who didn’t win went, ‘Oh, shit’. Don’t make that mistake.

“I was thinking, there’s no way I’m going to win this. And then they said my name and I went, ‘Oh, f---’! It was even worse!”

Prima Facie’s National Theatre production got a worldwide cinema release but now there’s an actual movie version: a UK-Australian co-production under the helm of BAFTA-winning director Susanna White (Andor), starring Wicked’s Cynthia Erivo.

“I went with my husband the other week. We were both crying at the end of it,” Miller says. “You sort of hold your breath through the second half, the whole way through … even though I know exactly what’s going to happen because I wrote the screenplay.”

Miller also adapted Prima Facie as a novel in 2023, and it’s an indication of its impact on the legal profession that lawyers for an accused rapist in Victoria tried – unsuccessfully – to argue for a mistrial on the basis of one of the jurors bringing a copy into the jury room.

Her new book is published on September 29. It’s the novel version of Inter Alia, the play that opened at the National Theatre as Rosamund Pike’s first stage role in 14 years, selling out before rehearsals had even begun. (Pike, like Comer, won an Olivier; the production heads to Broadway in December.)

A companion piece to Prima Facie, Inter Alia also tackles sexual assault law but from the point of view of a judge who prides herself on kindly treatment of alleged victims under cross-examination. Her perspective is rattled when someone close to her is charged with a serious crime.

I tell Miller I have sons, and read the book in an escalating mood of panic. She says that Inter Alia (the play) has spurred interrogation of the manosphere.

“It’s more than just a space that’s ugly. What it’s also doing to boys is actually co-opting their sexuality and their way of being in the world, telling them that there’s only one form of masculinity that matters.”

She is heartened by the level of discussion the play has opened up.

“People email me, saying, ‘We all went out for dinner afterwards and we talked about it at length’ …

“I’m as guilty as anyone. You know, raising teenagers, I never thought to talk to them about what porn they might consume. Because it’s not a comfortable conversation.”

Miller was shocked at how much she has enjoyed novel writing, “because I’m such a theatre animal”. Twenty-six years as a dramatist was a great preparation for writing novels, she says. “You know how to keep an audience’s attention. How to keep the plot moving forward.”

Miller’s other legal hit prior to Inter Alia was her one-woman portrait of US Supreme Court trailblazer Ruth Bader Ginsburg, RGB: Of Many, One. Its extended Australian tour gave Heather Mitchell a late-career star vehicle.

The play is finally to be staged in America. “I’m looking forward to seeing how the New Yorkers respond to it because, of course, she was one of them.”

The fact Miller will have two shows playing in New York next year, and that it’s merely a sidenote to this story, gets me thinking again about Miller and her imperial phase.

But I’m conscious this is the kind of phallocentric, male-journo thinking that’s at odds with the kind of heroism she is depicting in Strong Is the New Pretty.

“There is no single central character, which is what’s beautiful about this,” Giles says. “It sort of starts from a singular perspective and then refracts out as you gather more and more people who were part of that story.

“It’s what we’re trying to mirror in the staging of the play. So it becomes about a bunch of women coming together in a theatrical sense, creating something extraordinary out of nothing.”

“I think that’s how women manage often, how they actually get things done,” Miller says. “And I’m not saying it’s better or worse than the way men manage but [for men] there’s more of a hero’s journey where men rise to the top, and it’s like they were the one person that got it done …

“A new play is where you all hold hands and dream it into being. Because, you know, everything is brand new. And we’ve got a lot of incredible optimism and positivity and talent in that room.

“In a way, the women in the room are reminding me why I wrote the play.”

Strong Is the New Pretty is at Brisbane’s QPAC, September 1-19; Canberra Theatre Centre, September 24-26; Geelong Arts Centre, October 8-11; and the Drama Theatre, Sydney Opera House, October 22-December 5. Inter Alia is published on September 29 by Picador Australia. Prima Facie, starring Cynthia Erivo, premieres at this month’s Toronto International Film Festival.
