‘Someone is smoking weed’: Sabalenka halts US Open match due to cannabis smell

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 21:32:56 GMT

‘It’s tricky to handle when you’re trying to compete’

Alcaraz into fourth round after straight sets victory

Aryna Sabalenka briefly stopped her match at the US Open to complain about the strong smell of cannabis on her court as she comfortably reached the fourth round in New York.

Sabalenka, the two-time defending champion, continued her attempts to rebuild her form as she overcame a challenging test from Kamilla Rakhimova before winning 6-3, 6-4.

Early in the match, a smiling Sabalenka approached the chair umpire Eva Asderaki-Moore while leading 3-0, stating “Someone is smoking weed, do you mind … because it’s so strong,” Afterwards, Sabalenka laughed as she described her interaction with the umpire: “I was, like, Guys, you can do whatever, you can smoke whatever, you can relax as much as you can, but please, do not do it around the tennis courts. It’s a bit tricky to handle that smell while you’re trying to compete at your best.”

Cannabis is legal in New York and weed can be smelled around tournament grounds, as is the case all around the city. This has become a common talking point at the US Open in recent years. Although Sabalenka initially seemed to believe that the smoke may have been coming from a spectator in or right by the crowd, she later said she was unclear about its origins but the smell of cannabis was stronger than she had ever smelt it during her years of competing in New York: “That strong, yeah. Also, because it was a bit windy. I don’t know if it was, like, coming from the crowd or was from the outside because the wind blows it into the stadium. I don’t know. I just hope they’re going to be a bit more aware of that stuff,” she said.

Most importantly for Sabalenka, she has returned to the round of 16 without dropping a set and she appears to be finding some rhythm on the court. This victory was spearheaded by a stellar serving performance, with the Belarusian serving 10 aces and facing zero break points. She had arrived in New York in some of her most difficult form for years, having failed to reach a final since spectacularly winning Indian Wells and Miami back-to-back in March. Sabalenka will lose her No 1 ranking, which she has held for 97 weeks, unless she wins her third US Open title in a row and Elena Rybakina, the world No 2, loses before the semi-finals.

Although Sabalenka has put together a series of encouraging performances on-court, the added pressure on her shoulders has perhaps been revealed elsewhere. After her dominant second round win over Polina Iatcenko, Sabalenka clashed with a reporter in her post-match press conference when the reporter described her week before the US Open as “parties and fun”.

This was the second time during the tournament that a reporter had referenced pre-tournament obligations leading up to the US Open, prompting a forceful response from Sabalenka: “You guys are, like, a joke,” she said. “‘Parties, fun …’ like, why would you even say that? Why would you even think about that? What kind of question is that? Just because I posted, like, some activities with brands, and you think that I’ve been partying, not training?”

Sabalenka eventually ended the lengthy, heated exchange by imploring the reporter to: “Think before you say stuff.”

A tougher test awaits Sabalenka in the fourth round as she faces the home favourite Taylor Townsend, who followed up her great run to the fourth round last year with another excellent tournament in New York. Townsend defeated the 15th seed Diana Shnaider 6-2, 6-7 (3), 6-3 to return to the fourth round.

after newsletter promotion

Daniil Medvedev, the 2021 men’s singles champion, also continued to find his feet in New York as he reached the fourth round with a 6-4, 6-4, 6-4 victory over the 29th seed Arthur Rinderknetch.

Carlos Alcaraz, the men’s defending champion, continues to grow in confidence on his return to tennis from a four-and-a-half month injury layoff and he moved into the fourth round with a 6-3, 6-4, 6-1 win over Wu Yibing of China. Alcaraz, who until the tournament had not competed since injuring his right wrist at the beginning of April, had to hold his nerve and problem solve during some tight moments in the first two sets. However, he elevated his game in those decisive moments and he continues to show that he will be difficult to defeat despite how early it is in his comeback.

Alcaraz will next face the 20th seed Tommy Paul, an American player, who overcame the 15th seed Alexander Bublik 6-4, 3-6, 6-7(4), 6-1, 6-3: “To be honest, I’m better than I thought,” Alcaraz said. “Physically, I thought I was going to be bad after the first match but I’m recovering really well, I’m doing great things off the court out be in a good shape and right now I think my level is good. I’ve got the rhythm of the competition. Every time I step on to the court, I give it my all.”

St Helens miss out on playoffs after Charnley news caps Leigh’s perfect night

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 21:26:18 GMT

Leigh 48-10 St Helens

Charnley scores and agrees confirms extension

It ended not so much with a bang, but with a whimper. One of rugby league’s most extraordinary streaks has felt as though it was coming to an inevitable end for quite some time but as it transpired, St Helens’ 64-year run of making the playoffs ultimately concluded in a manner that summarises their fall from grace.

You have to go back to 1962 to find an end-of-season playoff series that did not include one of rugby league’s true heavyweight clubs. In the Super League era, they have won 10 titles and were champions of the world as recently as 2023. But this, sadly, is a shadow of that side – and indeed that club.

They have been outsiders all season long for the playoffs, and their hopes were emphatically ended here against a team who themselves have genuine Old Trafford aspirations. Without over a dozen first-team players, Saints’ defensive frailties that have plagued them all season were exposed brutally yet again to ensure they will finish seventh. History for all the wrong reasons.

But this was just as significant a night for Leigh as it was for St Helens. These two teams have been on contrasting journeys in recent years with Saints slowly slipping away from being the best team in the world, and the Leopards rising year-on-year to become a genuine Super League threat in 2026.

They scored eight tries, four in each half, to blow Saints away in crucial moments and book their playoff spot. They could yet finish fourth and get home advantage in the opening week should they beat Wakefield next Friday. After a slow start, Leigh look genuine contenders.

“We’ve got to rely on other teams winning over the weekend and then it’s still mathematically a chance,” their coach, Adrian Lam, said. “But we would have taken this a third of the way through the season so I’ve got to appreciate that.” His side were far too good when it mattered here, with their attack in devastating form all evening.

Super League’s all-time top try-scorer, Josh Charnley, opened the scoring with his 281st career try before David Armstrong doubled the lead soon after. There was a brief flurry of resistance from Saints but tries for Jacob Douglas and Tristan Sailor proved to be a false dawn. They collapsed again as half-time approached, with two more Leigh tries making it 24-10.

From there, it always felt unlikely at best that Saints could keep their season alive going into next weekend. “The group are very disappointed but they should be proud,” their interim coach, Eamon O’Carroll said. “The scoreline blew out but there were some St Helens traits in there. But there needs to be changes now.”

Those changes will be headlined by the arrival of the Australia coach, Kevin Walters, in 2027 – and he has plenty to work on based on this display. Leigh put the result beyond doubt as the hour mark approached when the outstanding Umyla Hanley scoring his second after Edwin Ipape barged over from close range.

The race of the night came in the men’s 1500m as the Australian Cameron Myers found his way out of a box on the home straight, swerved between Jakob Ingebrigtsen and Phanuel Koech, and then got his nose in front to win in 3:30.14.

This Diamond League final also doubled as the 50th memorial meeting to be staged in memory of Ivo Van Damme, the brilliant Belgian athlete who won silver medals over 800m and 1500m at the 1976 Olympics before dying in a car accident later that year, aged just 22.

Lewis had taken his place next to the king in time to see the Jamaican world champion Oblique Seville take the men’s 100m in 9.90sec, recovering from a poor start to beat the Commonwealth champion Emmanuel Eseme by three-hundredths of a second.

If Ipswich’s defending was less than watertight, Liverpool’s attackers were full of the speed and invention they sorely lacked for much of last season.

Once Barcola arrived in the second half, those velocity levels increased yet higher, Liverpool playing the attacking football, high on risk and entertainment, that the appointment of Iraola promised.

Travelling Liverpool fans were made to wait for their first glimpse of £123m Barcola, his being benched adding further suspense to a deal that took an entire summer to complete. Making his first start, Ronald Araújo, the former Barcelona captain in the right-back position Liverpool failed to fortify before the window closed.

Ipswich, having broken the home duck they waited until 30 December to break two seasons ago in their opening match with Sunderland, looked to show the “emotional discipline” their manager said they lacked in losing 5-2 at Old Trafford. Little of that was in evidence in their ruinous opening spell.

How long will Iraola’s doctrines take to embed? Perhaps not as long as feared. The club’s suit class, particularly departing sporting director Richard Hughes, has absorbed sustained heat for a botched squad construction. Though Isak, the most expensive player signed under Hughes, looks – at last – to be flowering. To follow his strike against Nottingham Forest, he had scored twice by the 10th minute. Assisted for both by barrelling surges from Cody Gakpo, who might have been at Manchester City or Tottenham had the runes been right, the finishes were of the gold standard Liverpool invested so heavily in.

After Victor Muñoz set off a long run stopped only by Issa Diop’s last-man tackle, Julio Enciso controlled the ball, standing on it, as if calling for calm from his colleagues.

Isak, who had a third first-half goal disallowed for offside, was making the runs that made his reputation, looking nothing like the sorry figure he cut in his debut, lost season before injury ruled him out for five months. Ipswich were being toyed with, and a no-look pass from their captain, Dara O’Shea, straight to Gakpo, betrayed a collective cognitive dissonance. Florian Wirtz becoming involved with the tricks and flicks offered another pointer that last summer’s huge Liverpool outlay may not have been so wasteful as it appeared in Arne Slot’s dog days. Iraola’s appointment came with a reputation for improving players, and should the Basque get the best from a player in a similar price bracket to Barcola and Isak, then his pronouncement he is happy with his squad will ring truer than it sounded this week.

Liverpool’s second half began with another Gakpo surge and a free Alexis Mac Allister header, as Ipswich looked to build of what had been an improved end of the first 45. Another gap in the Liverpool squad is a commanding defensive midfielder, and Enciso often found such empty spaces. Virgil van Dijk and Jérémy Jacquet mirrored each other in their calm, even if the apprentice did lose his cool a couple of times when confronted with the physical presence of Emersonn. Beyond the break, with O’Neil in full flow, barking at players and officials alike from the sidelines, Ipswich upped the rough stuff, more confrontational, less admiring of their opponent’s higher skill levels.

Alexia Putellas begins WSL ride as London City outclass Manchester United

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 20:51:57 GMT

There are few scenarios since Millwall Lionesses broke away from Millwall and became London City Lionesses that would have felt more surreal than the idea of Alexia Putellas captaining the side to a statement win in a Women’s Super League season opener in Bromley just seven years later.

Here we are though. Referees have to get used to the former Barcelona captain stooping to pick up the coin after the toss, as is her custom. Players must get used to eyes and cameras looking past them to focus on the influential No 11, and the two-time Ballon d’Or winner has to get used to playing with players not drilled in a very specific style of play from such an early age.

Of course it’s a step down to go from the four-time European champions to a team embarking on their second season in the WSL, but off the pitch, with owner Michele Kang’s commitment to giving female athletes the best of everything, the difference will be more negligible, even before the approved new world-class training facility is built.

Bromley may be about as far from the colossus of a stadium that is the Camp Nou as is possible, but the 5,402 sell-out was far closer to the average attendance of 6,168 that the European champions commanded across the course of last season, with most of their games played at the more modest Johan Cruyff stadium.

Putellas led the team out to a heroes welcome at the sold-out home of Bromley FC, her steely stare only broken to crack a quick smile and share some words with the mascot gripping her hand.

The last club game Putellas played was in the blazing sun in Copenhagen as Barcelona outplayed Lyon to secure a fourth Champions League title. In this corner of the outskirts of London, the midfielder experienced her first proper taste of her new reality and we got our first proper taste of ours. At 32 and with her very best years likely behind her, it is still an utter joy to have the magical player in the WSL. It was a solid rather than showstopper performance, Putellas outshone by teammates such as Rosa Kafaji and Lucía Corrales, who was unfortunately taken off late on after overstretching for the ball.

It is the ‘Putellas pull’ that demanded this fixture between the heavily invested-in side and the barely backed Manchester United be broadcast live on Sky Sports to open the WSL season.

Regardless of what you think of her movements in women’s football, Kang – who walked the perimeter of the stadium prior to kick-off taking photos with fans in her ‘Kang 27’ emblazoned home shirt – is the antithesis to Jim Ratcliffe, whose dismal references to his women’s team contrast sharply with the woman who is ideologically invested in giving female athletes the best of every thing because it is the right thing to do.

In the first half, Kang’s charges were a reflection of what that commitment can do to players. London City were on the front foot from the off, with Corrales forcing a save from Phallon Tullis-Joyce inside four minutes. Eder Maestre, tasked with gelling a squad stacked with new players, including former England goalkeeper Mary Earps, who was named on the bench for the opening fixture and is understood to be nursing an injury picked up in pre-season, had said the identity he wants to create for the side is “related to all those things we felt when we were playing football as children”.

That ethos was evident in their play, despite not always being pretty. They pressed and attacked aggressively, and that they broke the deadlock was not surprising.

Trump’s ‘retribution’ could now include Falklands as favor to Milei – and revenge on the UK

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 20:21:52 GMT

US president suggests he might support his Argentinian acolyte’s drive to reclaim sovereignty of disputed islands

Donald Trump has long embraced vengeance. “I am your retribution,” he declared to an admiring audience at the 2023 Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) as he commenced his march back to the White House.

It is unlikely Argentina, and far-flung holdovers of the former British empire, were on the US president’s mind at the time.

But the tide of international events in the past three and a half years have turned Trump’s vindictive mindset to the advantage of Javier Milei, the boisterous rightwing Argentinian president.

Trump’s notorious fixation with payback was almost entirely the trigger for Milei’s televised address to his fellow Argentinians on Thursday, as he stated his intention to reopen his country’s claim to a set of windswept islands in the south Atlantic – known to Britain as the Falklands, and to Argentina as the Malvinas.

The centuries-old dispute over the islands’ sovereignty has lain dormant since 1982, when the two countries fought a brief, but bloody, conflict that began after Argentina’s ruling military dictatorship invaded the territory.

Britain reclaimed them after troops in a naval taskforce dispatched by the then prime minister, Margaret Thatcher – ironically lionized by Milei as a political exemplar and inspiration – stormed the territory and eventually forced Argentina’s surrender.

An uneasy peace has reined in the generation since, although Argentina, which returned to democracy the year after the conflict, has never renounced its claim to the isles – despite the adamant insistence of their less than 2,000 inhabitants that they remain British.

This week, however, Trump suggested he is reconsidering US support for Britain’s sovereignty over the Falkland Islands. Why would the president go out on a limb to threaten this fragile peace? And why now?

Milei jumped on Trump’s comment that he was “reviewing” the US’s longstanding neutral stance on the territory’s sovereignty, which amounts to a de facto recognition of Britain’s control.

Fueling Trump’s animus is grievance that Britain, under former prime minister Keir Starmer, declined to support the US president’s decision to go to war on Iran, another irony given that country’s deep-rooted suspicions of Britain and its imperial past.

The president’s obsession that allies declined to help him in a war he never consulted them on runs deep and wide – from Westminster to Seoul – and has the potential to upend US relationships around the globe, if unchecked.

And Milei’s attempt to capitalize on Trump’s vengeance underlines the potential for ripple effects of this war to reach waters far beyond the Gulf.

In what has become a repetitive refrain, Trump laid bare his sense of wounded affront in an interview with a rightwing British cable channel on Thursday.

“Your country was not there to help me,” he told GB News. “We didn’t need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader, ‘Why don’t you send a couple of ships?’ He said, ‘We don’t have any.’ It was pretty sad, the whole thing.”

Milei’s opportunism could also be used by Trump as a bargaining chip – to lever more money from the cash-strapped UK treasury for defense spending and Nato contributions, after the new British chancellor of the exchequer, John Healey, recently suggested that it might not reach increased spending targets.

It is a sorry pass for the “special relationship”, fostered through alliances in two worlds wars and deepened during the cold war and subsequent conflicts. Yet Britain is hardly alone in feeling the heat of a wrathful Trump.

Vengeance has been targeted in recent months at numerous other allies, now regarded with more hostility by the White House than traditional adversaries such as Russia and China.

Annual joint military exercises with South Korea – a vital ally of Washington since the Korean war broke out in 1950 – were suddenly scaled down and cut short by six days last month, on Trump’s orders, because of his irritation that the Seoul government declined to join the fight against Iran.

He has repeatedly threatened to bomb or “blow up” the tiny Gulf kingdom of Oman, which has had friendly ties with the US for 200 years, if it impedes his efforts to reopen the strait of Hormuz, which Iran has closed to most commercial shipping.

The White House also announced the withdrawal of 5,000 US troops from Germany after the country’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, rebuffed pressure to get involved in the Iran conflict and said Trump had been “humiliated” in the conflict.

Threats of retribution have also been aimed at Spain, which has resisted pressure to boost defense spending, and Italy, whose prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, was a former Trump ally.

But Milei, a self-styled “anarcho-capitalist” who has paraded with a chainsaw to signify his attitude to public spending and attended Trump’s 2025 inauguration, remains on the US president’s good side.

Last year, the administration extended his troubled government a $20bn loan guarantee to stabilize the infamously shaky Argentinian economy – but premised the money on Milei’s party defeating the leftist opposition in forthcoming congressional elections, which it duly did.

This time there are no guarantees, other than that of never-ending turbulence at the hands of Trump. Such rough currents may be the “winds of change” Milei referenced in Thursday’s speech, delivered – Trump-style – with his cabinet members flanking him.

But he may have been aware the phrase had other, historical connotations – evoking the words of a famous speech in 1960 by then British prime minister Harold Macmillan in Cape Town, heralding independence for Britain’s former colonial possession in Africa.

“The wind of change is blowing through this continent,” Macmillan said then. “Whether we like it or not, this growth of national consciousness is a political fact.”

In his address, Milei suggested the sun was setting on Britain, just as it once did on its empire, citing multiple crises of a migratory, demographic and economic nature that are unlikely to be resolved. “It is clear that they are on a path of decline,” he pronounced.

He did not mention his own falling political popularity – a factor which may also have played a key role in the former military junta’s decision to seize the islands in 1982, as opposition grew against the backdrop of mass disappearances of political dissidents and multiple human rights abuses.

Then, too, Britain was grappling with tensions over immigration and race riots, soaring unemployment and long-term economic decline that Thatcher had been elected pledging to reverse. In the late winter of 1982, there was little sign that she was capable of doing so – until the Falklands conflict sparked a sudden upturn in her political fortunes.

But she had the solid backing of the special relationship, and her ideological soulmate, Ronald Reagan, in the White House. Andy Burnham, Britain’s newly installed Labour prime minister, must contend with the chill wind emanating from the menacing and destabilizing presence of Trump.

Kimi Antonelli: ‘The F1 environment is great but at times it can be very brutal’

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 19:00:15 GMT

Before his home grand prix, the Mercedes driver opens up on his rocky debut season and quest to become the first Italian world champion since 1953

If Kimi Antonelli feels any pressure as the favourite to take the Formula One world championship at just 20 years old and in his second year in the sport, it is imperceptible. He admits F1 can be brutal but a thing of beauty too, a labour of love for the Italian who has been a revelation this season.

Compelling and brilliant, that he is also endearing and likable marks Antonelli out as more than just a potential champion. Sitting in the Mercedes motorhome it is impossible not to be struck by how young he looks, the tousled hair, engaging smile and eyes gleaming with youthful enthusiasm. He speaks with an open candour, the air of a kid in a sweetshop who still can’t quite believe all those sherbet lemons are there for the taking.

It is striking precisely because so many F1 drivers lose this sense of exhilaration all too soon in their careers, and it is almost infectious. Yet for all that his F1 career has been brief after making his debut for Mercedes last season, it has been quite the ride since he climbed into a kart as a five-year-old.

“I do what I love to do, it’s something that I’ve dreamt of for such a long time and I want to enjoy it fully,” he says with the smile that it is very much the Antonelli default expression.

“But it’s different, because growing up you just see the races, the drivers driving, you don’t see what’s behind all of that. Last year I probably would have said different things compared to this year, especially because I think the F1 environment is very brutal. It’s great, but at times it can be very, very brutal.

“I feel like last year I suffered a bit from that when there was a lot of speculation about my future, it was difficult for me, but thanks to the team and to my family and all the support I had, I was able to overcome that, but that was a thing that as a kid I didn’t see it coming until I actually experienced it.”

A rocky debut season and public debate over his future in F1 – for all that it was never entertained at Mercedes – was borne with great fortitude and he has come out the other side a stronger character and delivered emphatically on his great promise. Antonelli leads the drivers’ championship, ahead of his Mercedes teammate, George Russell, and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton by a whopping 59 points.

The youngster has learned hard and he has learned fast. When he made a mistake on the penultimate lap at last season’s Qatar Grand Prix, with Lando Norris passing him, he was subjected to a torrent of abuse and absurd accusations that he had moved over for the British driver, who went on to take the title.

“After Qatar all the, let’s say, the hate … what was hard for me in Qatar was getting blamed for something that I would never do,” he says. “To get really criticised publicly, openly about something that I would never do on purpose, it was tough.”

Antonelli is admirable because he does not shy away from addressing these questions. He is self-aware to an extent that belies his years. If he must still be considered the kid in F1, he wears a personable maturity more comfortably than many of his contemporaries in the sport.

On track his driving has spoken for itself this season, not least in the five consecutive wins he delivered from the Chinese to Monaco grands prix, which has put him in such a dominant championship position. His team, from Toto Wolff down, recognise they have not only a special talent but also a special person, for whom being in F1 is a very simple and very human equation.

“I always try to be myself,” he says. “This is the way I am, I feel like it’s good with the mechanics, with the team, to joke around a little bit when it’s the right time. Just to create an even better environment and I think if you’re able also to connect in that way with the team all of us are able to enjoy even more the weekend together, working together.

“Of course there are certain situations where I might be a bit more serious than usual but at the end of the day myself is being positive, smiling, having fun, joking with the mechanics, with the team in general and then just driving the car as fast as I can.”

At which he excels. The competitive verve of his driving style is enthralling, even as the bravura approach might obscure what is clearly an immaculate touch in a controlled, intuitive balancing of a car at its very limit. It has put him in unprecedented territory.

The last Italian to win the world championship was Alberto Ascari in 1953 and the country has embraced their wunderkind in the German marque wholeheartedly. For all that Ferrari is a religion in Italy, in Monza Antonelli has brought Mercedes into the faith.

Yet the young man remains so grounded. That his father, Marco, a former driver, has played such a huge part in his career has been key and for which he deserves much credit as Antonelli acknowledges what is clearly a fundamental bond.

“My dad always comes to most of the races, we have a really strong relationship, he’s kind of my rock,” Antonelli says. “I feel like my dad knows me inside out. I always like to discuss with him because it’s what we’ve been used to since I was in karting.

“He’s going to give me advice and then if I decide to listen, good, but if I don’t decide to listen, it’s OK as well. He always tells me that I need to be also free to take my own decisions about things, that I don’t need to be stuck by what he says.”

This weekend Antonelli and Mercedes have already made one decision which is to put the title tilt first. The Italian is taking a raft of new engine components for which he will receive a penalty that means he will start from the back of the grid. He recognises that the overtaking opportunities at Monza made this the right choice, even as he deals with the weight on his shoulders as the home hero.

“Being Italian I know how we can think, how we can react and I know as an Italian when we get excited about something we create expectations – very high expectations,” he says. “But then when something bad happens then we’re like completely the opposite, we tend to exaggerate things. So I’m aware of the expectations, but I’m also happy about the support that I received.”

The bigger picture is the plan for this engaging young man, who only turned 20 late last month. Should it work out, and few would bet against Antonelli at this point, he hopes the Mercedes team will be singing from his songsheet of the Italian national anthem when he is world champion.

“I mean, they’ve got to learn it,” he says, eyes gleaming. “If I achieve the goal by the end of the year then I’m going to print the lyrics so then they can.”

Chelsea hit bullseye with Morgan Rogers as Arsenal rue what might have been

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 19:00:14 GMT

The Gunners will have a look at what they could have won when the former Villa man lines up against them, having made a flying start for Xabi Alonso’s team

Chelsea thought they had little chance of signing Morgan Rogers at the start of the summer. Xabi Alonso and the club’s recruitment team had the England international as a priority target but a deal seemed unlikely. Chelsea had endured a disappointing season, missing out on European football after finishing 10th, and their expectation was that Rogers would leave Aston Villa for Arsenal.

It was towards the end of the World Cup that Chelsea were made aware of a window of opportunity. Although Arsenal could claim to be London’s top dogs after winning the Premier League they dithered in talks with Villa, raising the prospect of another club stepping in.

Mikel Arteta talked about being bold in the market after Arsenal’s defeat by Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League final. Arteta wanted more in attack. A new option on the left was a priority; Leandro Trossard and Gabriel Martinelli were up for sale and everything pointed towards Arsenal making their move for Rogers at the end of June.

Yet the lines became blurred. Arsenal had a fee of £80m in mind, while Villa wanted more, particularly after Nottingham Forest sold Elliot Anderson to Manchester City for £116m. Time dragged on. How serious were Arsenal? There was also interest in Julián Alvarez, Vinícius Júnior and Bradley Barcola. Villa waited and the price for Rogers went up. Arsenal, beaten to the punch in the end, will have a look at what they could have won when Chelsea and Rogers visit the Emirates Stadium on Sunday.

Chelsea were decisive. They were tracking Rogers before he left Middlesbrough for Villa in February 2024. Joe Shields, one of Chelsea’s five sporting directors, worked with Rogers at Manchester City’s academy. The signing was not done on a whim. Chelsea have a good relationship with Villa’s owners and moved quickly after opening club-to-club talks a day after Rogers played in England’s World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina. The fee was £117m and Chelsea did not struggle to convince Rogers. Alonso wooed him and the deal was confirmed five days after negotiations began.

There was no last-ditch move from Arsenal. They signed Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge for £34m two days later and focused on other targets. When the window closed, though, Arteta’s options on the left looked a little light. Martinelli and Trossard left but only Tzolis arrived. Eberechi Eze and Noni Madueke are alternatives. It is hard not to feel that Arsenal could have done with Rogers, even though Chelsea have paid a high price for him.

It remains to be seen whether the 24-year-old can prove he merits becoming the third-most expensive player in English football history. For context, the fee is the consequence of the market threatening to rise out of control and the money spent on many players starting to feel meaningless. It is worth pointing out, too, that money flowed back and forth between Chelsea and Villa all summer. Even so the price will follow Rogers around, so it is just as well he has made an excellent start.

Rogers has been involved in four of Chelsea’s seven goals in their first two league games. He scored in the 3-2 win at Fulham and later combined with João Pedro to set up Cole Palmer’s goal. He created Pedro Neto’s goal in last weekend’s 4-3 win over Brighton and played a key role when Jorrel Hato played in João Pedro to score.

Chelsea have thrilled in attack so far, João Pedro, Rogers and Palmer combining to devastating effect. Alonso, an adaptable manager, wants more control but his transitional football has been a delight. Chelsea were mannered and controlled during Enzo Maresca’s time in charge. It is felt that Alonso has recognised the Premier League’s shift towards power and athleticism. Rogers fits into the Spaniard’s system. Thomas Tuchel loves Rogers for his connectivity and pressing. It is significant that England’s energy levels rose in their quarter-final against Norway after the introduction of Rogers and Djed Spence late in the second half.

Chelsea needed more strength, more speed. Rogers, able to play anywhere in attacking midfield or as a No 8, looks a better fit in Alonso’s 3-4-2-1 than Enzo Fernández, sold this week to Manchester City for £125m. He has played with Palmer as one of the No 10s but has a responsibility to drift left, a role that is unlikely to have suited Fernández. Arsenal’s impeccable defence will be tested by Chelsea’s front three.

The Rogers-Palmer partnership has clicked. They are old friends and banter over the “ice cold” celebration. Rogers is a bubbly character and can get on with anyone. Chelsea are keen to improve the culture in the dressing room. It is felt that Alonso has shifted the mood after last year’s rebellions. The squad are united. It is one of the reasons why Chelsea decided to sell Fernández on deadline day. They did not need the headache of reintegrating the Argentinian.

This is a fresh start. The signing of Rogers, who was the Professional Footballers’ Association’s young player of the year in 2025, was a sign of Chelsea’s intent. Rogers was one of the best players in the Premier League last season. He grew under Unai Emery and scored when Villa beat Freiburg in the Europa League final in May.

It was one of Rogers’ less eye-catching goals: a clever jab at the near post from a low cross. There was a period last season when he could not stop scoring from long range but Rogers has spoken about wanting scruffier goals and he arrived at the far post to open his Chelsea account against Fulham.

Rogers is embracing the challenge. At Arsenal he would have been slotting into the finished article. Arsenal have reached the summit. Chelsea are beginning their climb under Alonso. Rogers, who has played in the Championship and had a loan in League One, rather liked the idea of starting lower down.

Judge declares mistrial in Lindsay Clancy case after jury deadlocked again

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 18:41:51 GMT

Defense lawyer had asked for time to request emergency stay after jury was split 11 to one

Lindsay Clancy murder trial: live updates

The judge in the trial of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three young children, has declared a mistrial after the jury could not reach a unanimous verdict and remained deadlocked after a week of deliberations.

Jurors in Plymouth state court spent more than 38 hours in deliberations over the charges against the 36-year-old mom, which came on the heels of a weeks-long trial that directed national attention to maternal mental health issues that can occur postpartum.

The 12-person jury was made up of nine women and three men and, according to the notes given to the court, was split 11 to one.

After the jury returned without a verdict for the third time, Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial but was interrupted by a last-minute request from Clancy’s lead defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, who requested one hour to petition for an emergency stay to seek relief from a superior court judge.

That emergency filing with the Massachusetts supreme judicial court asked a single justice to order Sullivan to further question the juror arguing the juror was “biased” and, per jury notes, unwilling to follow the court’s instructions on reasonable doubt.

“Intervention is necessary in this case to avoid an avoidable mistrial of a case that is so time and labor intensive and that has captured so much public attention,” the filing reads, which also claimed that the court had “abdicated its responsibility to ensure the integrity of the jury”.

The filing also asked that the juror be barred from further deliberations if Sullivan determined that they could not follow the instructions issued by the court.

“A mistrial at this point is entirely avoidable, but only if the court does its job,” the filing says.

Additionally, the filing claimed the court “reflects a bias against those who suffer from debilitating mental illness”, arguing that mental illness is a “protected category” under the fifth and 14th amendments of the US constitution.

The filing was discussed with the Massachusetts supreme court justice Dalila Argaez Wendlandt during a Zoom hearing that was open to the public for viewing. Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague summarized what happened with the jury and their repeated notes indicating a deadlock before defense attorney Dana Goldblatt argued that the supreme judicial court had the discretion to order the trial court to make the inquiry of the juror. Wendlandt then said she would take the matter under advisement.

The petition was subsequently denied.

Clancy, a former neonatal and delivery nurse, had been accused of strangling her three children, Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, in the family’s Duxbury home in January 2023.

Prosecutors argued in opening statements that Clancy had “coldly and efficiently executed” her children, doing so with “no hesitation, with deliberate premeditation and extreme atrocity and cruelty” after she “drew her husband out of the house, their father, so that she had the opportunity and the time to carry out these murders”.

But Clancy’s defense team argued she was “suffering from psychosis” when she killed her children and allegedly attempted suicide by jumping from an upper window in her home, which left her partly paralyzed. Reddington told jurors that Clancy suffered from postpartum depression after giving birth to her third child, Callan, and been prescribed a cocktail of medications.

“This is a young woman who, with her husband, tried very hard to get the help she needed,” he said.

Clancy has not denied that she had killed her children but her not guilty plea was predicated on a lack of criminal responsibility because, as her defense team said, she was suffering from postpartum psychosis, which included auditory hallucinations that commanded her to harm her children, and undiagnosed bipolar disorder.

Under Massachusetts law, the defendant must have “retained the substantial capacity to appreciate the wrongfulness or criminality of their conduct and to conform their conduct to the requirements of the law” in order to be found guilty.

Throughout the trial, jurors heard from Clancy’s former husband Patrick Clancy, her mother and aunt, and an array of psychologists and treating physicians. The court heard that Clancy had been prescribed 13 different medications for anxiety and sleep, which the defense said may have exacerbated her symptoms of depression.

Clancy had checked herself into psychiatric clinic in the weeks before the killings. Later, on 24 January 2023, she had sent her then husband out for food and to collect pharmacy medications. In that time, police say she strangled their children with exercise bands. Her ability to orchestrate a window of time to carry out the killings, prosecutors argued, was evidence of premeditation.

Before resting his case last week, Reddington called forensic psychiatrist Dr Phillip Resnick to testify that Clancy had “severe depression” and a history of anxiety, which increased after the birth of her children to the point that she “felt she couldn’t function”.

“At the time of the crime on Jan 24, 2023, Ms Clancy was frankly psychotic,” Resnick said. “She was clearly psychotic on that day.”

After the declaration of Clancy’s mistrial, prosecutors have the option of trying her again. The court has set a status conference for 9am ET on 29 September.

Clancy’s criminal trial will be followed by a civil claim brought by both Lindsay and Patrick Clancy against her medical and mental healthcare providers. The former couple claim the providers committed medical malpractice by failing to properly diagnose, treat and monitor her severe postpartum psychiatric condition.

After formally declaring the mistrial, the judge thanked the jury for their time and consideration.

“Each one of you knew how long the case was going to go. You knew how difficult the case was going to be to listen to facts-wise, but still, you braced for that duty,” Sullivan said before dismissing them.

He also indicated that should there be a re-trial, he would want it to happen “sometime in the fall”.

Plymouth county district attorney Tim Cruz told reporters that Clancy’s had been “an emotional trial for everybody”.

“This was and has always been about getting justice for those three little babies,” Cruz said. “We’re here at this courthouse today because those children are not. Our priority has always been to fight for Cora, for Dawson and for Callan.”

Cruz also praised assistant district attorneys Jennifer Sprague and Shanan Buckingham, who he said “are both mothers themselves – and went home to their families after each long day in court”.

Reddington addressed reporters outside the courthouse, too, saying that Cruz “knows he was crushed”.

“I’m representing a woman who is a fantastic, wonderful individual,” Reddington said. “This woman is so brave, so awesome. She sat there through seven weeks of the trial, where nobody had anything bad to say about her except the two prosecutors.”

Reddington also thanked the jury, “minus one” – referring to the holdout juror who he says he “hope[s] they can sleep at night”.

In response to how Clancy’s parents are doing after the mistrial, Reddington said: “Not good.”

“They know that they were robbed by one [juror] for whatever [their] agenda was,” Reddington remarked. “And I got a funny feeling that [the jury] would have gone on for another week if they had to. So I hope that [juror] can sleep well at night.”

“If we didn’t have that one individual, we would’ve had a verdict and we would be out of here,” he continued. He added that Clancy is “like a a daughter to me”.

It was not immediately known for what outcome the 11 decided jurors had voted.

Donald Trump also weighed in on the trial, telling reporters at the White House that the case was a “horrible tragedy” and a “terrible situation”.

“I assume there’s going to be another trial,” the president said. “She did a horrible, horrible thing. Can’t be worse.

“There’ll be a price. It’s going to be a mental institution or jail or something ... It’s too bad.”

In the US, the national maternal mental health hotline is 1-833-852-6262. In the UK, the Pandas foundation offers support via Whatsapp on 07903 508334. In Australia, the national maternal and perinatal mental health hotline is 1300 726 306

‘‘Never Forget’ is not a slogan’: Mamdani designates 9/11 as a Day of Remembrance and Service

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 18:36:44 GMT

The New York City mayor will sign two executive orders honoring those impacted by the attacks, as he faces campaign to exclude him from the 25th anniversary commemoration

New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani is set to designate September 11 as a Day of Remembrance and Service ahead of the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks.

Mamdani’s office announced on Friday morning that the mayor will sign two executive orders honoring victims, first responders, survivors, city workers and families affected by the attacks. The orders will also strengthen the city’s ability to protect New Yorkers and maintain essential services during emergencies.

The first executive order is expected to designate time on September 11 for a moment of silence honoring those killed in the attacks, as well as those who have suffered health consequences in the years since. It will also encourage city agencies to hold memorial ceremonies, educational programming and other remembrance activities.

The designation would mark the first city-level action of its kind by a New York City mayor, Mamdani’s office said.

The second executive order will overhaul the city’s emergency continuity plans for the first time since 2007. It will also create a new interagency team to coordinate the city’s response and continuity planning.

In a statement on Friday, Mamdani said: “I am honored to establish the City’s first Day of Remembrance and Service on September 11th to remember those we lost on that horrific day and the first responders, families and city workers whose lives were irrevocably changed in the aftermath. Through this executive order, we are calling on New Yorkers to honor their memory through service and deep reflection.

“We must also recognize that remembrance carries a responsibility to strengthen our city, protect New Yorkers and ensure that government is prepared to deliver for people no matter the circumstances. ‘Never Forget’ is not a slogan. It is a commitment that we must carry forward through action. And that is precisely what these two executive orders demonstrate,” he added.

The city’s fire department commissioner Lillian Bonsignore echoed similar sentiments, saying: “Service was the legacy of those who answered the call on September 11, 2001, and those who have died since. The greatest tribute we can pay them is to continue serving one another with compassion, courage and a shared commitment to building a stronger New York.”

Mamdani’s announcement comes amid a wave of attacks, some Islamophobic, targeting the 34-year-old democratic socialist, who is the city’s first Muslim mayor.

A recent petition with more than 98,000 signatures, including from family members who lost relatives in the attacks, calls for Mamdani to be excluded from September 11 commemorative events marking the 25th anniversary.

Among other claims, the petition accuses the mayor of supporting individuals whose public statements or records are viewed as “dismissive of American institutions or insufficiently critical of extremist ideologies”.

Former New York governor George Pataki, a Republican, has also said Mamdani should skip the 9/11 memorial.

But other families and local lawmakers have pushed back. Elizabeth Miller, whose father was killed in the attacks, told CBS earlier this month: “The focus should be on where are we in this world, 25 years later?”

“Mayor Mamdani has assured 9/11 families that he wants to be there to honor our loved ones, and I think he should be allowed to do that,” added Miller, the project director of September 11th Families for Peaceful Tomorrows, a remembrance organization.

In a separate statement, the organization said: “We strongly condemn the anti-American accusations and Islamophobic sentiment underlying the effort seeking to prevent him from being at Ground Zero.

“For decades, we have firmly maintained that Ground Zero is sacred space and should never be used as a platform for political speech or partisan politics. Ground Zero remains a burial ground.”

Meanwhile, city council speaker Julie Menin called the push to exclude Mamdani “absolutely inappropriate”, adding: “I think mayor [Mike] Bloomberg made a terrific decision in making sure that there were not political speeches because, again, it shouldn’t be politicized … So, those that are trying to politicize this, what is happening on the 25th anniversary, I think that that is unfortunate.”

Responding to a question about how he felt about the petition a few weeks ago, Mamdani told reporters: “I will proudly honor the families, the survivors, the first responders, forever impacted by that horrific terror attack, by standing alongside them at this year’s 9/11 commemoration, reaffirming that we will never forget the solemn day felt by all of us who call this city home, and frankly, by all of us who call this country home.”

Even before taking office, Mamdani faced Islamophobic attacks on the campaign trail, including from his political opponents, former governor Andrew Cuomo, House Republicans who have called for his deportation, as well as Donald Trump.

Farage seeks to shore up damaged leadership as scandal engulfs Reform conference

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 18:16:10 GMT

Splits emerge within party after resignation of officials reported to police for apparent plot to evade donations law

Nigel Farage sought to shore up his damaged leadership on Friday as he attempted to distance himself from two of his most senior officials reported to the police for apparently plotting to evade the law on foreign donations.

As the scandal engulfed Reform UK’s party conference in Birmingham, Farage was forced to suspend close aides Dan Jukes and head of policy James Orr after an undercover investigation by reporters from a group called Verbatim.

He later acknowledged Jukes and Orr had made “human error” and were “not authorised” to act in the way they did when trying to orchestrate donations to benefit the party from a fake US businessman, who was not permitted to give money.

The Met police are now assessing the evidence after a complaint that Farage, Orr and Jukes may have broken political funding laws, with sources suggesting a full investigation is highly likely to be launched. They all deny wrongdoing.

One possibility would be for the police to extend an existing Met investigation into whether Reform took donations channelled through an intermediary from potentially impermissible sources, which the party and donors deny.

Orr is an associate professor of divinity at the University of Cambridge who had been working for Reform, reporting directly to Farage, since February. In relation to the undercover footage of Orr, a spokesperson for the university said Cambridge was “looking into these matters”. Jukes is Farage’s closest aide, and has been at his side for more than a decade working on communications and strategy.

Farage had been introduced by Jukes to the would-be donor from the US promising to give £500,000 despite not being eligible, who was really an undercover reporter. The Reform leader then appeared to endorse the scheme for the impermissible US donor to give money through his son, a UK intermediary, by saying “thank you, both” and “all above board”.

After dismissing the sting as a “hoax”, Reform began an organised campaign to limit the damage to Farage personally before his main conference speech, after a summer of scandals over his finances, including an undeclared gift of £5m.

Addressing the allegations, the Reform leader responded by reading out a legal statement in which he dismissed the allegations as “a little local difficulty” and described the reports as “an exercise in entrapment”.

Farage claimed Orr and Jukes had merely been “contractors” who engaged in “loose pub talk, including a couple of boasts that simply were not true”. One party figure, Nadine Dorries, claimed Jukes had merely booked transport and carried bags, despite being a senior adviser integral to Reform’s operations and success for many years.

When it was put to Farage that he had thanked the bogus donors and understood what was going on, he said: “It was the middle of the byelection. I was told I had to go and meet these people. I didn’t have to, but I did. I was told they had a global family trust headquartered in London. I asked the question: is this all above board?”

The Reform leader also insisted that the party’s internal processes would have stopped any impermissible donors and said neither Jukes nor Orr should have been carrying out fundraising. He said a suggestion by Jukes in the footage that other foreign donations had been channelled through UK intermediaries was not true and the donors did not exist.

The pair were caught out after being filmed by undercover reporters from the group Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, and broadcast by Channel 4 News on the eve of Reform’s party conference.

In the footage, Orr and Jukes appeared to help orchestrate an impermissible donation of £30,000 from the fake US donor, which was used to pay for polling that would benefit Reform and made front pages of national newspapers. The money from an American company was transferred to the polling company JL Partners after being organised at the behest of Reform to boost its policies and political narrative. It was not declared to the Electoral Commission.

Jukes went on to discuss whether the US businessman could give £500,000 through a UK intermediary, who was an undercover reporter, and introduced the would-be donors to Farage at a lunch in Clacton over oysters and champagne.

Jukes issued a statement: “This was entrapment over a prolonged period of time by individuals using selective editing who had their own agenda to discredit Reform UK.”

Orr said: “I have agreed to step down from my current role at Reform UK pending the outcome of the party’s internal investigation into the conduct of the program, with which I will cooperate fully.”

The Lib Dems have asked the standards commissioner to investigate Farage’s conduct.

The row comprehensively overshadowed the first full day of the party’s conference with every Reform politician repeatedly questioned over the scandal.

It also exposed splits at the top of the party, with Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, strongly distancing himself from Jukes and Orr. He told reporters “anyone who supports Reform is disappointed”, and added of the investigation: “It’s just not something I am personally involved in.”

He also launched a personal video about his backstory, leading to speculation he could attempt to run for the leadership as a rival to Robert Jenrick or Richard Tice if Farage were to be forced out over his financial scandals.

However, some Reform insiders are convinced Farage will part company with Yusuf before long, partly over his ambition and combative style on social media, including one post on X that saw him accused of racism towards a Somalia-born Labour councillor. Farage is understood to have used a rude term about Yusuf recently in relation to his troublemaking on social media.

One senior Reform figure said they believed Yusuf would have to go as a precondition for some sort of reconciliation with Rupert Lowe, whose party, Restore Britain, has eaten into the party’s voters on the hard right. Farage has recently condemned Lowe as vindictive, but some of their friends believe a rapprochement could be possible if Yusuf were no longer in the party.

Reform had wanted the main event to be Farage announcing a deal with the hard-right French National Rally president, Jordan Bardella, to return small boats crossing the Channel if both parties achieve power. However, a press conference was dominated by questions about the foreign donations scandal.

Farage’s main speech was later delayed by security concerns after climate protesters disrupted Tice’s stage appearance. More activists later repeatedly interrupted his address. While waiting to go on stage, the Reform leader danced and sung with the crowd.

He began his speech by calling for Andy Burnham to hold a general election and accusing Labour of planning to put up taxes.

The speech was light on policy but Farage at one point hinted he could look at the way judges are appointed in future – suggesting the party could look at a system of political appointments as is the case in the US.

‘I can’t be bought,’ Nige tells Reform’s faithful – however different it may look

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 17:50:45 GMT

Just as the party leader had hoped to change the narrative, along came Channel 4 News to spoil his conference fun

Why, oh why, oh why? You could almost feel Nigel Farage’s frustration. Why was it always him? Surely it was about time someone gave him a break. There he was trying to earn some money from a Thai crypto billionaire and a gold bullion dealer, and yet still Reform kept getting linked to dodgy cash.

It was almost as if a pattern was emerging. First there was the £5m gift, then the Posh George donations via Dicky Tice, and now Channel 4 News had done a sting on him and two of his most trusted aides in which it looked as if they were happy to break the law on political donations. Life can be so damned unfair at times. Always kicking you when you are down.

The headlines from Reform’s party conference in Birmingham were meant to be all about Nige declaring a national emergency the moment he got in to No 10. Instead he was dealing with a rather more pressing crisis. Every time he tries to persuade the country he’s running a serious party and that it isn’t a one-man band, something seems to happen to make it look like a dodgy, third-rate clown show.

Operation Failed Clean-up was initially left in the hands of Richard Tice and Lee Anderson. Imagine how bad it has to be for these two to be left in charge. Dicky is one of the least plausible politicians you can hope to find, so he didn’t even appreciate the irony of claiming it was all an establishment plot run by leftwing eco activists.

As for Lee, he was adamant that the two Reform members involved – James Orr, a Cambridge associate professor and supposed brains behind the party, and Dan Jukes, Nige’s trusted right-hand gofer for more than a decade – had been out of line and suspended from the party. More than that, they weren’t coming back. More than that he couldn’t say as an investigation had been started. So who was leading the investigation, he was asked. “I don’t know because the investigation hasn’t started,” Lee replied. Sometimes he runs Dicky a close second.

Others were equally as confused. Danny Kruger was in a more forgiving mood and thought there might be some way back for Orr and Jukes once the Reform investigation had exonerated them. Nadine Dorries speculated that maybe they hadn’t known they would be breaking the law. Though the undercover footage rather indicated they had known exactly what they were doing. That accepting money from foreign donors was not an alien concept.

Nige was just baffled. Fed up. Couldn’t believe how this had happened. Orr and Jukes were just contractors. Freelance labourers who had been brought in to paint the kitchen and had overstayed their welcome. He didn’t even know them, had barely met them. Even though both had been the closest of mates with him. Nige is never slow to throw comrades under the bus. It’s the narcissist’s first line of defence. Self-protection at all costs.

At a lunchtime press conference, he had more to say. First he announced he had a spontaneous statement to make that sounded as if it had been carefully worded by his lawyers. It’s probably been an expensive day for Nige. It was a hoax. No laws had been broken. No money had been taken. Except Reform had allegedly taken £35,000 to pay for the opinion poll, and the film suggested they would have been more than happy to take the £500,000 if it had been genuine. Details, details.

It was all a misunderstanding. James and Dan had just misspoken. And he couldn’t believe he had been caught on film having a “man of the people” champagne and oysters lunch with them and the undercover journalists in Clacton. Because he had only ever been in Clacton once in his life. What were the odds? “It was just some jack-the-laddery,” he said. “Pub talk.” Quite right. Which one of us hasn’t spent a long time chatting about crimes we were going to do and their exact modus operandi every time we have a couple of drinks?

Still, at least some things about the Reform conference were business as usual. The queues. Who would have guessed that 8,000 people might turn up at once when you had already sold 8,000 tickets? This came as a surprise to the organisers. And to the member who had turned up dressed as Richard I. Where better to find support for a crusade against Muslims than at the Reform conference. First we take Birmingham, then we take Baghdad.

With the conference already running an hour late before it had even started, it was left to Jeremy Kyle to fill in. He interviewed one punter who told him that all woke people should be hung. This was a little extreme even for Jezza. And there are plenty of people he would like to hang. Finally, though, we were up and running. First a tribute to Ann Widdecombe, then Anderson being given licence to try out his standup routine. Suella Braverman was a proper man, he insisted. Don’t call us, Lee. We’ll call you.

Then came Zia, the self-appointed shadow home secretary who is too unpopular in his own party to be allowed to stand for election. All he really wanted to talk about was small boat crossings. The audience whooped regardless.

The guest speaker was Jordan Bardella, the president of the far-right National Rally party in France. Not the sharpest pencil. He started by congratulating Nige on his brilliant win against the establishment bin in Clacton. It’s possible he doesn’t understand English humour. He then praised the Brits for standing up to Hitler in the war. A bit rich from a man whose party was founded by Nazi collaborators. The session closed with a handshake for Nige as they signed a new version of the entente cordiale.

Much of the afternoon was a write-off. Matt Goodwin, Sarah Pochin, Dicky. I mean, who really cares? They are all lightweights. That just left Nige to round things off. Eventually, after yet another unscheduled delay and some 80s wedding filler songs. Cue some tacky smoke and pyrotechnic effects and the appearance of the Messiah. “I can’t be bought,” he declared on the video above him. Except it rather looks as if he can.

The rest of the speech – with a few interruptions from protesters – was standard Nige. He would change the world in 100 days and sack any ministers who failed. There’s going to be a lot of ministerial vacancies. There was the invention of a reality where he was the Divine. It was all just lazy. Boring. Just one reference to the ongoing crisis. “The party has done nothing wrong,” he said. Mmm. With respect, that’s not something he gets to judge.

Cambridge University asks former chief crown prosecutor to open Arday review

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 17:48:21 GMT

Nazir Afzal to focus in review’s first stage on support given to professor in immediate period before his death

The University of Cambridge has asked Nazir Afzal, a former chief crown prosecutor for north-west England, to lead the first part of its review into the death of the scholar Jason Arday.

Arday died at his home in south London on 14 August, nine days after his resignation as a Cambridge professor amid swirling allegations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career.

Prof Deborah Prentice, Cambridge’s vice-chancellor, said the time since Arday’s death had been “a period of profound sadness and reflection” for the university, and she sought to defend her institution from criticism.

“We worked very hard to support Professor Arday during an appalling period of external criticism and focus but given the devastating outcome, we are all asking ourselves whether we could have and should have done more. This review will answer that question,” Prentice said.

“We are committed to ensuring that any recommendations arising from the review are addressed and adopted with clear accountability for delivering necessary changes.”

Arday was named professor of sociology of education at Cambridge in 2023, with the university highlighting his appointment as the university’s youngest ever black professor at the age of 37.

Arday denied accusations of plagiarism levelled against him but on 5 August the university said it would hold an investigation into his academic qualifications. Arday resigned hours after the investigation was announced.

Prentice said the review would be in two parts, with the first, led by Afzal, to focus on the support given to Arday in the immediate period before his death.

Afzal said: “I am honoured to have been asked to lead part one of this important independent review. At its heart is a person, a family and a community who have been profoundly affected by Professor Arday’s death. It is important that we approach this work with both rigour and humanity.

“My responsibility will be to listen carefully, examine the evidence thoroughly and understand what support, interventions and protections were available to Professor Arday in the period before his death. We must be willing to ask difficult questions, including whether more could and should have been done. This work will be conducted independently and with urgency.”

Afzal, a University of Birmingham graduate, is the chancellor of the University of Manchester, having been head of the CPS in the north-west of England during which he prosecuted child exploitation rings in Rochdale. In 2022 he led an independent review into London fire brigade that exposed a culture of misogyny, racism and bullying.

Prentice said: “I am very grateful to Nazir for agreeing to lead this part of the review. He is a highly respected legal professional who will ask challenging questions about the support that was offered to Professor Arday during his time at Cambridge.”

The university said the review’s second stage would consider “the wider context of Professor Arday’s time at the university”, including the recruitment of senior academic staff, the university’s response to allegations of research misconduct, and the support it gave to academics “subject to extraordinary public and media scrutiny”.

Cambridge said it would appoint an independent external chair for the second part and an expert panel “including individuals with lived experience” to advise the review.

It said part one of the review was expected to report within three months, and the second part within six months of establishing the expert panel.

Earlier this week, Jacqui Smith, the minister responsible for higher education, told parliament that she was “more than just keeping an eye” on Cambridge’s response to Arday’s death. Smith said England’s higher education regulator, the Office for Students, had the powers to investigate further if necessary.

Readers respond to Paul Sagar’s article suggesting a ‘Care First’ year for students in exchange for 50% off university fees

I am sorry that Dr Paul Sagar experienced his injury, but grateful for his moment of enlightenment (The big idea: Could this policy fix the care system and slash student debt at the same time?, 30 August). It is the sort of suggestion that family carers such as myself have been making for years, having been failed by the statutory services for decades.

It needs backing up with some infrastructure: more special schools, more special colleges, better provision in mainstream schools for children with special needs via smaller class sizes, and through more care villages/intentional communities with accommodation, not only for those needing care and support but also for the staff and volunteers on the same site, and housing for family carers.

For our family, enlightenment came more than 60 years ago when my younger brother was born deafblind with additional complex multiple disabilities. When my parents asked the authorities which special school he could attend, the reply was devastating: there was nowhere in the north of England that could cope with the severity and complexity of his disabilities. My parents were left in despair.

Thankfully, we embarked on a tour of the UK as a family with our car and caravan in search of a special school that could help. By some form of divine intervention, we came across the Camphill Rudolf Steiner school in Aberdeen.

My brother started there at the age of five and a half, and within a few weeks was toilet-trained and feeding himself – something that the officials at South Shields town hall had said was impossible.

The houseparents at the school were supported by a team of unwaged voluntary workers, many of whom were from other European countries and doing their “civil service” – an alternative to military service in their own country.

Our family was saved by the conscription policies of other countries and the civilian alternative provided by Camphill. The young voluntary co-workers gained a lifetime of experience and expertise, a confidence in working with and supporting vulnerable children and adults, and training in social care, communication and life skills, as well as learning English with an Aberdonian twang. Simon BurdisMorpeth, Northumberland

Paul Sagar is right to think that radical solutions are needed to transform social care in the UK, but social care deserves more consideration than an amped-up Duke of Edinburgh award. Care work is too often unfairly maligned as unskilled work and kept on low wages by an economy that favours profit over worker wellbeing.

These proposals to incentivise participation in social care work through student debt forgiveness and voluntary service won’t change that without engaging with the poor working conditions and pay in the sector. Rather, we need to consider what an economy that centres care in all its decisions looks like.

Moving away from extractive capitalist models of care provision is an essential part of this, and one that Andy Burnham has acknowledged. So too is a new narrative about care as being valuable, alongside meaningful support for the 6 million unpaid carers and an investment in care work and conditions. Our welfare state, public services and communities all have a role to play in a more caring economy, and we shouldn’t have to twist anyone’s arm to know that. Hannah WebsterCo-founder, Care Full, and former unpaid carer

Paul Sagar’s “Care First” proposal assumes that almost any school leaver can become a suitable carer after training. But caring is not easy or interchangeable work. It requires patience, judgment, emotional maturity, safeguarding awareness and the ability to preserve someone’s dignity during intimate or distressing situations.

What evidence suggests that school leavers motivated principally by reduced university fees would remain in demanding social care roles for a full year?

Social care already has a retention crisis. More than one in five domiciliary care staff leave their roles annually. Turnover rises to 38% among workers under 25 and 43.5% among those with less than a year’s experience. Recruiting a rotating supply of school leavers would do nothing to address the low pay, insecure hours, exhausting travel and working conditions driving experienced carers away.

Most importantly, people needing care have a right to choose who supports them and to expect competence, continuity and genuine commitment.

The proposed reward is also remarkably unequal. At current fee levels, one year in social care could earn a student up to £14,685 in tuition-fee reductions. A family carer providing at least 35 hours of care a week receives only £4,495.40 a year through carer’s allowance – and many receive nothing.

After more than 30 years as an NHS midwife, I left my career to care full-time for my mother, who has dementia. I lost earnings, pension growth and the freedom to work normally. If care is worth thousands when performed temporarily by a prospective student, why is sustained care provided by relatives valued so little?Jacqueline HyltonLeeds

After deciding that I wasn’t going to take photos when not working, we were on a whale-watching trip. I was the only one who saw the whale. Everyone else was looking at their mobile phones. Greg LewisClovis, California, US

In the absence of a personal camera, in the late 1960s, the commonly used alternative for young lovers to record their undying devotion to each other was the photo booth.

Apparently they were used by some to provide passport photos, but I recall that on Friday and Saturday evenings in Birmingham city centre, they were an essential part of a good night out. Not only would you get four photos to share; the curtain also provided a few moments of privacy, although only from the waist upwards! Alan PaylingTorquay, Devon

The Guardian view on Reform’s funding scandal: Nigel Farage has questions to answer

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 16:52:08 GMT

An undercover investigation raises issues around foreign money, political transparency and the rightwing populist party’s fitness for power

Reform UK’s conference was to open showcasing a party ready for government. It did so with two top aides removed after an investigation aired on Channel 4, its finances under police scrutiny and seven in 10 voters, polls suggest, regarding its leader, Nigel Farage, as sleazy – double the number who thought the same of Andy Burnham. Reform, a rightwing populist party, says it will take power back from a corrupt establishment. The latest scandal raises a question: does Reform oppose the influence of big money – or just who benefits from it?

Undercover reporters from Verbatim Investigations, founded by journalists from the US Center for Climate Reporting, pretended to be a wealthy American father and his UK-based son who wanted to donate to Reform. In the UK, foreign donations are banned from politics. But that allegedly was ignored. Verbatim’s team filmed their meetings with James Orr, a Cambridge academic specialising in ethics, and Reform’s head of policy, as well as with Dan Jukes, Mr Farage’s close aide. Both have been “removed” from their posts.

Reform officials allegedly commissioned £32,500 of polling, arranged for what they believed was a US company to pay the bill, hid the party’s role and used the results to generate favourable newspaper headlines. Verbatim wired the money from a US firm to pollsters JL Partners, whose boss was filmed saying that he should have disclosed that his client was Reform. JL Partners admits procedural “weaknesses”. When the supposed American benefactor later explained the arrangement to Mr Farage over lunch, the Reform leader’s filmed response was not alarm but celebration: “It worked. Boom.”

The second main allegation is that the American father was willing to provide Reform with £500,000 through a “permissible” British intermediary – his son. This, if true, would be unlawful. At the lunch Mr Farage does not say that the father cannot be the cash’s source or that the son can legally only donate his own money. Rather, he is filmed saying “thank you both” when it was explained.

Gavin Millar KC, a noted media lawyer, told reporters that “there is enough being said, in the presence of Mr Farage and to Mr Farage, for it to be a red flag – for it to be understood as the reality that this money is coming from an American in a disguised form. And he should be questioning that … On the contrary, he seems to be quite happy to receive the money.”

In response, Reform says that it has “broken no laws”. Mr Farage told LBC that while his party had done “nothing wrong”, the footage looked bad and hence party aides were suspended. Reform has not offered much of an explanation, preferring to claim that it has “been the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign-funded climate change activists”. Political opponents have reported Reform to the police and the Electoral Commission.

Reform’s problem is not that two aides forgot about the rules. It is that senior figures appear to have understood them, discussed how to circumvent them and assumed that nobody able to stop them would find out. A party accused of plotting how to get around the law is now promising to impose a “national emergency” so that judges and officials will not get in its way. That is a telling and ominous reveal about how Reform understands power.
