UN votes to adopt new world map that shows Africa’s true scale

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 16:49:29 GMT

Togo-sponsored resolution called to phase out traditional map that depicts continent as similar size to Greenland

The United Nations has voted to adopt a resolution for the world to formally phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe in favour of one that more accurately displays Africa’s size.

In a session at its headquarters in New York, the UN general assembly officially retired the 16th-century Mercator projection in favour of one based on the more accurate 2018 Equal Earth design.

At the session, 164 countries voted in favour of the resolution. Only the US voted no, with its representative saying the resolution was “superfluous”. There were six abstentions.

UN resolutions are non-enforceable, so countries and institutions will not be mandated to use only the new projection or forbidden from using the old one. However, the outcome is expected to result in an update of classroom curriculums and everyday technology given the wide usage of the Mercator projection in education, technology and governance.

Togo, which spearheaded a campaign for the resolution on behalf of the African Union, said the resolution “recognises and affirms that disproportionate cartographic representations, particularly those resulting from the Mercator projection, have had lasting cognitive, educational, cultural, geopolitical and socioeconomic effects, contributing to a drastic reduction in the perceived size of Africa and other regions of the world in the global collective imagination”.

Speaking before the resolution passed, Robert Dussey, Togo’s foreign affairs minister, said: “This discussion is not a political discussion [but] a scientific discussion, because there is scientific proof so we all have to accept the reality.”

The Mercator layout was introduced by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate the seas. Almost five centuries later, it remains the global standard.

Because of its projection style, however, regions near the equator appear significantly smaller than they are, whereas high-latitude areas look much larger. For example, the map shows Africa as being similar in size to Greenland, but the continent is 14 times larger than the Danish territory.

“You could fit the United States, China, India, Japan, Mexico and much of Europe into Africa and still have land to spare,” says a petition on Change. org for the #CorrectTheMap campaign, which has more than 11,000 signatures. The African Union endorsed the campaign in August 2025 and then asked Togo to spearhead its adoption.

On Friday, before the vote, France’s foreign minister spoke in support of the resolution. “[We] will abandon the Mercator projection in favour of map representations tailored to specific uses, more faithful to actual surface areas and in line with the recommendations of cartographers and scientists,” Jean-Noël Barrot said during a speech at the Sorbonne University in Paris, in a move seen as part of France’s push to increase goodwill among its former colonies. France will now use the Eckert IV projection, which is close to the Equal Earth projection recommended in the resolution.

Historians and geographers have said for years that the Mercator projection is rooted in western stereotypes. Activists have echoed this, with some coining the term “cartographic colonialism”.

Some argue that the map has subtly shaped international power dynamics by minimising the physical presence of the global south and visually inflating northern hemisphere nations while shrinking equatorial regions. This is said to have reinforced systemic biases in international trade, development priorities and educational frameworks.

One of the Mercator projection’s most prominent critics was Arno Peters, a German historian, who launched the Peters world map based on the Gall–Peters projection in 1973. It has often been used as an alternative to the Mercator map.

Togo’s #CorrectTheMap campaign promoted the use of the 2018 Equal Earth design, which was developed by an international team of cartographers. Supporters say it will help to reverse perceptions of Africa and decolonise global curriculums.

Some analysts agree. JJ Enoch, a London-based senior associate at JS Held, a geopolitical risk advisory firm, said the Mercator projection visually diminished Africa’s true scale. He linked the campaign to a quest by African nations for “greater influence in global institutions and greater control over how the continent is represented”.

He said: “Adopting an equal-area map … would provide a more accurate basis for education and public understanding, while signalling that Africa’s demographic, economic and geopolitical importance should no longer be viewed through inherited and distorted conventions.”

Togo’s government is planning an event in Lomé, the Togolese capital, with Unesco, the African Union and tech brands such as Google Maps during the first quarter of next year to map out the implementation of the resolution.

Speaking before the vote, Dussey said: “To those who say why now, I say: why not? When we look at the world map … it is time for us to change the narrative.”

He added: “It’s time for us in Africa to take responsibility to change what we can change ourselves.”

‘There’s no plan’: as instability in global bond markets rises, what are the knock-on effects?

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 16:49:28 GMT

From mortgages to inflation, concerns about the public finances of major economies have wide-reaching consequences

When Donald Trump was asked recently about the threat of rising interest rates on US government debt, he told baffled reporters: “The ultimate intervention is our military. And if we have to use that, we will.”

Perhaps not surprisingly, his bellicose words did not soothe fractious bond markets, and his resumption of the bombing campaign against Iran only made matters worse.

The past fortnight has seen a wave of instability sweeping through government bond markets in major economies – with knock-on effects for millions of borrowers. The interest rate, or yield, on 10-year US government borrowing hit 4.8% on Friday, up from 4.64% 10 days ago. At one point midweek, the 30-year yield touched its highest level since 2008.

Neil Shearing, the chief economist at the consultancy Capital Economics, said one impetus for the current wobble had been markets taking a fresh look at the state of US public finances. “There’s been a recalibration,” he said.

Total US government debt has surged past $40tn (£29.5tn), and annual deficits are forecast to be an eye-watering 6% of GDP for the foreseeable future.

Such figures were long deemed barely to matter given the status of US government bonds, or treasuries, as the ultimate safe-haven investment. But as the events that led up to the 2008 financial crisis revealed, things don’t matter in the markets until they do.

“I think we are starting to see a more realistic reassessment of the fiscal pressure in the US,” Shearing said. “What marks the US out is that there’s not really an acknowledgment of the fact that there might be a problem. There’s no plan.”

Russell Jones, a veteran bond market analyst at Llewellyn Consulting, said: “The thing about economics is that often markets delay the judgment and, you know, you can’t really time when they suddenly decide that that’s enough.”

The US treasury secretary Scott Bessent’s recent fumbled attempts to intervene in financial markets – to help Tokyo prop up the yen and then to calm bond yields – have only added to the sense that policymakers are panicking.

Layered on top of these concerns is a more immediate worry about inflation taking off again as a result of renewed hostilities in the Middle East. Oil prices have risen back above $90 a barrel since the US and Iran resumed tit-for-tat attacks.

That has increased expectations that central banks will have to raise interest rates – another factor that puts upward pressure on yields.

Every pronouncement by policymakers is being closely scrutinised for clues, including a key speech by the new Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, last Friday that was read by markets as signalling a willingness to act.

The European Central Bank is expected to lead the charge with a rate rise next week, but markets are telegraphing higher borrowing costs across major economies.

That includes the UK, where investors are now pencilling in three quarter-point rate rises over the next 12 months, and Japan, where the decades-long period of deflation and rock-bottom rates is finally coming to an end.

A dramatic expansion of borrowing by AI “hyperscalers” in the US, to help fund the massive planned expansion of datacentres, has offered investors an alternative home for their cash – and raised questions about the market’s ability to absorb so much debt simultaneously.

Recent calculations by the investment group Vanguard put the value of debt issued by five major tech companies at $135bn (£100bn) this year, up from an average of $35bn between 2020 and 2024.

There is potentially an even more fundamental explanation for an upward shift in borrowing costs, too – based on the growing prevalence of inflationary shocks not just as a result of geopolitical chaos but because of the climate emergency.

Some economists, including the Bank of England policymaker Swati Dhingra, have argued these increasingly regular shocks, as a result of extreme weather events and resulting economic upheaval, could lead to structurally higher interest rates.

Whatever the causes of rising bond yields, the impact is already rippling out worldwide. Public borrowing has increased dramatically in recent years as policymakers have stepped in to cushion consumers against Covid shutdowns, wrestled with sharply higher energy prices since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and stepped up defence spending. That means small changes in global interest rates can have an outsized impact on government budgets.

In the UK, where £1 in every £12 of public spending already goes on debt interest, Andy Burnham, the prime minister, was pressed this week by the opposition leader, Kemi Badenoch, about the rising cost of government borrowing.

Higher yields on gilts, as UK government bonds are known, will feed through into predictions of higher interest rate costs for the Treasury ahead of the new chancellor John Healey’s autumn budget.

David Aikman, the director of the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, urged the government to take the opportunity to implement spending cuts and/or tax increases to help insulate the UK from higher borrowing costs.

“There will be a lot of talk about the fiscal rules. I think that’s slightly missing the point,” he said. “The big point here is we’ve just got a lot of debt, whether you’re missing the rules or not. And it means we’re really vulnerable.”

On the other side of the world, Australian policymakers have been wrestling with similar challenges. Bond yields have breached 15-year highs just days after the country passed A$1tn in government debt.

The timing of the two milestones comes at a difficult time for a Labor government that is under pressure to rein in historically high levels of spending.

Falling house prices in a property-obsessed nation are adding to a mood of discontent. Bets have firmed that the Reserve Bank of Australia could deliver another interest rate hike later this month to tame stubbornly high inflation.

Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, has been at pains to highlight Australia’s relatively strong budget position internationally. Australia’s debt is equivalent to about half the size of the economy, which pales against other advanced nations. Similarly, the commonwealth is running deficits, but of less than 1% of GDP.

Chris Richardson, an independent budget expert, said Australia’s government indebtedness wasn’t “bad by world standards”. “But it’s still a lot of debt. And the higher cost of money means the difficult choices that were there already are that much harder.”

For developing countries, these issues are all the more urgent. The International Monetary Fund warned earlier this year that these economies had become more exposed to the risk of higher interest rates, because of the growing importance of lending from short-term investors such as hedge funds, which tend to be more flighty during periods of market volatility.

Matthew Martin, of the advocacy group Development Finance International, said: “A lot of these countries are very near the edge, and if they have to go back to the markets and refinance another bond at 1% or 2% higher than it was before, that will mean even less money to spend on climate action, health and education.”

If higher yields are sustained, the effects will be felt far beyond the world’s treasuries, muddying the maths for corporate investments and putting upward pressure on mortgage rates, which in the UK have already started to rise.

Aikman argued corporate balance sheets worldwide looked less shaky than before the global financial crisis. “We’re not in the place we were in the run-up to 2008,” he said. But he pointed to “pockets” of concern, including the huge scale of debt-fuelled private equity projects that could prove vulnerable in a world of higher rates.

By the end of the week, the sell-off sweeping global bond markets appeared to have eased, for now. But it left yields at levels significantly higher than three months ago – and delivered a painful reminder to policymakers, including Burnham, that in globalised financial markets their plans can be buffeted by forces far beyond their control.

The Guardian view on music and drama education: reversing elitism starts at school

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 16:49:26 GMT

The number of students taking creative subjects at A-level and GCSE is at a record low. The arts must not become the preserve of the most privileged

How many of the young people who attended Reading and Leeds festival or a Prom this summer will be picking up a guitar or clarinet when they return to school? New figures suggest not many. The number of students taking A-level music is at a record low: under 5,000, a drop of nearly half from 15 years ago. “We are facing the worst-case scenario prospect of A-level music disappearing from English state schools entirely,” warned Deborah Annetts, the chief executive of the Independent Society of Musicians. Music GCSE entries have also fallen. It has the widest attainment gap for disadvantaged students of any subject. Private violin lessons are beyond the purse strings of most parents.

The statistics for drama are similarly bleak. A-level drama entries have almost halved in 10 years, with by far the biggest drop in state schools. Forty per cent of state schools no longer even offer music or drama GCSEs. Leading universities have been forced to close music departments and arts courses. The number of teachers training in creative subjects has also declined sharply over the past 15 years. It is no coincidence that the Ebacc, which prioritised core academic subjects at the expense of the arts, was introduced by the Conservatives in 2010. No wonder the worlds of music, theatre and television have become so privileged.

“How did British singers get so posh?” asked a recent piece in the New Statesman. Exceptions such as Adele, Raye and Olivia Dean are all alumni of the Brit school, the only state-funded vocational school for the performing arts in the UK. “Learning an instrument and getting up on stage … is now a luxury not every child can afford,” Ed Sheeran wrote in an open letter last year, asking the government to commit £250m of funding for music education. Its 600 signatories included Elton John, Harry Styles and Stormzy. Alison Balsom, the world-class classical trumpeter, has said that her career would not be possible for a state-school pupil now. Julie Walters and Michael Sheen have spoken out about the challenges facing children from working-class backgrounds hoping to become actors.

Sir Keir Starmer was hailed as the most musically accomplished prime minister since Ted Heath, playing four instruments as a child and becoming a junior exhibitioner at the Guildhall School of Music. “To everyone who makes music happen – this government is on your side,” the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, has promised. Scrapping the Ebacc last year was a welcome start. Other plans include the National Centre for Arts and Music Education, finally launching this autumn. Andy Burnham, an English graduate and music fan, has already put vocational education on the agenda. Now he must take up the baton for the arts. Mood music is not enough.

Every child should have the right to discover their gifts and fulfil their potential. Music and drama help develop discipline, confidence and social skills, and enhance wellbeing. The creative industries – a source of great economic value and soft power on the world stage – must be accessible to all. Reversing elitism in our recording studios, concert halls and theatres starts at school.

As Femi Koleoso of the jazz quintet Ezra Collective put it in their acceptance speech at last year’s Brit awards, giving a young person a trumpet or a saxophone might be the solution to many of society’s problems: “Because when you do that, you give them a dream, an aspiration and a goal.”

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 16:35:43 GMT

Kooij claims stage win at Tour of Britain

Wout van Aert won his fourth career stage at the Vuelta a España amid scorching heat on Friday, while Enric Mas kept the red jersey.

On a hot and sunny day in southern Spain, Van Aert beat fellow breakaway rider Valentin Paret-Peintre to claim the hilly 192km jaunt from Almuñécar to Loja.

The elite Belgian rider stopped the clock after four and a half hours of racing. It was Van Aert’s first win of this edition after he won three stages in 2024. It added to his long list of triumphs, which includes 10 stages of the Tour de France and several one-day classics. It was also the fourth team win for Team Visma Lease a Bike at this edition.

Mas, the Movistar leader, kept his lead of one minute 45 seconds over the four-time winner Primoz Roglic. They crossed in a group around three minutes after Van Aert.

Riders had to handle more heat as thermometers recorded 36C (97 F) in Loja, where the stage finished. One rider compared the heat to having a “hairdryer blowing in your face”. Another said he spent the day pouring water over himself at every opportunity.

“It was a very tough stage because of the heat and the hard pace,” the American rider Sepp Kuss, of Visma Lease a Bike, told broadcaster RTVE in fluent Spanish. “If you tried to attack, you just cracked. But we all had to compete in the same conditions. I must also thank the organisers for adding extra spots where we could grab water. If not, it would have been impossible.”

Mas has led the race since the Tour de France champion, Tadej Pogacar, withdrew following a crash last Saturday. Mas has finished the Vuelta as runner-up on three occasions, in 2018, 2021 and 2022. He is trying to become the first Spanish rider to win the home race since Alberto Contador in 2014. The key to Mas finally coming out on top will likely rest on him having a big enough lead to withstand Roglič during a time trial on stage 18.

Friday’s stage 13 was just south of Granada, where the three-week race will finish on 13 September. On Saturday, riders face a 154km (95m) stage from Jaén to Sierra de la Pandera. “Our goal tomorrow is just keeping the red shirt for the next day,” Mas said.

This year’s Vuelta is entirely in southern Spain and without any of its classic mountain finishes in the country’s greener north.

Olav Kooij edged out Tim Merlier in a chaotic sprint to win stage three of the Tour of Britain in Beverley. Kooij began his charge well down in the pack but, with Thursday’s stage winner Merlier finding himself boxed in, the Dutchman spotted his opportunity down the left and, by the time he belatedly found some room, Merlier could not respond.

It was an eighth career stage win for Kooij at this race, putting him second in the Tour of Britain’s record books alongside Edvald Boasson Hagen, two behind the all-time record held by Sir Mark Cavendish.

After a second consecutive sprint finish to end the 181km stage from Hull, the stage one winner Lewis Askey continues to lead overall. Askey leads by 12 seconds from Tim Wellens, with Matteo Trentin a further seven seconds back in third.

Sex symbol in a 70s tank top: how Richard O’Sullivan blazed a trail for funny, frisky, cheeky chappies

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 16:21:37 GMT

The star of Man About the House scored an unprecedented run of hit series during the 70s and 80s, bringing a youthful vitality that audiences – and tabloids – loved

Richard O’Sullivan, star of 70s sitcom Man About the House, dies aged 82 Dandies, docs and robbers: a life in pictures

Having started as a child actor – first appearing on screen aged seven – Richard O’Sullivan, who has died aged 82, went on to a major TV career playing still relatively youthful characters, representative of the social and sexual freedoms that grew from the liberations of the 1960s.

Between 1972 and 81, he appeared in more than 100 episodes of peak-time ITV comedies as funny, frisky men in their 20s and 30s. The first of these was Dr Lawrence Bingham in the hospital sitcom Doctor in Charge, radiating a cheeky charm that led to his career-defining casting as Robin Tripp in Man About the House, in the mid-70s and its spin-off, Robin’s Nest, a few years later.

In the first, Robin shared a flat with two young single women: Chrissy (Paula Wilcox) and Jo (Sally Thomsett). The living arrangements were platonic, partly to appease the TV regulator – from whom formal approval had been sought to show a “mixed” house – but also to establish a sexual tension unusual in mid-evening shows. In the sequel, Robin had qualified as a chef and, again daringly for the TV times, was living with a woman to whom he was not married.

The attractiveness of screen actors has become a contentious question amid valid concerns about performers being objectified for looks rather than talent. But O’Sullivan had both – with a role in the Richard Burton-Elizabeth Taylor movie Cleopatra, a Hollywood career at one point seemed possible. But, as remained the case from Poldark in the last millennium to the Poldark remake in this one, casting has often been calculated to make viewers fantasise. In Man About the House, O’Sullivan, Wilcox and Thomsett offered something for every viewer, as long as they were heterosexual.

Indeed, a running gag in Man About the House was that Robin was gay, a ruse designed to neutralise the living arrangements in the eyes of their landlords (Brian Murphy and Yootha Joyce as George and Mildred), although the humour depended on Robin projecting randy straightness.

The sexiness of O’Sullivan’s onscreen persona – that even the period male fashion for knitted tank tops did little to dampen – was helped by reports of relationships with female co-stars and front page red-top newspaper coverage when Tessa Wyatt, O’Sullivan’s onscreen girlfriend in Robin’s Nest, left her then husband, DJ Tony Blackburn, to replicate the role off-screen.

Man About the House spawned probably the most formidable franchise in British TV, with Robin’s Nest running alongside Murphy’s and Joyce’s own spin-off, George and Mildred. Core audiences of tens of millions for O’Sullivan’s two instalments gave him an audience-drawing power on which ITV was keen to continue to capitalise, casting him as another telegenic rebel, a legendary highwayman, in Dick Turpin, which ran from 1979 to 82.

Approaching his 40s as that series ended, O’Sullivan faced the challenge of moving on from representing the fun of the young. Although the title of Me and My Girl in the 1980s flirted with offering more of the sitcom same, his character in this was a grey-haired widower and the female lead his teenage daughter, played by Joanne Ridley. The impact of this programme was helped by unusually short gaps between series due to fears that Ridley would age faster than the teenager she was playing.

When Me and My Girl ended, O’Sullivan had starred in five successive hit series, with the recognition and wealth that such exposure brings. Sadly, there was to be little more of either. Due to declining health, O’Sullivan’s final screen credit was in 1996 and, after a stroke in 2002, he was cared for at the admirable Brinsworth House entertainers’ retirement home in London.

A career ended by ill-health would be a misfortune for any performer but a small consolation in O’Sullivan’s case is that an actor who specialised in projecting youthful vitality and energy remains forever so on rerun channels.

The Trump White House’s fetish for gamer culture has moved up a level with new arcade

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 16:15:50 GMT

A string of distractions on the US government’s own website invite you to catch pixelated migrants – showing gaming’s potential to be nastily weaponised

The Trump White House on Thursday released a horrible little propaganda arcade via its website, a collection of nasty riffs on popular games. Wrapped in the cutesy, nostalgic aesthetic of early-90s pixel art, these mindless fascist diversions are harmless-looking, but their intent is stomach-turning: this is the appropriation of play in service of propaganda. It’s just the latest in a series of attempts from Trump’s administration to use video game memes and imagery to further its messaging.

Having riffed on Halo and Pokémon in social media ads last year, inviting potential ICE recruits to “stop the flood” and “catch ’em all”, this time the administration has ripped off a series of recognisable games. Flappy Bill, perhaps the least gross, is a version of the old mobile hit Flappy Bird, except here you’re an eagle with a scroll in its claws. Supply Line could almost be an educational game about healthy food in schools, where you sort junk food off a conveyor belt destined for school lunches, except for some reason you play as a boxer who becomes more bloodied with every seed-oil containing, ultra-processed food item that you fail to punch into the garbage chute.

Then come the really nasty ones: Build the Wall, which warps Tetris into a game where you must fortify the southern border to keep out “the coming horde”, and an evil little take on Snake where you patrol the Rio Grande, collecting brown people who then follow you around in orange jumpsuits. The final game is Trump Savings Tycoon, where you “fill your kids’ Trump accounts” by catching bills and gold coins in a net. (The algae-beset Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool is depicted in the foreground, inaccurately coloured in blue.)

I have played all of them, so that you don’t have to. Build the Wall and Rio Run are actively disgusting, built around the naked dehumanisation of migrants, but mostly these games are just embarrassing. Like most things that come from the Trump White House communications team, they are mean-spirited, unimaginative and lazy. I have a strong suspicion that they are vibe-coded using AI, and I almost hope that they are, because the idea of humans spending their precious time on Earth making these horrid, half-arsed games makes me even sadder than playing them did.

Anyone involved in the creation of the original games that the White House Arcade is ripping off is surely cringeing. Members of the original Halo team were moved to speak out on social media after the White House posted a picture of Trump as Master Chief last year; I wonder if Sega will have anything to say about this trailer, which opens with a digital chorus singing “Magaaaa”, soundtracking the sorry collection with music that sounds a lot like Sonic’s Green Hill Zone.

The leveraging of video games and their imagery for political influence has been under way for some time, beginning perhaps with 2014’s Gamergate, an online harassment movement that was stoked by Steve Bannon and far-right website Breitbart. Trump, alongside other rightwing regimes, has had an enormous head start on this front. “The use of video game content, culture and aesthetics for communication is a feature of Trump’s White House, rather than a bug, because much of the modern political right emerged from toxic game communities,” says George Osborn, author of Power Play: Video Games, Politics and the Battle for Global Influence.

“Activists who shaped the Gamergate movement have become an established part of the political right … Until now, it seemed to be restricted to social media posting. I estimated that video game-coded posts had approximately twice the reach of a regular White House Instagram post, suggesting it was able to simultaneously rile up audiences offended by its post and delight supporters. But the deployment of an arcade on its website marks a change of course … Now, it appears that Trump’s White House is ready to use games to begin to try to win over audiences – escalating from appropriating video game culture to ensnaring the medium itself for its own ends.”

Artists and activists have been using video games to put across political messages for a very long time. I have played games about escaping war-torn countries; about examining the paperwork of desperate people at the border of a fictional eastern bloc country; about running a dictatorship or taking one down. Governments, however, are new players in this space.

These games, in line with the Trump administration’s wider social media and communications strategy, are culture-war shitposting. They are almost entirely valueless, and exist more to rile us up than to actually persuade anyone of anything. If we attach too much outrage to them, we are being drawn into someone else’s game; it is deeply unlikely that a round of Rio Run is about to radicalise anyone who isn’t already fully on board with Trump’s whole schtick. But at a time when the Saudi Arabian wealth fund now co-owns one of the world’s biggest game publishers alongside an investment firm run by Donald Trump’s son-in-law, gaming’s propagandist potential should not be a blind spot.

How much does Donald Trump care about winning the midterms? Apparently, not much at all

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 16:01:18 GMT

Such is the US president’s narcissism that he would see a Democratic victory as proof that he’s indispensable – meanwhile, his every decision spells calamity for voters

What is Donald Trump playing at? If it’s true that the best way of understanding the behaviour of an organisation is to assume it’s controlled by a secret cabal of its enemies, perhaps that same logic extends to the current conduct of the president of the United States. Maybe he secretly wants Republicans to lose the looming midterm elections that will decide the balance of power in the US for the next two years and for which the first postal ballots were sent out today.

That’s not as mad a theory as it sounds. Indeed, there are at least two reasons why Trump might either be unbothered by Republican defeat in November or even covertly desire it. We’ll come to those, but let’s start with a pattern of behaviour that is hard to explain as anything other than calculated self-sabotage.

At the centre of it is the single act that is already defining Trump’s second term: his reckless, failed war of choice against Iran. No matter how many times he declares mission accomplished or claims to have destroyed the Iranian military or to have reopened the strait of Hormuz, the facts keep telling a different story. In the past week, the two sides shifted from an economic standoff back to a shooting war, with the US firing on Iranian targets that included a wedding party, killing four, and Tehran striking out all over the neighbourhood, hitting Iraq, Kuwait, Jordan and Bahrain.

The impact on US voters is severe, felt most directly through rising petrol prices and grocery bills. But look at the graph measuring the cost the US government must pay to borrow money: it’s been a steep upward climb since 28 February, the day the war began, hitting a fresh high on Tuesday. For consumers, that rise translates into an expected jump in interest rates. It means that many of those casting ballots are likely to be doing so just as they start paying more on their credit card bills and mortgages. Given that Trump was elected in November 2024 on a promise to bring down inflation, it’s hard to think of a worse environment for a governing party about to face the voters’ verdict. And that’s before you consider the disenchantment of the Maga faithful, who thought the whole point of Trump was an end to forever wars in the Middle East.

And yet, Iran may not even be the most electorally damaging of Trump’s foreign adventures. He is, and it would once have been absurd to write this sentence, leading his country into a state of war with … Canada. It’s easy to laugh at the petty gestures, such as Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario as Lake America, a move shamefully followed, and therefore endorsed, by Apple and Google in their map apps. But the economic confrontation is serious – and seriously damaging to Republicans’ electoral prospects.

For which US states are hit hardest by Canada’s “dollar-for-dollar” response to Trump’s tariffs? Why, it’s Michigan, Ohio, Maine, Iowa and Texas, all of which just happen to have key senate contests this year. Republican candidates in those states now have to explain why a crucial and previously friendly export market – Canada takes nearly a third of Iowa’s exports, for example – has suddenly turned icy.

What’s odd is that Trump’s trade wars are also wars of choice, and they are hurting especially badly what should be a reliable Republican constituency: farmers. Take Iowa: Democrats have not won a senate seat in that farming state for nearly 20 years, yet now, thanks to Trump’s tariffs, they have a genuine shot.

Still, perhaps the most egregious illustration of Trump’s apparent determination to ruin Republican chances in the midterms is his support for datacentres. Few issues have seen their salience rise so quickly and in such a clear direction: almost overnight, they have become objects of fear and loathing across the country and across the political spectrum, with seven in 10 Americans saying they would not want one anywhere near where they live. Even among Republicans, there is deep concern over their environmental impact, energy consumption and water use. For others, datacentres have become a lightning rod for a broader anxiety over AI and what it may do to our jobs and our lives. Either way, they are kryptonite to voters.

So where does Trump stand? “The only reason that communities throughout the USA should not want data centres is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” the president posted on Monday. In that remark, he not only put himself at odds with most US voters, he insulted them too.

It’s almost a talent, this ability of Trump’s to land on the wrong side of so-called 80/20 issues, siding with one-fifth of the electorate against the rest. Likewise, strong majorities oppose his vanity projects, whether demolishing the East Wing of the White House to build a ballroom or putting his signature on the dollar bill, yet he persists not only in doing them but in talking about them constantly.

And all the while, he has hobbled his party by endorsing radioactively unpopular candidates. Few politicians in the US are more tainted than Ken Paxton, who as attorney general of Texas was impeached by his fellow Republicans on a long list of charges that included bribery and abuse of public trust. Yet who did Trump back as the Republicans’ senate choice in Texas? As a result, now even that red-state stronghold is shaky.

after newsletter promotion

Put it all together, and these look like the actions of a man who has no fear of the blue wave that seems to be coming and who could not care less if it sweeps away the Republicans’ current majorities in Congress. That’s curious, given how useful it has been for Trump to have Capitol Hill serve as a rubber stamp that, combined with a largely pliant supreme court, has allowed him to rule with the scarcely fettered power of a would-be autocrat. What could explain the insouciance?

One answer is that Congress’s most potent weapon – the power of subpoena and investigation – holds no terror for Trump because he knows that the House and Senate have no means to enforce their will. They have no police or troops at their command. They can issue their writs and summonses, and he will simply ignore them – comforted by the near-blanket immunity he has already been granted by the supreme court. If Congress goes after his aides and advisers, he will instruct them to follow his lead, on the promise of a comprehensive presidential pardon protecting them from any and all legal consequences. The only real weapon Congress has – impeachment and removal from office – he knows they will never use. If senate Republicans could acquit him after the 6 January insurrection, as they did, he knows they will never vote to convict him of anything, no matter how great the crime.

But that only goes so far. It explains why Trump does not fear Republican defeat in November, but not why he would actively seek it. For that, one has to look into the abyss that passes for the president’s soul. The bestselling new book Regime Change, by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, spells it out: “If Republicans were wiped out in the 2026 midterm elections, or in 2028, he could simply boast that they couldn’t win without him” on the ballot paper. Such is Trump’s narcissism, he will take an epic Republican defeat in two months’ time not as a repudiation, but as a compliment. And, it seems, he is doing all he can to earn it.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

Russia strikes Ukraine intelligence HQ in ‘major escalation’

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 15:37:52 GMT

Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he has told SBU to deliver ‘appropriate, tangible response’ to Kyiv strike

The head office of Ukraine’s SBU intelligence agency has been hit in a Russian drone attack, sending plumes of black smoke rising into the air in the heart of Kyiv.

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he had instructed the SBU to deliver an “appropriate, tangible response” to the strike, while the foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, described it as a “major escalation”.

The streets around the SBU headquarters were cordoned off shortly after Friday’s attack, with armed officers patrolling the area.

Numerous ambulances and emergency services vehicles were stationed around the site, which is close to St Sophia Cathedral, a Unesco world heritage site.

“Unfortunately, a Russian drone hit the central building of the SBU on Volodymyrska Street in Kyiv, opposite the St Sophia Cathedral,” Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram. “The drone was aimed directly at the office of the Head of the Security Service in that building.”

Kyiv has been under a barrage of daily drone and missile attacks from Russia for over a week. Zelenskyy on Friday called for Russia to halt its attacks during a visit of US negotiators, Steve Witkoff ‌and Jared Kushner, to the city on Sunday and said Ukraine would guarantee the safety of Russian airspace while they were in Moscow.

Ukraine is facing a critical shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors which can shoot down incoming threats. Many of the recent Russian strikes have been by new-model jet-powered drones which can reach speeds of 250mph, making them hard to intercept.

It is rare for government buildings in central Kyiv to be reached by Russian strikes, especially in broad daylight. The explosion from the hit on the SBU building could be heard from several blocks away.

The incident is likely to intensify the escalating attacks that Moscow and Kyiv have been launching at each other in recent weeks in efforts to destroy each other’s resilience and morale. It will also raise questions about Kyiv’s ability to defend its key infrastructure against Russia.

Sybiha said the attack was “a major escalation that demands resolute responses” and called on international partners to “unequivocally condemn these actions and step up pressure on the Putin regime”.

At least nine people were injured in Friday’s strike, according to Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko.

Stanislav Zavertailo, the co-owner of the nearby Zavertailo cafe, said one of his customers was injured in the strike, which sent shockwaves through his premises, shattering all the windows.

“It’s a normal cafe,” he said. The customer was “eating one of our famous poppy seed rolls” when the attack occurred, he added.

Staff and customers rushed into an underground shelter after the strike, fearing a double-tap attack, a tactic which Russia has employed, in which a second drone is sent in soon after the first, hitting emergency service workers.

An hour later, there had been no second strike, but Zavertailo said he did not feel at ease. “We are all waiting for another attack,” he said.

The SBU is responsible for coordinating complex operations against Russia, including last year’s Operation Spiderweb which destroyed aircraft worth billions of pounds inside Russia.

Friday’s hit was “awful” said a Zavertailo cafe employee who had recently emerged from the underground shelter. As “a person who lives in Ukraine for all this time, it’s just hard”.

The strike came two days before Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were expected to visit Kyiv for the first time.

US-led diplomatic efforts to end Russia’s four-and-a-half-year invasion have stalled in recent months as the US has shifted its focus towards the war with Iran.

Canary staff not paid amid fears for news website’s future

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 15:27:35 GMT

Outlet faced significant financial challenges after it had funds blocked by bank without explanation

Workers at the leftwing news outlet the Canary fear it will not survive beyond this year amid access to funds being blocked and allegations of financial mismanagement and internal turmoil.

The site, which was founded in 2015 against a backdrop of the wave of support for the then Labour leader, Jeremy Corbyn, appeared set to expand after a multimillion-pound injection of funds last year.

But the outlet faced significant financial challenges in July after it announced that it was unable to pay staff and contractors as a result of Lloyds Bank unexpectedly blocking access to “a substantial amount” of its money. The bank did not give a reason.

A number of staff at the outlet were not paid again at the end of August. “Any payment difficulties have been solely due to our ongoing debanking issues,” a Canary spokesperson told the Guardian.

Some journalists at the Canary, however, have said they believe the banking issues had been used to distract from wider financial mismanagement.

They claim the funding, believed to be more than £2m, has been squandered on projects including a short-lived newspaper and the purchase of other websites.

Staff at the outlet, where there are about 50 full-time and part-time jobs, have moved to unionise by forming a branch of the National Union of Journalists (NUJ). Over the summer a full staff meeting was told that the new funding had all but gone and they were all facing the possibility of redundancy, with about £400,000 left to see the Canary through to December.

Since the Canary faced issues with access to its funds, staff say they have been notified that late payments of pension contributions by the company have been reported by the National Employment Savings Trust (Nest), the government-backed workplace pension scheme that helps employers meet their legal duty of automatic enrolment.

It is understood that tensions have also risen after, in the spring, workers say, they were asked by management to sign “non-negotiable” non-disclosure agreements, and told that if they refused they would be subject to changes to their employment contracts.

The site describes itself as anti-austerity, anti-Zionist and pro-freedom of expression, among other things. Steve Topple, the outlet’s chief executive, told staff in May that he and others in the management team had serious concerns about the integrity of the Canary as an organisation “and also the level of reputational risk”.

“We are at a time when we are doing things that are putting a massive target on our backs, and I am expecting the full force of the system to be placed upon us in due course,” he wrote in a message which also said he would not tolerate the leaking of confidential information beyond the organisation.

Staff at the website said in 2022 that they had “overthrown” management and were running the organisation as a cooperative. That structure was later dissolved.

Some had hoped that the title’s longer term future had been secured after Cecil Hetherington, the founder of the Northern Irish classifieds website Used Cars NI and chair of the house-sale platform PropertyPal, became a major shareholder, contributing an estimated £2m.

“We were told originally that Steve had taken on a donation from Cecil Hetherington, but then the ‘debanking’ happened and things changed,” said one worker, referring to the period in which funds were blocked by Lloyds.

“Payments have been late for the last three months, wages and invoices have been late. Even basic stuff hasn’t been taken care of, with the result that the website went down at one point.

“We have undoubtedly made mistakes in our internal communications, and we apologise to everyone in Canary Media Limited and our readers for that. We are currently in discussions with our employees to address their very understandable concerns and would appreciate the privacy to do that.”

As AI madness encroaches, we need human connection more than ever. But we’ll have to fight for it

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 15:00:11 GMT

We don’t want the isolating, automated outputs tech lords are selling us. We’re yearning for a shared frame of reference

I have a cherished memory of a family trip to the movies. In the Australian tradition, we bought choc-top ice-creams, chattered through pre-show trailers and a hush fell on the full house as the movie started.

It was Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, on film, only a couple of weeks ago, months after its release.

In an AI-supercharged world of algorithmic recommendations and atomised cultural space, I’ve come to suspect The Odyssey’s ongoing popular appeal is no longer its Greeks with gifts, or superstar director.

It’s the increasingly rare opportunity to share even a single cultural reference with other people. Despite our human instinct for interaction, we live in a global moment where health authorities believe social isolation is an epidemic.

Yet in the same city of my fun night at the cinema, this week it was news that Australia’s Macquarie University has introduced an AI chatbot into the weekly teaching of two mandatory psychology subjects.

Displacing human beings from what should be stable jobs isn’t the only outrage here.

As someone whose dainty, addled, depressive brain obliges tender care from trained professionals, Macquarie, please record this data in your feedback corpus: I cannot trust or validate the insight of a supposed expert whose contact with adult realities has been compromised by being taught by a machine.

If I want a chatbot to talk me out of a panic spiral, I’ll consult it within my already-paid-for subscription service when I’m freaking out at midnight like a normal person, thank you.

Far more positive social impacts can be measured from Australia’s academics’ union, this week taking strike action at the University of Sydney against the encroach of AI madness.

“We want enforceable protections against AI being used to cut jobs, intensify workloads, undermine academic and professional judgement, or replace work and human interaction that are fundamental to a university,” said the NTEU’s Vince Caughley. Solidarity, brother. My gratitude extends to Australia’s writers’ union, the AWG, as well as its entertainment and communications union, the US actors’ union and Writers Guild of America, Canada’s performance union, Germany’s service workers union and actors’ union, an alliance of Italy’s dubbing unions and all industrial organisations striking AI-use agreements not merely to protect their members’ workplace rights, but to remain on the side of public opinion.

Because studies repeatedly suggest consumers don’t want the isolating, automated outputs being sold to them.

In the world of commercial literature, one study found “consumers perceived human-written books more positively in all investigated dimensions than ones written by AI”. While other researchers have found the intrusion of AI titles to Amazon is now as many as 20% of its ebook catalogue, the same study shows they only made up 12% of sales and 10% of bestsellers in their genre. A considerable underperformance.

In music, global consultancy Bain learned that 62% of consumers would not engage with music generated by AI.

French streaming service Deezer revealed fully AI-generated music constituted as much as 18% of its daily uploads but amounted only to about 0.5% of listening – while the Guardian reported that up to 70% of those streams appeared fraudulent.

Bain found the only majority tolerance for AI content was in video games: 71%did not want AI in their books, and 65% did not want it in their news and magazines.

Similarly, in sales, studies show that telling customers beforehand they are engaging with chatbots in outbound calls reduces purchase rates by 79.7%. In 2025, Deloitte learned 74% of customers preferred human interaction even for routine banking questions. In another international 2025 study, chatbots were the least popular form of customer service engagement: a mere 8% of respondents chose them voluntarily.

Consumer sentiment backlash is registering faster than the slow pace of democratic governance. Governments have struggled with the speed of tech encroach, with regulation lagging in the face of relentless economic and political pressure from the world’s most aggressively overcapitalised, cashed-up dipshits who own all this stuff. Australia is considering its approaches to AI regulation, but it does not have it yet.

Friends, we missed the boat on regulating social media. Nazis, radicalisation, deadly health misinformation and addictive and dangerous products sailed in.

As more comprehensive AI regulation is debated, the Australian government is mooting community calls for default opt-in obligations on platform algorithms, to stop the use of apps being conditional on what preferred form of slop its tech lord wants to shove into your consciousness.

We should all support it, if just to take a wild, political stand for authentic preference over forced consumption. Elon Musk has mooted making an “AI Odyssey”, and if you think the algorithm he paid $44bn for will let you escape that horror show, there are some relevant scenes from A Clockwork Orange I suggest you try to catch at a midnight screening.

Cinema, writing, education, psychology and, yes, even shopping and banking facilitate human interactions.

Unless the clients of AI’s robots are also robots, I have to ask: just who are y’all making products for?

Van Badham is a Guardian Australia columnist

Brydon Carse has been left out of England’s white-ball squads to face Sri Lanka at the end of the season and told to “work through the issues” that led to him being handcuffed by police outside a bar in Derby last month.

Carse, 31, is being investigated by the Cricket Regulator regarding the late night incident in August that prompted his removal from England’s plans for the ongoing Test series against Pakistan. Derbyshire police are also looking into an alleged assault that night, albeit Carse’s involvement is not currently known.

In the meantime, Carse is technically available for England selection but has been left out of the Twenty20s and one-day internationals against Sri Lanka that start in Southampton on 15 September. Henry Crocombe, the uncapped seamer who has claimed back-to-back hat-tricks for Sussex in the past week, has taken Carse’s place in the ODI squad.

An England spokesperson said: “Given recent events, we feel it is important for [Carse] to work through the issues that led to the Derby incident and take time for a proper reset. This decision does not prejudge the outcome of any investigation.”

Though a close friend of the white-ball captain, Harry Brook, and centrally contracted, it would appear Carse has fallen foul of the England management at large as they attempt to change the image and culture of the men’s national teams. Joe Root, the Test captain, had previously asked his players to be “role models”.

Jacob Bethell will also miss the white-ball fixtures against Sri Lanka after recently undergoing surgery on the knee problem that has kept him out since mid-July. Bethell is not expected to be fit until the limited overs tour of Australia in November, with Derbyshire’s Aneurin Donald now earning a maiden T20 call up.

If selected, Donald would become the first Glamorgan product to play for England since Simon Jones during the 2005 Ashes, even if he has moved counties since. The 29-year-old struck 489 runs in this year’s T20 Blast at a remarkable strike-rate of 230 and went on to shine in the Hundred for the runners-up, Trent Rockets.

There is a third Test against Pakistan to complete first, however, with the tourists having now begun life under their new interim head coach, Mike Hesson. Sarfaraz Ahmed was stood down from the role after going 2-0 down at Lord’s last Sunday, while seven members of Pakistan’s touring party were also dropped.

As Pakistan’s white-ball coach, Hesson had only flown to the UK to attend the Pakistan Cricket Board’s official reception with King Charles at Clarence House on Wednesday. “It’s been pretty challenging,” said the New Zealander. “I was heading over to see the King and be part of a nice occasion. That got expedited.”

After holding one-on-one talks with the remaining squad members this week, and then drilling them at Edgbaston’s indoor school due to rain, Hesson believes a fresh start has occurred. Of the seven players being flown in, three were still due to arrive in the UK on Friday.

As for the departed, Hesson tried his best to explain.

In essence, three of the seven dropped – Imam-ul-Haq, Mohammed Rizwan and Salman Ali Agha – were told their tour was over immediately after the defeat at Lord’s. Hesson claims he was not privy to this decision by the high performance director, Aaqib Javed, nor was he able to share the precise reasons why.

Richard O’Sullivan, star of 70s sitcom Man About the House, dies aged 82

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 14:30:59 GMT

Actor, who also played title roles in Robin’s Nest and Dick Turpin, dies peacefully at Royal Variety Charity care home

Richard O’Sullivan obituary

Sex symbol in a 70s tank top: how Richard O’Sullivan blazed a trail for funny, frisky, cheeky chappies

Richard O’Sullivan, known for his role as Robin Tripp in the 1970s TV sitcoms Man About the House and Robin’s Nest, has died aged 82.

The actor, who was also famous for playing the title character in the TV series Dick Turpin, died peacefully with his family at his side at the Royal Variety Charity’s care home on Friday, the organisation said.

His son James O’Sullivan paid tribute to him, saying: “My dad was as funny and charming in real life as he appeared on our TV screens over the years. Always kind-spirited, good-humoured, a doting grandfather and a wonderful dad – I will miss him dearly.

“Although much of his career happened before I was born, I was fortunate enough to be able to enjoy and witness his incredible talents on the countless reruns of his shows that made him the respected and loved actor that he was.”

O’Sullivan had lived at the Royal Variety Charity’s Brinsworth House in Twickenham for 23 years. His son thanked the “incredible team” there for their “love, kindness and care”. He said: “They have been truly amazing and will always hold a special place in my heart.”

O’Sullivan’s career began when he appeared in The Yellow Balloon as an eight-year-old in 1953. He later appeared in Peter Hall’s production of Love’s Labour’s Lost at the Royal Shakespeare theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1956.

He appeared in two films with Cliff Richard in the 1960s: The Young Ones in 1961 and Wonderful Life in 1964. In 1963, he starred opposite Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton in Cleopatra in the role of Pharaoh Ptolemy XIII.

Man About the House ran for six series from 1973, following the trials and tribulations of a man sharing a London flat with two single women, Chrissy, played by Paula Wilcox, and Sally Thomsett as Jo.

Giles Cooper, the life president of the Royal Variety Charity, said: “Richard O’Sullivan was a master of effortless charm and impeccable comic timing, bringing pure warmth, wit, and unforgettable joy to millions of living rooms as a true giant of British television. He will be sorely missed by us all at the Royal Variety Charity.”

‘Like a tired boxer, battered by applause’: as Andrew Scott’s biopic premieres, Richard Eyre remembers Ian Charleson’s superb, near-death Hamlet

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 14:03:50 GMT

In 1989, the Chariots of Fire actor took on the incredible task of playing Shakespeare’s prince while terminally ill from Aids. This weekend sees the world premiere of Elsinore, a new film about the episode, itself heavily-tipped for awards

Ian Charleson was one of the finest actors of his generation and an important figure in the fight for gay rights. Yet the extraordinary circumstances of his final performance as Hamlet, just months before his death, are less familiar.

Now, a new film is bringing that haunting production back to life. Elsinore, directed by Simon Stone and starring Andrew Scott as the Scottish actor, will premiere at Telluride this weekend before opening the London film festival in October.

Charleson was 40 and terminally ill with Aids when he was cast as Hamlet in Richard Eyre’s 1989 production at the National Theatre, after Daniel Day-Lewis abruptly left the role. Charleson had first played Hamlet 15 years earlier and persuaded Eyre to let him reprise it, despite the director’s misgivings about his health.

“Ian was very bright, very witty, mischievous,” Eyre told the Guardian. “He was beyond good-looking. He was beautiful, and he had a beautiful singing voice.”

Eyre remembered sitting with Charleson in the National’s canteen a year earlier, when the actor was starring in Cat on a Hot Tin Roof. “He said, ‘I’m hungry for the big Shakespeare roles’. So when Dan had his breakdown” – Day-Lewis believed he saw the ghost of his father onstage – “I thought, I will approach Ian. We met, and then I realised Ian was was very ill. But I thought I will go with him anyway.”

The cast, crew, and audience were told that Charleson’s face was swollen after a sinus operation. In reality, he was suffering from septicaemia, enduring painful acupuncture during rehearsals and, later, chemotherapy.

“Ian’s beautiful face was actually deformed by the disease,” Eyre said. “But I just thought, he is determined, and I felt determined, and it was sort of an act of love for a friend. Most people told me I was absolutely insane. The press were characteristically loathsome in their probing. I just stubbornly stuck to my decision. In retrospect, it was the right one. He was heroic, and utterly brilliant in the part.”

The production ran for six weeks and was widely regarded as one of the finest Hamlets seen on stage. The day after Charleson’s last show, Ian McKellen refused the Evening Standard award for best actor and gave his statuette to Charleson instead.

Charleson died on 6 January 1990, eight weeks later, having asked that Aids be recorded as the cause – an unusually public act at a time when the disease was feared and stigmatised.

Eyre has written of how fitting it was for Charleson to play Hamlet in the last months of his life. “Do you think I can go on as Hamlet looking like this?” Charleson asked him. “You’ll get better,” Eyre replied. “We have to be positive,” Charleson said.

“Hamlet is a poem of death,” Eyre wrote. “It charts one of the great human rites of passage – from immaturity to accommodation with death. Hamlet grows up, in effect, to grow dead.”

Born in Edinburgh in 1949, Charleson trained at the Bristol Old Vic. He played Eric Liddell in Chariots of Fire, which won four Oscars including best picture, and also appeared in the following year’s best picture winner, Richard Attenborough’s Gandhi.

Charleson seemed to have all the ingredients of a major film career: he was handsome, charismatic and intelligent, with a formidable technical ability. Yet his film career never took off as expected. Instead, he repeatedly returned to the stage, performing Shakespeare, Tennessee Williams, Chekhov, Sam Shepard.

Michael Billington, the Guardian’s former chief theatre critic, remembers Charleson as Eddie in Shepard’s Fool for Love at the Cottesloe in 1984. Initially unconvinced by his interpretation, Billington later came to remember the performance for its “mixture of masculinity and sensitivity”. Charleson performed Cat on a Hot Tin Roof, he said, with “the same blend of supposedly contradictory qualities: athleticism and delicacy”.

Charleson was gay at a time when being openly so could damage an actor’s career. Diagnosed with HIV in 1986, he took part in Before the Act, McKellen’s 1988 anti-Section 28 gala, alongside Judi Dench, Vanessa Redgrave and Stephen Fry.

Scott, who played Hamlet 150 times in London in 2017, has found himself returning to the role while portraying the actor who performed it at the end of his life.

“The idea that Ian was doing this when he was so sick is still, to my mind, just completely mind-blowing,” Scott told People. “And his decision to do it was just incredibly courageous.”

Scott said he was moved by “the opportunity to play a part that Ian and his contemporaries would not have gotten while they were working actors.”

He added: “I wanted people to be able to understand that he was trying to live – it’s not about fetishising his death. He was so full of life and fun, and he did this extraordinary thing.”

Critics and industry insiders are heavily tipping Scott for a best actor Oscar nomination following early praise for his performance. Eyre called it “brilliant”. “He looks like Ian, and he touches the heart like Ian,” he said.

Charleson’s most celebrated performance was never preserved on film. What remains are recollections, photographs and accounts of an actor performing with extraordinary intensity while his body failed him.

Eyre recalled that Charleson had flu and missed two nights, but felt guilty: “If they pay you, you should turn up.” His final, Monday night performance, Eyre wrote, was “like watching a man who had been rehearsing for playing Hamlet all his life. He wasn’t playing the part, he became it.”

At the curtain call, Charleson stood “like a tired boxer, battered by applause”.

A few weeks before he died, just before Christmas, he wrote to Eyre: “One day when I’m better I’d love to attempt Hamlet again, and all the rest; and together we can revitalise Shakespeare. Anyway I hope this is not a dream and I can’t tell you how much of a kick I got out of doing the part, if only for the short time I could …”

Chat to strangers and let your kids be bored: how to embrace a ‘slow September’ – and enjoy life more

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 14:00:10 GMT

The pressure to self-optimise at the start of the new school year can lead to disappointment and burnout. Instead, here are seven ways to slow things down and reap the benefits

It is a hangover from our school days that September can feel like a time for getting back to the grind. As in January, there is a sense that we should return as better workers, partners, friends and parents. This sense is even stronger now a culture of optimisation – has taken over – evidenced by the fad for adding “maxx” to everything. Yet that can lead to disappointment and burnout, which Mental Health UK reports up to 91% of adults were at risk from over a recent 12-month period.

One antidote to this drive is to embrace a slower way of living. Rather than always rushing from one activity to the next, we could be enjoying life.

“In the age of digitisation, from work to socialising, we are seeing everything intensify,” says Heejung Chung, a professor of work and employment at King’s College London. “But by doing everything, we’re also creating a culture where it’s seen as normal. So you are not only creating a standard for yourself, but for everyone else as well. There is a creeping set of collective expectations that we can do everything, especially women, and we need to change it.”

So say “no” to self-optimisation this September, and instead embrace these practical ways to slow everything down – from work to parenting.

More often than not, we feel as though we don’t have enough time to converse with strangers in our daily lives, whether that be the woman next to you at the bus stop or the barista making your coffee. Yet taking the time to mindfully have a conversation with someone we don’t know has tangible benefits.

In Once Upon a Stranger: The Science of How Small Talk Can Add Up to a Big Life, Dr Gillian Sandstrom argues just this. “Research shows that even tiny conversations with strangers improve our mood,” she explains. “They naturally slow you down, so you start paying more attention to the people around you and your surroundings. They also help you learn new things – I’ve met someone who rescues bats at Durham Cathedral, and a publican who taught me that asparagus squeaks.”

Sandstrom points to a 2012 study, Giving Time Gives You Time, which shows that when you spend time on other people, you end up feeling as though you have more time yourself. “When we’re busy, we feel like we can’t spare time for other people, but if we never take that time, we’ll never stop feeling busy,” she adds. “It’s counterintuitive but it works.”

One literal way to slow down is to start walking at someone else’s pace. “If you’re with a child, an older adult, or even your dog, let them set the pace instead of pulling them along,” says Sarah Hodges, therapy network manager at the mental health and meditation app Headspace. “When we stop rushing to keep our own schedules, we often notice things we would have missed, like the small moments, conversations and connections that make life meaningful. Research on mindfulness and attention shows that when we slow down and intentionally notice what is happening around us, we can reduce stress.”

Prof Mark Williams, founding director of the Oxford Mindfulness Foundation, also suggests walking with an upright posture. “Most of us walk leaning into the future, mentally rushing towards whatever comes next,” he says. “Research shows that simply standing or walking a little more upright can positively influence how you feel.”

If you are a parent who is preoccupied with ensuring your child is always busy, you might be doing them a disservice. “Being bored is part of the human experience,” says Stephanie O’Dea, author of Slow Living: Cultivating a Life of Purpose in a Hustle-Driven World. “This is how creativity, imagination and independence begin. A child saying they are bored isn’t an indictment of your parenting.”

Allow them the space for imaginative play. “A child is more likely to play independently if you spend time with them beforehand,” says Dr Maral Amani, a paediatric physical therapist and child development expert. “A helpful response the next time your child says, ‘I’m bored,’ is to resist immediately solving the problem. Instead, try offering confidence. You might say: ‘Hmm, I wonder what you’ll come up with.’ This communicates that you believe they are capable of finding something to do on their own.”

Another suggestion is to invite your child to help you with whatever you’re doing. “If you’re folding laundry, cooking dinner or putting dishes away, you could say: ‘Do you want to keep me company and tell me a story while I do this?’” says Amani. “Sometimes children aren’t looking for entertainment, they’re looking for connection. Inviting them into your everyday activities shows them that ordinary moments can be meaningful.”

Many of us feel we always need to be productive, even during our downtime. Yet there is much joy to be had in actual leisure time, whether that is doodling, kicking a ball around the garden with your child or listening to music. “Do something with no goal beyond enjoyment,” advises Hodges. “Research on rest and recovery highlights the importance of activities that allow us to step away from constant achievement and performance. Doing something simply because we enjoy it helps restore our energy and reminds us that our value is not only tied to what we accomplish.”

Sign up to Inside Saturday

Rosie Nixon, the author of The Pro Method: Pause, Reflect, Organise – Three Simple Steps to Reinvent Your Life, a new book about how to overcome burnout, also recommends doing a “joy audit” of what you actually like doing, and sticking to those activities. “Take a minute to pause and reflect on what genuinely fills your cup, and enables you to cope with the more demanding aspects of your life,” she says. “Then deprioritise anything that isn’t serving you any more – whether that’s friendships, or social media accounts you are following.” And if there’s a TV series or book you’re just not getting into, don’t feel you have to complete it.

Our always-on work culture means many of us feel as though we can’t take a break during the working day. But as Chung has discovered through her research, having sufficient time away from work makes you a better worker the next day. “For athletes, resting their body isn’t optional; it’s how they are able to perform so well,” she says. “The brain works in much the same way. If your job involves creative thinking, problem-solving or knowledge work, rest isn’t wasted time. It’s what enables you to perform at your best.” For this reason, she argues that working long hours into the night will affect the quality of your work not only at the time, but the next day too.

Yet finding time to pause during the day can feel impossible. “Finishing one task simply acts as the trigger to begin the next,” says Williams. “So one particularly useful moment to pause is immediately after completing something.” He recommends taking a “mindfulness minute” , whether that be 10 slow breaths, or walking to refill your water bottle.

Claudia Hammond, author of Overwhelmed: Ways to Take the Pressure Off, suggests scheduling your meetings for five past the hour, so that you always have five minutes to catch a breath between hour-long calls. “A recent study found that micro-breaks of just two minutes each hour – where you stare out the window, or doodle, or lean your head back in your chair and shut your eyes – are great for mood and therefore productivity and concentration,” she says.

Many believe that in order to have a meaningful experience with our friends, we must be dining at a restaurant, going to an exhibition or attending a party, but some of the most meaningful interactions happen when we’re doing very little at all. “Organising seeing friends can start to feel like a job in itself,” says Hammond. “Especially if there are conflicting priorities, or somewhere requires a deposit, or is fully booked. So it’s a question of remembering that you don’t need to do something massive: it can be as simple as going for a walk.”

The same can be said of hosting. Remove the pressure to cook a gourmet meal and design a tablescape. Instead, focus on the joy of sharing a meal together – whether that’s something homemade or a takeaway.

“September is about fortifying yourself for the winter, and delving into the pleasures of home and slowness after the freneticism of summer,” says cook and food writer Jago Rackham. “Eat slow-roasted meats and poached fruit, do as little as possible to the excellent seasonal ingredients, and plan long lunches and early dinners to catch the last of the light.”

If you think you don’t have time for mindfulness, try to incorporate it into what you are already doing. “You can build these small moments of awareness into everyday life without adding anything else to your schedule,” says Williams. “If you’re eating lunch, really pay attention to the experience of eating. When you’re walking, ask yourself: ‘What else is here, apart from all the thoughts in my head?’ You might notice an interesting roofline, a bird perched on a fence, or the way the light falls on a building. Appreciation is incredibly valuable. It brings a little more positivity into the day, and we know that being in a positive mood increases creativity too.”

Wide-legged trousers for men are having a moment. Just ask Gary Neville

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 14:00:09 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Neville may have been mocked for wearing them on Monday Night Football, but he is actually bang on trend

From Kylian Mbappé’s World Cup style to Erling Haaland’s hair tie, football has had many viral fashion moments in 2026.

Perhaps the one that speaks to the fashion crowd, and a larger debate happening in menswear right now, is Gary Neville being mercilessly teased on Sky Sports’ Monday Night Football for sporting wide-legged trousers.

As a producer played Baggy Trousers, by Madness, Neville’s chino-style, wider-legged black slacks were mocked by fellow pundit Jamie Carragher, who compared Neville to Frank Worthington, the forward from West Yorkshire whose dandyish off-pitch style raised eyebrows in the 1970s.

“I went shopping in London,” Neville explained as Carragher jogged along to the Nutty Boys’ hit. “This guy styled me. I think they’re pretty cool, you know.” He predicted that Carragher would be wearing a pair soon.

Neville seems to be on to something. Because as far as the cut of your trousers goes, girth is greater.

Nick Pope, the site director at Esquire, said: “In terms of what people are actually wearing on the street, it is the wider silhouette.” Retailers from Cos to Next and Marks and Spencer are going great guns selling wider-fitting trousers in the menswear aisle.

The width currently in style can’t quite be described as “baggy trousers”, however. Pope said what Neville wore was a relaxed 90s fit for today, like the trousers seen on A$AP Rocky at the Tribeca festival in New York City in June.

The silhouette dominated men’s fashion week for autumn/winter 2026-27 among designers including Dior, Prada and Saint Laurent. On the red carpet, the style has been seen on fashion magnets such as Connor Storrie (at the Golden Globes) and Joe Alwyn (at the Baftas).

The classic football pundit dress code grew out of newsreader style: a suit and tie. It was a safe option for the footballer turned television presenter who could not show up wearing their home kit. But Neville and fellow presenter Jamie Redknapp donning a wider leg on Sky Sports speaks to a moment where TV dress codes are morphing.

James Andrew, the editor of FourFourTwo, a football magazine, said: “It’s more relaxed now.”

Pope added: “I think punditry is becoming more fashion forward in the sense that they’re wearing knitted polos and chinos. But it’s still very tonal and sensible.”

Paul Monks, who dresses the pundits for Sky Sports, including Monday Night Football, said he believed the clothes should echo the easygoing feel of the show and its audience.

“We want what we do on screen to feel relevant to the viewer,” he said. “The way people dress generally has become more relaxed. You see far fewer men wearing suits day to day now, so it wouldn’t make sense for television to become more stiff or overly formal.”

The wardrobes of pundits, as well as the England star Jude Bellingham and managers such as Pep Guardiola, have started to have an impact on everyday style.

Pope said: “They’ve become these unlikely style influencers for middle-aged men. Someone like Gary Neville is probably quite aware of that.”

The viral incident illustrated Neville’s growing interest in fashion: he has a clothing collection with Hawes & Curtis.

Corina Gaffey, a stylist, said: “Gary seems receptive to switching up his on screen style, trying different brands, silhouettes and cuts. He’s obviously in tune with fashion and interested in it.”

Pope predicted there would be more collaborations between footballing and fashion. “I think we’re going to see more pundits with their own lines,” he said.

One-nil to wider leg trousers, then.
