Woman, 45, killed in Florence in seventh alleged femicide in Italy since mid-August

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 13:56:14 GMT

Lorena Isceri was thrown off a motorway bridge, allegedly by ex-boyfriend Federico Vella

A 45-year-old woman abducted and thrown off a motorway bridge near Florence has become the seventh alleged femicide in Italy since mid-August.

Lorena Isceri was abducted on Thursday afternoon, allegedly by her ex-boyfriend, Federico Vella, in the Rifredi area of Florence, before being forced into the boot of his car and driven towards a bridge on the A1 motorway.

Isceri, who worked in the veterinary sector, still had her phone and managed to call an emergency helpline, telling operators she had been abducted.

Vella, 38, stopped the car, snatched the phone and allegedly threw her off the bridge, before jumping off himself.

After Isceri’s call to the helpline, police traced her phone signal but arrived too late to prevent her murder. Officers are establishing whether Isceri was killed before she was thrown off the bridge.

Isceri’s mother told SkyTg24 that she had last heard from her daughter on Thursday morning, and said she sounded fine. When asked about the relationship with Vella, she said Isceri had spoken to her about it and was “very afraid”.

Italian interior ministry data had indicated a downward trend in femicides during the first six months of 2026.

Figures compiled by the feminist alliance Non Una di Meno showed that as of 8 August, 40 women had been killed so far this year.

But numbers have risen since 15 August, Italy’s Ferragosto national holiday, with seven women, including Isceri, killed by a current or former partner.

Giorgia Meloni’s ruling coalition, which on Friday celebrated becoming the longest-serving government in the history of the Italian republic, had pledged to crack down on gender-based violence after the strong public reaction to the killing of Giulia Cecchetin, a 22-year-old medical student, by her former boyfriend, in November 2023.

Two years later, the government approved a law that for the first time introduced a legal definition of femicide in criminal law, punishing it with life in prison, while increasing sentences for crimes including stalking, sexual violence and the sharing of intimate images without consent.

However, a campaign to educate schoolboys about healthy relationships was thwarted after the government made it conditional on parental approval.

Luisa Rizzitelli, the Italy coordinator of One Billion Rising, which campaigns to end violence against women, said: “Perhaps Meloni is right to celebrate her government’s longevity, because there is precious little to celebrate in terms of concrete results.

“The approach to the tragic issue of male violence against women has been based on security policies while completely lacking strategic, structural programmes for training and prevention. The stubborn refusal to implement sex and relationship education in schools is a major factor fuelling the epidemic of femicides in Italy.”

In the UK, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123 and the domestic abuse helpline is 0808 2000 247. In the US, the suicide prevention lifeline is 988 and the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is on 13 11 14 and the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines can be found via www. befrienders. org

Nigel Farage meeting a ‘shadowy foreign donor’? It can only be another establishment stitch-up

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 13:50:46 GMT

The only thing more dodgy than Reform’s financial dealings is the egregious lunchtime combination of oysters, Guinness and champagne

How many sarcastic air quotes is too many for quoting Nigel Farage’s suggestion that Reform have been ““““““““hoaxed”””””””” by some undercover investigators into appearing to seek to get round electoral law to bag a £500k donation from a foreigner, as well as commissioning off-the-books polling and failing to identify it to newspapers? I don’t feel eight was too many. I could run to nine. Amazing, really, that it’s been as long as a few weeks since Farage had a crash-out and forced a byelection. All any of us wants is for Nigel to once again resign after a staged shitfit and ask a few thousand members of the public to judge him.

For whatever reason, though, the law of our country does not amount to an “ONLY THE PEOPLE OF CLACTON CAN JUDGE ME” tattoo, and so it is that as Reform’s conference gets under way today, the party has been reported to the police for allegedly using foreign money to fund its activities. It’s all based on a covert sting carried out by Verbatim – an investigative group founded by journalists from the non-profit Centre for Climate Reporting – and broadcast last night on Channel 4 News.

Though Farage has some very significant walk-on parts in this secretly filmed footage, the chief protagonists in the hokey cokey are James Orr, the party’s director of policy, and Nigel’s right-hand man Dan Jukes. Jukes is one of the many Farage aides to physically resemble an Apprentice candidate who crashes out in week four after miscalculating quantities in the sweetshop task. Still, he’d make a lovely Rolf in a regional production of The Sound of Music. And, happily, would now have the time to really commit to the role.

“If Nigel makes it to No 10,” he honks at one point during filming carried out by an undercover “donor”, “you’re having a pint with who’s effectively going to be his chief of staff in No 10. If that isn’t a business interest, I don’t know what is.” As it turns out, the guy is effectively having a pint with someone the party chair, Lee Anderson, this morning said was “gone” with “no chance of them coming back”. Slightly less definitively, the official party statement said that Jukes and Orr had stepped down pending an internal investigation. Can’t imagine what form that will take. I always picture Reform’s internal affairs department as a toy phone ringing out in an abandoned wendy house.

But perhaps this sort of thing is the job of flailing enforcer/terminal shitposter Zia Yusuf, who this week could be found branding a possible Labour byelection candidate for Keir Starmer’s vacated Holborn and St Pancras seat as something other than the tireless community servant her career has thus far marked her out as. Or as Zia put it: “The front runner being foisted on the people of Holborn by Labour to replace the former Prime Minister Keir Starmer in our Parliament was born in Somalia. Do you understand what is happening?” If not, certainly one to discuss with that much-vaunted recent defector to Reform, the Iraq-born Nadhim Zahawi. Still, the episode does at least confirm Yusuf as the biggest Pick-Me in British politics. He’s really not like the other children of immigrants, you see – he actually enjoys being racist for approval.

Back to the undercover investigation, though, which a highly defensive Reform statement whinges was “perpetuated by foreign-funded climate-change activists posing as would-be party donors”. Foreign-funded! That’s a bit rich in the circumstances. But the real standout bit of footage for many will be the moment when Orr laments: “We just don’t have British resident donors, British entities, that would support us. That’s the grim reality.” From the horse’s mouth, then, comes apparent confirmation that Reform is funded by foreign-based money for reasons on which we can only speculate.

It’s often the incidental details that seem most weirdly illuminating. Take the scene when the fake American donor finally journeys to some sort of Clacton beer garden, where he and Farage and co seem to have settled themselves in one of a row of cursed teak gazebos. Here, Nigel chortles about “Guinness with a champagne top”, confirming his undying addiction to an even more annoying brand of alcohol-based identity politics than a Gin O’Clock poster.

He’ll no doubt be butching it out with a drink at the Reform conference this weekend. The rest of the country might do well to once again ponder the 64,000-of-indeterminately-sourced-dollars question: why does this sort of thing keep happening to Farage and his party? Is it because of a byzantine conspiracy involving climate activists, “the establishment”, the deep state and Big Gazebo? Or is it because they are just endlessly, repeatedly and ineptly dodgy? Watching the footage, it’s fairly difficult to conclude anything other than that we are dealing with a bunch of preposterously self-regarding amateurs.

We’ll have to see if this latest exposure further fans the anger that has been radiating off Farage all summer, ever since his undeclared £5m gift from a Thai-based crypto billionaire was revealed. As discussed here before, I am ever-more convinced that Farage is too mentally fragile for the highest office – indeed, leading anything other than an insurgent party seems to be either spinning him out or finding him out. Today’s attempt to shift focus saw him promise to declare a “national emergency” in the event he becomes prime minister. On the basis of all we keep discovering about him, you can’t argue with that.

Man jumps out of first-floor window to escape kidnappers in Lincoln

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 13:16:33 GMT

Five jailed after targeting victim and subjecting him to ordeal linked to past relationship breakdown

Dramatic footage shows a kidnapped man jumping from a first-floor window into a tree before running into the street and, by chance, coming across a police car.

Lincolnshire police said the ordeal of the unnamed man had been “horrifying” and the presence of a marked police vehicle “may have saved his life”.

DC Liam Henderson said the CCTV footage captured a desperate moment in which the victim “quite literally risked everything to get away from those holding him captive”.

Lincoln crown court heard that the victim had been targeted and subjected to a terrifying ordeal linked to a past relationship breakdown. On 4 July 2025, he was lured to an address in Market Rasen where it soon became clear he would be unable to leave.

Inside the address were Brad’Lee Ranyard, Nathan Gladwell, Jackson Nicholson, Craig Ranyard and Danielle Thompson. For hours the victim endured violence and intimidation, police said. He was “repeatedly assaulted, threatened, humiliated and tormented” by his captors, who filmed the abuse on their mobile phones and laughed.

The next day the man was forced into the back of a Isuzu pickup truck and driven along back roads to a property in Lincoln. He arrived at 7.30am and was again held against his will.

At 11.23am the man seized his opportunity. He can be seen diving from the window into the tree, before getting to the ground and running into the street. Footage from a police car, which had turned into the street, shows the man running towards it saying: “Let me in, let me in”.

Police said the officer immediately recognised the man’s distress, realised he was fleeing a dangerous situation and took him to safety.

Henderson, who led the investigation, said: “This was a sustained and deeply distressing ordeal in which a man was subjected to violence, threats and humiliation at the hands of people who appeared to find amusement in his suffering.

“The victim showed remarkable courage in seizing the opportunity to escape.”

Henderson said it was sheer chance that a police car had entered the street. “That moment changed the course of events and allowed officers to get him to safety when he needed help most,” he said.

“We often hear concerns that victims may feel alone or that help will not arrive when it is needed. This case is a powerful reminder that when someone reaches out for help, we will do everything we can to protect them and bring those responsible to justice.”

Police said the victim had given permission for the footage, which also shows the arrests, to be shared.

A judge at Lincoln crown court gave nine-year jail terms to Brad’Lee Ranyard, 20, and Nicholson, 25, for kidnap and false imprisonment. Craig Ranyard, 42, was jailed for five years and three months after being convicted of false imprisonment.

Thompson, 38, was jailed for four years and nine months after being convicted of false imprisonment. Gladwell, 36, was jailed for three years and seven months after being convicted of false imprisonment.

‘I’m used to doing the impossible’: George Lucas unveils new LA museum – what’s its story?

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 13:00:07 GMT

Spaceship-shaped gallery, featuring works from Banksy, Norman Rockwell and Frida Kahlo, is devoted to ‘visual storytelling’ – and is finally ready to open

“I’m used to doing the impossible,” George Lucas said on Wednesday. But “this one almost broke my will”.

The film-maker was describing the decades of work that went into his latest project, the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, as it was unveiled to the press in Los Angeles eight years after breaking ground, following attempts to build it in two other cities. Shaped like a spaceship and towering over the nearby University of Southern California – Lucas’s alma mater – the long-awaited institution finally opens on 22 September. It aims to be a testament to visual storytelling across all kinds of media – paintings, comics, murals, photography, sculpture.

The result is 100,000 sq ft of gallery space featuring a striking variety of pieces, ranging from works by Judy Baca, Norman Rockwell, Diego Rivera and Banksy to the Wizard of Oz’s Cowardly Lion costume to drawings of Asterix and Garfield. What unites the seemingly disparate works is their function: to tell a story, often in a single frame, as Lucas’s co-founder and wife, Mellody Hobson, told members of the press on Wednesday.

Visual storytelling “is the art that surrounds us”, said Ryan Linkof, the museum’s senior curator. “It is the art in the visual history that we assume every day, often without even realizing it. Newspaper photographs, advertisements, book covers, comic books, posters, street art, movies.”

The couple sees this storytelling as fundamental to the human experience. Narrative art “depicts the myths that anchor us, the stories that we believe in”, Hobson said; pictures, Lucas added, make those myths feel real. All that “creates a group of people with a common belief system, and that common belief system allows them to work together and not kill each other”.

The Lucas museum is divided into two sections, one containing most of the galleries and a pair of cinemas, and the other housing its mural collection as well as a research library. With its sleek, flying-saucer-like design, it’s impossible not to think of Star Wars, though the museum’s architect, Ma Yansong, says he was inspired more by tree canopies and clouds. A plaza between the sections offers shade as well as an oculus: a round opening that allows visitors to “see the sky and the universe”, Yansong told the media.

The museum’s construction is a saga of its own. Lucas began collecting art in the 1970s and over the years combined his collection with Hobson’s, Bates said. About 20 years ago, according to Bates, Lucas began working toward the museum’s creation. Plans for it to be built in San Francisco or Chicago fell through. Finally, the project broke ground in Los Angeles in 2018, and eight years later, it is ready to open. LA, Hobson told the media, is “where we believe we were always meant to be”. Bates agreed: “The largest, most popular form of narrative art is cinema. So what better space for it to be than the home of storytelling?”

The ground floor features a brief tour through thousands of years of visual storytelling, beginning with an immersive reproduction of cave paintings before moving to paintings, mosaics and sculptures – some original, some reproduced – depicting stories from ancient civilizations and the Bible. The exhibition sets the historical context for the museum’s core collection, mostly from the 20th and 21st centuries, reached via round glass elevators that do nothing to dispel the Star Wars aura.

The galleries here are sorted into an odd mix of categories. There are rooms that focus on medium – the comics room contains strips from Krazy Kat, Little Orphan Annie, The Adventures of Tintin and Superman; the children’s stories room contains art from Where the Wild Things Are and fairytale illustrations; the manga room features Astro Boy and a portrait of Pikachu.

Other rooms are divided by theme: the “community” area contains neighborhood scenes by Ernie Barnes and a Frida Kahlo self-portrait; the “childhood” area hosts a Margaret Keane painting, Children of Paris, and a Picasso drawing titled Little Girl; “civic life” features photography of a 1968 sanitation workers’ strike and a painting by Shepard Fairey and Ernesto Yerena Montejano opposing immigration raids.

Still other galleries are organized by single artists – NC Wyeth, Jessie Willcox Smith, Maxfield Parrish – and others by genre: science fiction, fantasy, adventure. And while this is very much not a Star Wars museum, it has plenty to offer fans, including an exhibit that focuses on modes of transportation in the films and contains vehicle models, production artwork and costumes. (There are other surprise nods to the films around the museum.)

Finally, there is the mural room, with some of the museum’s most memorable pieces. A video traces the length of Judith Baca’s mural of the region’s history along the Los Angeles River; nearby are several Banksy works on walls that have been extracted and hung in the space. There’s also a huge image of the French artist JR’s Kikito, an installation that shows a child looking over the US-Mexico border wall.

Each work has a small plaque giving its title and year, the artist’s name and the materials used. But there isn’t much else on the walls to tell visitors what they’re viewing – no blurbs or lengthy descriptions. That was deliberate, Linkof said. Lucas and the curators didn’t want a “heavily mediated” experience, telling people “where to look, how to look, what to think, how to understand and interpret something”, he said. “We’re encouraging people to have their own individual encounters with works of art and take away what they feel like speaks to them.” That said, those who are curious about a work’s origins or context can scan the images with their phone to get a brief description of who made the work and why.

Many of the artists here are well-known, but as the museum’s leadership emphasizes, they often don’t receive the same institutional respect their peers do. John Romita Jr’s Spider-Man panels don’t tend to appear in museums that also feature the Sistine Chapel ceiling, re-created here with backlit photography. “Rockwell in his day was not considered an artist, more an advertising illustrator, but actually, the process, the level of depth in those images – he is one of our greatest storytellers,” said Tracey Bates, the museum’s CEO, in an interview. With the museum, Lucas and Hobson – who call the Sistine Chapel “God’s first comic book”, Bates says – hope to elevate the standing of these visual storytellers.

“How many of us here in this room have learned to face our fears because of the work of Maurice Sendak, or learn moral lessons while studying EH. Shepard’s drawings of the 100 Acre Wood?” Bates asked. “George calls it the People’s Art, and this museum is its home.”

Russell Howard announces ‘devastating’ death of baby son

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 12:59:39 GMT

Comedian and his wife, Cerys Morgan, set up charitable foundation in memory of Felix, who died shortly after birth

Russell Howard has announced the death of his baby son, in what he described as the “most devastating time of our lives”.

The 46-year-old comedian said his family had been “changed for ever” after their “beautiful baby boy”, Felix, died shortly after birth.

In a statement on his Instagram account, Howard said: “During the most devastating time of our lives, the hospital staff who cared for us showed extraordinary compassion, kindness and humanity. They helped us navigate an unimaginable heartache and gave us support when we needed it most.”

Howard praised the support he and his wife, Cerys Morgan, had received from a bereavement midwife named Lauren, who he said had experienced a similar tragedy.

“Her care meant more to us than we can ever put to words,” he added. “During our time in hospital, Felix was placed in a cool cot, which meant that my wife and I were able to spend precious hours with our beautiful boy.

“Those hours are among the most precious memories we have of Felix.”

Howard and Morgan, who is an NHS doctor, have set up the Felix Foundation, in memory of their son, to help other families facing the same “devastating circumstances”.

To help launch the foundation, Howard will host a special charity gala at the O2 in London on 8 February featuring a lineup of friends and colleagues made up of Michael McIntyre, Jimmy Carr, Aisling Bea, Guz Khan, Greg Davies, Mo Gilligan, Michelle Wolf and John Bishop.

He said of Felix: “We miss him dearly, every single day but we take some comfort in knowing that his name will stand for kindness, compassion and laughter and that his legacy may help other families through the darkest moments of their lives.”

The foundation will aim to relieve the needs of parents, siblings and other close family members affected by miscarriage, premature birth, stillbirth, neonatal death or related bereavements, including by providing funding for specialist facilities, training or other forms of support.

‘I didn’t know if I’d ever have sex again’: inside Sharon Horgan’s excruciating post-divorce comedy

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 12:00:07 GMT

Horgan’s hilarious new show probes the perils of ageing and the horror of being single again – and it has sex scenes so wild you’ll be laughing for weeks. The creator and her co-stars open up about Youth

When Sharon Horgan walked into HBO to pitch her new series, Youth, she basically just said “sandwich generation” to them. Alex, the protagonist, is squished between a teenage son and two elderly parents. That’s the classic; the rest of it – the recent divorce, the dating hell, the busy, creative professional life full of pricks – is the icing on the sandwich (if you like). Horgan had been incubating some of the characters for five years, but “honestly”, she tells me, “I said about three sentences and a week later, they said yes. I’ve never had that experience before.”

You might think you can imagine it, but Youth is unlike any portrait you’ve ever seen in the gallery of (for brevity) menopausal women doing everything for everyone. There’s an urgency and valour to it that is very much drawn from Horgan’s own experience. “Everything just changed for me when I hit my 50s,” she says. “I was very bamboozled but I really had a hunger to make time count.” Not every situation is lifted directly from her own life, post-divorce – she’s also borrowing from her friends, she emphasises – but in general terms, the pressures, the worries, the outrages, the surprise and the delight are all so exquisitely drawn that even if it’s not Horgan herself, you hope someone, somewhere, is living this in real life.

I caught some of the shooting on a blowy day in April this year, in east London. Horgan and her co-star Rupert Friend were filming a crux scene. Friend plays Patrick, slightly younger than Horgan’s Alex, a little indecisive and shambling. “He’s not a Prince Charming character. I don’t think I’m the answer to all her ills,” he says, walking around a little park in between takes. Patrick wants to be with Alex, but he also thinks he wants children and there’s no way she’s going back there again, even if she could. “Sharon flips the proverbial biological clock on its head,” he says. “Men think it doesn’t apply to them because they ostensibly can make children all the way through. He’s never considered that it’s not his clock.”

Nothing passes between Alex and Patrick that’s overstated or even out of the ordinary, unless you count the fact that she gets hit by a cyclist as she walks away. But when it slots into the finished show, it is, like every other scene, hilarious. I just do not know how Horgan does what she does – which is what every one of her co-stars says about her. “She could have chemistry with a toaster,” says Aran Murphy (yes, son of Cillian), who plays her son. “She’s so fizzing with energy.” Rupert Friend puts the emphasis on her agility: “Sharon’s just brilliant at writing. She’s able to do that dance between jokes and pathos in a way that I don’t know anyone else can do.” But it’s Horgan herself who, in an absolutely unboastful way, explains it best: “I’m allergic to sentimentality. I can’t abide anything that is sweet or schmaltzy. But I love genuine emotion. I love to make people feel things. As much as I love the laughs, I’d feel like I’d failed in some way if I wasn’t giving people pain.”

Murphy’s Ruari is a gift of a part, the most believably wrecking-ball 18-year-old son you’ve ever seen. Some things he wrecks on purpose (the last day of secondary school), some he wrecks by accident (his first week at university; his life), but the stakes are agonisingly high and the actions all plausible. Horgan has a lot to say about parenting kids this age, “even though I do not have a son, I have daughters” (Sadhbh, 22, and Amer, 18). “Gen Z have that awful feeling of being the last generation. They’re here at a point in time where they’re being told that everything’s fucked and AI’s going to take your jobs. I sometimes don’t know how to get out of bed in the morning, but they’re the ones who care the most and feel things the most.”

Murphy is pretty reserved in real life (he speaks to me by Zoom from Italy, where he is on holiday), and the performance he turns in is one of the most thrillingly angry teenagers ever. “We really got lucky with Aran,” says Horgan. “There’s nothing about him that isn’t real. It made life so much easier to be working with someone who you literally can’t see acting.” She wanted Ruari to be “complex but not in a Dawson’s Creek way – a real boy who’s a little bit broken. All Alex wants is for him to normalise. But what’s normal?”

Besides, Ruari is probably saying the same about his mother, who he is furious to discover still has gentleman callers. Patrick isn’t Alex’s only love interest; there’s also a sex scene with Tim McInnerny (Percy from Blackadder) that I am still laughing at weeks later. None of the relationships, fleeting or otherwise, are at all a classic love story – Rupert Friend says ruefully, “I’m really the best of a bad bunch, which I am happy to take as the quote for my gravestone” – but the men are drawn so truthfully that you can’t help but love them all slightly (apart from the ex-husband, and even he’s not a bad guy, more of an emotional no-mark).

“When I found myself divorced,” Horgan says, “I genuinely thought I’d be alone for ever. I didn’t even know if I’d ever have sex again. There’s that extreme fear of being alone and being lonely. But at the same time, you think you have a freedom as well. You do suddenly think: ‘My kids have finished school, I’ve got some time to try and get this right.’” Alex’s love life is anything but over, yet this isn’t a “you go, girl” tale where every woman remains perpetually 35 through Botox and force of will. “You put yourself out there in a slightly different way,” says Horgan. “It’s still incredibly difficult, as a woman of that age, to find someone – the men who are left are either institutionally single or they’re divorced or they’re looking for someone much younger.”

The subplot of Alex’s ageing parents, meanwhile, is so honest it’s exhilarating. Dramedy tends to be respectfully saccharine about the elderly, and skate over the inconvenient bits: the stubbornness, the denial, the endless hospital appointments. But (I’m allowed to say this, being an orphan – Horgan’s mother is still alive, her dad died in 2023), those bits are almost the whole of the experience. “There is a huge amount of non-cooperation there,” she says, “and why shouldn’t there be? Ageing is hard. It’s harder when it begins to affect you mentally. When you’ve always been sharp as a tack, or when you begin to lose your mobility and you’ve always been a fucking go-getter. Losing those basic functions is brutal.”

after newsletter promotion

But from Alex’s point of view, “all the planning, all the phone calls, it becomes such a huge part of your life. As it goes on, you’ll see how it affects her sibling relationship as well. I wanted to explore that all so much but you run out of time and space. That could have been a whole show.”

Alex works in publishing, and there are some fabulous performances by her authors – Anne Reid, as a grande dame of airport fiction, turning her hand to erotica, alongside Harriet Walter as her ice-cold daughter. “I could talk to you about Anne Reid for the entirety of the interview,” Horgan says. “It’s hard to even mention her and not just wax lyrical about being aged 91 and still delivering work on that level and still caring so much.” Damian Lewis, within 30 seconds of arriving on screen, has distilled everything that is bad about publishing, celebrity, London, private members’ clubs and the world. “Everyone who came on to do their bits was influencing the show,” says Horgan. “I was writing it at the same time as making it, which was hell.” On the upside, it meant she was building relationships with her co-stars as she wrote, and incorporating those connections. Friend remembers deep conversations about what love actually is. “We talked about how heartbreaking it is to think about things in terms of if they fail. You know, if you meet and immediately think: ‘We could date, but if we date we might break up.’ Why do anything? Everything has a pessimistic possibility, and Alex is always considering it, but it’s no way to live.”

Pulling, Sharon Horgan’s 00s comedy, and Motherland, a decade ago, did the same thing – which is to say, if you’d asked: “Do you want to see a show about three single women? How about a school-gate show about neurotic middle-class people and Chardonnay and mini Babybels?” I’d have said: “No, not at all, sounds drab and also too close to home.” But then when they landed, they were all I wanted to watch. Youth is technically about the grinding sandwich years, when everything gets harder at once, and then your joints stop working. But it’s really about the sheer bliss of being alive when so much happens that is funny, stitched together by a fearsomely long to-do list.

Youth is on HBO Max from 21 September.

Andy Burnham presents his new government as more leftwing than Keir Starmer’s. In reality, it’s barely moved at all

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 11:57:11 GMT

The prime minister talks the talk about reversing decades of privatisation and austerity, but we’re yet to see any policies to this end

If Starmerism sought to present the Labour government as more rightwing than it is, Burnhamism seeks to do the opposite.

The change in rhetoric is certainly stark. Unlike his sulking predecessor, the new prime minister offers both an analysis and a vision. British stagnation and decline, Andy Burnham correctly told the House of Commons, can be explained by a series of “wrong turns” taken from the 1980s onwards: the privatisation of economic power, the deindustrialisation of the country and the ruinous austerity that followed the 2008 crash.

The solution, Burnham suggests, is public control of the essentials, the devolution of power and the rebirth of industry – to rebuild living standards and the economy and give long-abandoned communities a future. Keir Starmer, by contrast, had no vision, relying instead on a technocratic image of competence that was swiftly shattered by one fiasco after another. That left him defined by his opponents, and the electorate baffled as to where his government was headed.

The Starmer project foregrounded all of the government’s reactionary elements and buried its social-democratic features. Stringent fiscal rules, the assault on the winter fuel allowance, the attack on disability benefits, the construction of one of Europe’s most punitive asylum regimes, the arrest of pensioners who opposed Israel’s genocide: all became headline policies by design.

Now consider what they shouted least about: the semi-nationalisation of the railways, the creation of the publicly run Great British Energy, modest improvements to workers’ and renters’ rights, and some progressive taxation measures, such as hiking capital gains tax.

That was for a reason: defining itself against the left was the core strategy of Starmerism. When, in opposition, Starmer committed to retaining the Tories’ two-child benefit cap – even though it plunged hundreds of thousands of children into poverty – his advisers believed, as the journalist Andrew Marr put it, that “the public will notice him standing up to the left”.

Starmer junked the radical policy commitments he made to become leader and claimed Labour had gone “from a party of dogma to a party of patriotism” and “from a party of protest to a party of public service”. Labour voters defected en masse to Zack Polanski’s Greens, first in the Gorton and Denton byelection and then in June’s local elections. Starmer’s strategy of insulting progressive voters and their values succeeded in plunging Labour into an existential crisis.

Burnham, then, takes the opposite tack, having understood that, in the Britain of the 2020s, the left is a significant political constituency that Labour must appeal to, rather than wilfully alienate. He bemoans the Starmerite purge of leftwingers, such as economist Faiza Shaheen and former Labour mayor Jamie Driscoll. He sells himself not as a factionalist but as “a Labour politician that’s about unifying people”. Notably, when Jeremy Corbyn asked the prime minister a question about rent controls in the House of Commons, Burnham called the expelled former leader “my right honourable friend”: by parliamentary convention, “friend” is reserved for members of one’s own party.

The presentation has certainly changed. But what about the substance? When he stood in the Makerfield byelection in June, Burnham said that public ownership “is what should be done” in the case of Thames Water. Last week, he backtracked: “I’ve deliberately talked about public control rather than necessarily nationalisation.”

It is certainly true that “public control” has been his preferred formula. It allows voters – who overwhelmingly support nationalisation – to believe it means public ownership. But as he told Newsnight this year, it could mean anything from “much tougher regulation” to “public ownership”. That simply allows the existing approach to be rebranded.

During his byelection campaign, Burnham demanded that the government’s £39bn Affordable Housing Programme be entirely reserved for council and social housing. In office, his government allocated 40% of the first £10bn tranche to other types of housing – continuity with his predecessor’s approach.

Before his victorious return to parliament, Burnham had backed a £500,000 cap on donations to political parties. In power, he has U-turned.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

While just a few months ago, Burnham had said he had “long been persuaded” by the case for a land value tax, and proposed it as a replacement for the “iniquitous” council tax, as prime minister he declared: “That won’t be happening.” He has already embraced fiscal rules that block the investment needed for resource-starved public services and infrastructure.

Burnham apologised for Labour’s positioning on Gaza, but notably only for its record in opposition. He avoided stating that Israel had committed war crimes, with all the legal obligations that would impose on the government. His new foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, now touts sanctions on illegal settlements in the West Bank, but these are small, piecemeal measures that avoid imposing tough measures on Israel itself.

If vibes are your thing, then Burnhamism is a political sensation. Alas, what should matter is the substance. Our prime minister is correct that Britain took a series of wrong turns from the 1980s onwards. The logical conclusion arising from that is that the country needs a new economic model. Burnham has traced the path that led Britain here with admirable clarity. What remains unclear is whether he is prepared to leave it.

Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist

Katseye review – petulant hyperpop bops from a girl group in crisis

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 11:51:22 GMT

O2 Arena, LondonFans scream ‘eat zucchini’ as if their lives depend on it as the six-piece’s remaining members strut their way through chest-rattling hits, ludicrous bangers and flaccid flops

It takes a certain amount of resilience to be a Katseye fan. Since debuting three years ago via the boot camp meets reality TV show The Debut: Dream Academy, the multinational K-pop hybrid girl band have put their so-called Eyekons through the wringer. Last month alone they lost their second member to a “personal health and wellness” related hiatus, with Sophia joining Manon (who stepped away in more mysterious circumstances back in February) on the sidelines. Weeks later, they landed their first US No 1 album with Wild, a collection led by the carbonated dance-pop rocket Pinky Up – a song referred to by the band’s many online detractors as “skibidi toilet music” (ie slop).

Even as this debut arena tour arrived in the UK, there were fears the newly reshaped quartet might be reduced to a trio after Megan sprained her ankle. But if the fans are worried, they don’t show it, their ear-piercing screams drowning out the opening Hootie Frutti, a sonic melange that somehow makes Brazilian funk sound leaden. By the time petulant hyperpop bop Internet Girl kicks in they’re screaming lines like “eat zucchini, eat zucchini” as if their lives depend on it.

A now healed Megan, Lara, Daniela and Yoonchae do their best to reward the enthusiasm. They lock into the featherlight early single Touch, which recalls their K-pop peers NewJeans, while last year’s breakthrough single, Gabriela, is given a delicious flamenco makeover. The choreography is frenetic throughout, aided by 10 dancers, but the minimalist staging – just a raised platform and a short runway – means the focus is very much on the songs themselves. That causes problems when the best they can muster is Animal, a flaccid Ed Sheeran co-write, or My Way, a song so dated it’s essentially a refried X Factor winner’s single.

Things pick up when the band are allowed to unshackle themselves from the rigid choreography. The strutting new-wave of Bel Air – a resuscitated Charli xcx demo from 2013 – offers up flashes of their individual personalities, while a chest-rattling Gnarly, complete with its “I’m the shit” hook, shows how well they can sell ludicrous bangers as long as they stay just the right side of goofy. Not that the fans care a jot; to them, Katseye can do no wrong and the skibidi toilet music is simply part of the charm.

Drones, teargas, riot squads: why has the UK gone to war against asylum seekers already fleeing conflict?

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 10:21:42 GMT

Burnham and Macron have committed to going further in the crackdown on French beaches. But little is being done to offer refugees safe alternative routes

Garang*, 18, is one of thousands of refugees recently caught in the crossfire of French riot police, who threw teargas and beat them with batons when they boarded dinghies to travel to the UK. He is a victim of a war in his home of South Sudan – and one being fought on France’s northern shores.

He borrows a phone from anyone with credit who will let him try to call home, where his family is displaced. Garang doesn’t have enough money on the £10-a-week allowance from the Home Office to make a long-distance call. All he wants is to speak to his mum, to hear her voice, and let her know he is alive and safe in the UK despite the violence he has faced.

On Thursday, stopping more people like Garang from reaching the UK in small boats topped the “to do” list of the prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, when they held talks. The leaders agreed they were making headway in reducing small boat crossings in the English Channel but now needed to go further.

How much further can the war on refugees go? Along with the use of teargas and beatings, there are now surveillance drones and more French officers to tackle dinghy launches from other parts of the coast. The UK government is increasingly using military terms such as “surge” and “neutralise” in relation to small-boat crossings. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has vowed to continue to be “relentless” in this battle. Burnham said the government wanted to “prevent smugglers exploiting vulnerable migrants”, but was silent on alternatives to offer to these vulnerable people.

When the government tried to seal off the lorry route for people crossing from France into the UK a decade ago, ministers did not foresee its replacement with small boats. The maritime option required greater reliance on smuggling networks, which have vastly increased in size, complexity and profits. Worst of all are the optics, which have been seized upon by the right – shots of overcrowded dinghies carrying people in orange lifejackets bobbing up and down against the blue horizon.

These images have fuelled anger, with some Britons believing that most refugees are shunning other countries to beat a path to our door. In fact, the number of irregular arrivals to Europe in the last year has dropped significantly, and the UK ranks 16th in Europe per head of population for asylum claims. According to this newly released data, a majority of asylum seekers do not arrive in small boats – 41% were already in the UK and held a visa or other leave prior to claiming and 20% arrived by other routes, many likely to be clandestine means, such as lorries.

Channel crossings so far this year from France to the UK have dropped by more than 40% compared with the same period last year. Countries such as Turkey and Iran tower over us in terms of the number of refugees they take in.

But the UK government continues to pursue its war against refugees on the beaches of northern France. Home Office data shows that those in small boats overwhelmingly come from war and conflict zones: Eritreans fleeing indefinite military conscription; Afghans escaping the Taliban; Iranians who have opposed the regime or converted from Islam to Christianity, trying to dodge execution; and Sudanese crossing the desert to escape a brutal civil war. Nobody steps into an overcrowded dinghy that might end their life if it capsizes unless they are desperate.

Nigel Farage and Reform UK have poisoned the public discourse on people fleeing war, people who run because they don’t want to be killed or to kill others. The UK government can shift the dial. Instead of boasting about the paraphernalia of war deployed against refugees who have experienced unimaginable horrors, ministers can restore the humanity of those seeking refuge. Along with promoting safe routes, it can remind people of how few refugees in absolute terms are arriving here seeking safety – and of what they have been through.

As for Garang, he is still desperately trying to get through to his mum on the phone, relying on South Sudan’s hopelessly overwhelmed phone network. A few days ago, he managed to reach his brother, but by the time he had run to find their mum, the call disconnected. Just as Garang wants to tell her he’s OK, he wants to know the same of her. “Now I know she’s alive I will not give up trying to call whenever anyone lets me use their phone,” he says. “All I want is to speak to my mum.”

UK hits back at Argentinian Falklands claim and insists islands remain British

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 09:24:46 GMT

Ed Miliband says Britain’s position remains ‘unwavering’ in response to remarks by Argentina’s president

UK politics live – latest updates

British ministers have hit back after the Argentinian president said “winds of change” favourable to his country’s claim to the Falklands were “blowing around the world”.

The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said the UK would “resolutely uphold” the self-determination of the islands after the Argentinian president, Javier Milei, said his country needed to take them back.

Miliband said in a post on X: “The UK’s position on the Falkland Islands is unwavering. The islands are British and will remain so because that is the overwhelming position of the Islanders.

“Their right of self-determination is paramount, grounded in international law and we will resolutely uphold it.”

Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said Milei’s statement “tells us more about domestic politics in Argentina than it does about the Falkland Islands”.

He added on X: “The Falklands are British because Falkland Islanders choose to be British. Our commitment to the Falklands is absolute and unshakeable.”

Lucy Powell, the education secretary, also insisted the islands were British, adding: “We will defend the right of those who live in the Falkland Islands to determine their own future.”

The latest diplomatic spat over the south Atlantic archipelago came after comments by the US president, Donald Trump, who has cast doubt on American support for British control of the islands.

The US has traditionally remained neutral on the Falklands’ sovereignty, while recognising Britain’s de facto control over them.

Britain and Argentina fought a war over the islands in 1982, when British forces defeated Argentinian troops, who had landed there to stake a territorial claim.

In more recent years, the British oil company Rockhopper and the Israeli company Navitas have been developing the Sea Lion oilfield, 140 miles to the north of the islands.

Asked on Monday whether he could review British sovereignty over the islands as a way to push the UK to spend more on defence, Trump said: “I always review every position. That’s just one of many.”

On Thursday, when questioned about whether the US would back the UK in the event of an Argentinian invasion, he referred to the government’s refusal to let him use British bases in his initial attack on Iran earlier this year.

“Don’t forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the strait of Hormuz, and you weren’t there to help me,” he told GB News. “Your country was not there to help me.”

He added: “The Falklands is very interesting because your country is not the same country it was 20 years ago, 25 years ago. That was a long time [ago], you went there and you just took it back very quickly. There was no games, so I don’t know if you’re prepared to do that.”

On Thursday night, Milei highlighted Trump’s comments, saying: “President Trump declared that the US is re-evaluating its historic position in relation to the Malvinas [the Argentinian name for the Falklands].”

He added: “The US is considering this change of position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come.”

He also said companies developing oil “behind the back of the Argentine government” would be barred from doing business in Argentina.

Rockhopper’s shares dropped 7% in early trading on Friday.

Jackdaw gasfield set to be approved by ministers this month, sources say

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 07:55:07 GMT

Energy secretary could recommend new North Sea drilling next week, as ministers also consider approval for Rosebank oilfield

Ministers are poised to approve a controversial new gasfield in the North Sea this month, according to government sources, and are considering approving a major oilfield later this year.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, will give her recommendation to approve the Jackdaw field off the coast of Aberdeen as soon as next week, according to people close to the decision, and the formal approval could follow a week after.

Meanwhile, officials are looking for ways to make sure any proceeds from the separate Rosebank project – if it is approved – go towards clean energy projects, as happens in Norway.

Officials have not yet finished their analysis of Rosebank’s environmental impact, but some close to the process believe they will soon decide the project should be approved.

Both projects have become emblematic of the government’s commitment to the North Sea, with green campaigners calling for them to be abandoned while the US president, Donald Trump, urges the prime minister to open them up.

A spokesperson for the energy department said: “The North Sea remains a vital national asset, supporting jobs, growth and the UK’s energy security. We are clear that oil and gas will continue to play an important role in our energy system for decades to come, alongside transitioning to clean power to protect jobs and tackle the climate crisis.”

Consultations on both Jackdaw and Rosebank, which the industry says will provide 10% of the UK’s oil and gas output at their peak, closed last month, since when Fahnbulleh has been considering her response.

Campaigners say the fields would produce as much as £336bn worth of damage to the economy as a result of the carbon pollution from the oil and gas that are produced.

Both fields have licences to operate, but environmental approval was rescinded after a judge ruled the companies running them – Shell and the Norwegian company Equinor – needed to account for the carbon emissions that would be produced by burning the oil and gas they produce.

The companies resubmitted their applications for environmental approval earlier this year. Granting those environmental permits would not violate Labour’s manifesto commitment not to issue new oil or gas licences, but many of the party’s MPs are opposed to the projects entirely.

Since he entered Downing Street, Andy Burnham has signalled he has concerns about the way in which the move to green energy has affected workers in the north east of Scotland, telling MPs this week: “I know that people have struggled with the impact of transition.”

Officials stress final decisions have not been made for either Jackdaw or Rosebank, but those close to the process say Fahnbulleh is likely to signal her approval for Jackdaw as soon as Monday.

She will give her recommendation to the North Sea Transition Authority, which officials hope will issue the formal approval as soon as a week afterwards. Some in government think the NSTA process could take several weeks, however.

A decision on the £8.7bn Rosebank field, which is the biggest undeveloped field in UK waters and is estimated to contain as much as 500m barrels of oil or oil equivalent, is likely to come later in the year.

Fahnbulleh is likely approve that project if the environmental impact assessment allows it, according to sources, but is looking at ways to redirect the proceeds from it to clean energy projects in the UK. One option would be to put the tax revenues from the project into the national wealth fund, which has been set up to fund green energy schemes and other infrastructure projects.

Some in government warn this will be difficult, though, because the consenting process is already advanced and it could prove legally complex to change the terms on which the project is approved. The money has also already been accounted for in the Treasury’s forecasts, given the projects have their licences, meaning the chancellor, John Healey, would have to redirect it from other parts of government spending.

When does rage help us, and when does it harm us? Ukraine has taught me the answers

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 07:00:00 GMT

Fury at Russia’s death and destruction has fuelled art, action and resistance. But eventually, rage’s fire is all-consuming

Twice, I have heard Ukrainians perform Verdi’s Requiem. Once in Lviv, last Maundy Thursday, and once last month, under the great dome of St Paul’s Cathedral in London. In St Paul’s, performed by the Ukrainian Freedom Orchestra with the Philharmonia Chorus, the great Dies irae – “day of anger” – unfurled in an operatic gale of fury, reverberating so powerfully around Wren’s lofty spaces that the music felt like thunder echoing between mountain peaks.

In Lviv, where it was performed by a Ukrainian chorus and orchestra, the evening began with a call to remember the war dead. Lviv’s lay a mile up the road: 153 graves when I first visited in autumn 2022, and by this year more than 1,000. Ranks and ranks of soldiers killed in their 20s, 30s and 40s, each grave planted with flowers and plants, flags flying above. On that occasion, Dies irae – in the more sober acoustic of the Lviv Philharmonic Hall – seemed to contain the furious ache of grief. Certainly I have never heard a more wrathful day of anger.

I have thought a lot about Ukrainian rage. This was a rage against Russia and Russians, and it burned with a fury that was at times hard to step close to. Ukrainians, too, have sometimes been taken aback by the depth of their anger. Oleksandr Mykhed, an author now in the armed forces, has written a wartime alphabet book for children in which L stands for lyut, rage. He defines it as a “special mixture of feelings when the desire to defend what is yours, hatred for the enemy and enduring love for your own people are mixed in equal proportions”. This complicated, extreme cocktail of feelings is not a peacetime emotion, nor an easy one.

I found myself making sense of it through literature, specifically Homer’s epic poems. Epics need fuel to motor them on their poetic journey. They also need delay, so that they become long poems, not short ones. In the Odyssey, the fuel of the poem is desire – the desire to get home – and the delay is the divine malevolence that brings many obstacles in Odysseus’s path. But in the Iliad, set during the Trojan war, Achilles’ rage is the fuel of the poem: first his outrage as a subordinate insulted by his commander, later the raging grief of a man who has lost his dearest friend in battle. Grief and rage are cousins; that is also clear to me in Ukraine.

It would be wrong to suggest that Ukrainian rage is like Achilles’. His veers beyond the human, into the supersize, mythical emotional zone inhabited by the children of the gods. But I found myself thinking about the vastness of this Homeric rage when encountering the fury of Ukrainians at civilians killed, cities bombed, people raped and tortured. The poet Iryna Shuvalova, in an interview with the writer Kateryna Iakovlenko for Suspilne, the Ukrainian national broadcaster, said rage was “pouring out of us as a reaction to the incredible trauma, the blow, the provocation, the terrible losses”.

Shuvalova’s poem February – referring to the month of the full-scale invasion in 2022 – begins gently, wryly, by pointing out that “we planned to get through February / like any other month— / only shorter”. But then the invasion begins, and “instead, the river roars and grabs us by the legs / this red slippery foaming / February-fury”. The translators, Amelia Glaser and Yuliya Ilchuk, used the phrase “February-fury” to mimic the echo in Ukrainian between lyutyy, the word for February, and lyuta, raging. For me, the immediate resonance of Shuvalova’s blood-soaked river is Homer’s Scamander River, choked in blood and the corpses of the war dead.

And what is the “day of anger” that powers Verdi’s Requiem? The words, no longer often used as part of a requiem mass, are from a medieval Latin poem that summons up the chaos and terror of the Earth’s final dissolution. The intensity of its expression – the visceral, gut-felt outpouring – that I heard in those Ukrainian performances of the work reminded me of Homeric wrath, although it is a rage that has a different force. The anger of the Dies irae is a kind of world-fury produced when everything is disrupted, put out of order by human actions. A world locked into war, perhaps.

I am not a Christian, and the values of Homer’s Iliad are alien to me. But I think perhaps there are different orders of rage. Some rage is trivial and petty; the everyday rage of frustration and aggression. But Mykhed told me of a generative rage: a rage that produces action, that fuels resistance. His rage provided him with the impetus and energy to write his book The Language of War. He told me that he wanted his rage-filled book about the first year of the full-scale invasion of his country to be “a time capsule for myself so that I know where I’ve been, when in five years or 10 years, my rage won’t be so sharp”.

The feeling, he said, is specifically “not hatred, it is rage, because hatred doesn’t give you power, it’s more chaotic. But rage gives you words.” In 1981, Audre Lorde wrote urgently of the fury provoked into flame by racism – a fury that could alienate and be resented by white people. Black women, she wrote, “tremble their rage under harness”. But pulled into service, channelled towards action and words, anger “is loaded with information and energy”. So it has been for Ukrainians: rage turned into action fuelled resistance.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

But now, in 2026, Ukrainian rage burns low, at least among my friends. The fire cannot be sustained; it would consume you in its overwhelming heat. What is left? Fatigue, emptiness, an alertness to the dreadful idea that however bad things are now, they could get worse. “I feel like anything is possible – nuclear war, anything,” Iakovlenko told me. “Everything that was written in books and in films is actually happening to us.”

Sasha Dovzhyk, the director of Index, Ukraine’s Institute for Documentation and Exchange, told me that she felt “pure spite and grit and grim determination and a memory of what it felt like to have feelings and a loyalty to that past version of the self who felt rage”. She missed rage, she told me. Rage and grief gave her the power to write her forthcoming book, Apocalypse Baroque: Tales from Ukraine at War, which mixes genres – documentary and fairytales – with rageous energy. Maybe rage sometimes brings one too close to the perilous realm of myth, to the destructiveness of an Achilles. But if you can tame the wild horse of rage, it can be ridden, for a while.

Charlotte Higgins is the Guardian’s chief culture writer and the author of Ukrainian Lessons: Art in a Time of War, published by Jonathan Cape. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop. com

In Complex Cases, Consensus Can Be Hard to Reach

The New York Times September 04, 2026

Lindsay Clancy Trial

Advertisement

Supported by

Hung juries are not common, but the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy was emotionally wrenching and uniquely complicated.

By Jacey Fortin

As Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial came to an end on Friday, there was no shortage of drama.

The courthouse in Plymouth, Mass., was thronged with observers. Ms. Clancy’s lawyer butted heads with the judge and made a doomed appeal to prevent the declaration of a mistrial. Audience members gasped.

But the most pivotal decision took place behind closed doors. After spending nearly 40 hours in deliberation — and half of those in deadlock — jurors said they could not come to a unanimous verdict on whether Ms. Clancy should be held criminally responsible for strangling her three children in 2023. A single juror was said to be at odds with everyone else in the room.

It was a remarkable outcome, said Valerie Hans, a Cornell law professor who studies jury behavior. “Hung juries are not frequent,” she added. “Maybe one out of every 20 cases in criminal courts results in a hung jury.”

Jury verdicts in serious criminal cases across the United States must be unanimous, a rule that was affirmed in a 2020 Supreme Court decision interpreting the Sixth Amendment of the Constitution.

“It’s entirely an artifact of history and tradition,” said Christopher Slobogin, a law professor at Vanderbilt University. He added that the standards for criminal cases were high because a guilty verdict could result in a deprivation of liberty.

Dr. Hans says that failures of consensus are most likely in cases where the evidence is close — that is, not clearly favoring either side — and complex.

The Clancy trial seemed to fit those parameters. Jurors sat through four weeks of emotional, often harrowing, testimony. They watched expert witnesses reach opposite conclusions on Ms. Clancy’s criminal culpability in the death of her children. Her lawyer, Kevin Reddington, argued for an insanity defense, claiming that she had been in the throes of postpartum psychosis.

The jurors, nine women and three men, wore increasingly grim expressions as their deadlock dragged on, even after the judge, William Sullivan, delivered a set of instructions on Wednesday known the “dynamite charge” in a last-ditch effort to nudge them toward a verdict.

Professor Slobogin said it was notable that Judge Sullivan’s efforts had failed. “Typically, if there is a hung jury, the judge is able to convince the jury to go back and reach a unanimous verdict,” he said.

But on Friday, the jurors said in a note to the court that “with a heavy heart,” they had been unable to reach a consensus.

According to Dr. Hans, the jurors probably took their work very seriously. “People can be very flippant outside the jury context,” she said, “and yet there’s something about getting sworn in as a juror that is sobering.”

That extends beyond the courthouse, she added: Research suggests that people who serve on juries tend to become more civically engaged after the trial ends.

For now, the jurors’ work at the Plymouth courthouse is done. Ms. Clancy still faces murder charges, and prosecutors will decide whether to try their case all over again.

If they do, a brand-new jury will be sworn in.

Jacey Fortin covers a wide range of subjects for The Times, including extreme weather, court cases and state politics across the country.
